ASRS:1786853.n: Had a gear up incident. Landing gear would not go down. After manually trying to pump the gear down for over an hour I decided to belly land the plane at ZZZ. All precautions were taken and an emergency landing was made on Runway XXR. No injuries but plane has extensive damage. My student and I took off in his airplane from ZZZ and flew to ZZZ1 where we added some fuel to the airplane. Then we took off and flew to ZZZ2 where we began an ILS practice approach. On final the gear would not extend. We went missed and flew around for an hour and forty five minutes trying to get the gear and flaps to extend. Only the nose gear came down. We decided to land at ZZZ2 so called approach for landing. They immediately turned us over to the tower where we explained our situation. WE then landed on [Runway] XXR on the nose wheel and the tail tiedown ring. It stayed on the tiedown ring until it was almost stopped then came to rest on the left wing. We departed the airplane with no issues. There was very minimal damage to the plane. Later we discovered the ELT battery was due for replacement 60 days earlier.
ASRS:1786853.s: A pilot and student experienced a landing gear failure during an ILS practice approach at ZZZ2, resulting in a belly landing on Runway XXR. The aircraft sustained minimal damage with no injuries, though the reporter later discovered the ELT battery was overdue for replacement.

ASRS:1786858.n: As I was pre-flighting the aircraft before the passengers were boarding, I noticed that ALL of the cleaners onboard the aircraft did not have a mask on around their nose and mouth. Most of the cleaners had their mask only around their chin, some didn't have any mask on. This is a federal mandate, and a company requirement to wear a mask, yet the rule is not being followed. There's no enforcement. Plus, there was no air connected to the aircraft, so there was stagnant air. This was an unsafe environment. I see this on just about every flight, which is 1-4 legs/day. I'm also seeing at least 20% of the passengers in the boarding area or walking in the concourse not wearing any mask, and some are just wearing the mask around their mouth only. There is no enforcement. I'm seeing this at every airport I've been to in the domestic system. This Federal Mask Mandate is a complete joke. Airports are not safe if 20%+ of the passengers are not wearing masks. These people are not drinking or eating, so there's no reason why they are not wearing a mask.
ASRS:1786858.s: A pilot reported that during pre-flight, cleaners and passengers were not wearing masks as required by federal mandate and company policy. The pilot described the environment as unsafe due to lack of enforcement and stagnant air from disconnected ground power.

ASRS:1786864.n: Description of Event: The aircraft with PIC as above and one passenger was returning to ZZZ from a 1-hour cross-country flight that originated at ZZZ1. The flight was uneventful in VFR weather, with altitude from 2,000 feet to 1,600 feet after takeoff and climbout until approach. Flight path was as depicted in the charted course, following VFR altitude restrictions as required within ZZZ2 Mode C airspace, and with ADS-B Out active on 1200 a required. Visibility was observed to be 10+ miles with a solid cloud cover (overcast) at 9,000-12,000 feet. Winds were variable 6-9 knots at approximately 230-260 degrees from surface to flight altitude. Within 10 nm on the approach to ZZZ on a vector of 220, while monitoring ZZZ voice radio on 123.00, little traffic within the airport operations area was observed or noted on the radio. At approximately 8 nm from ZZZ, an inbound aircraft was announced on my ForeFlight display through the ADS-B In signal at my 7 o'clock, 400 feet below and overtaking. That Cessna 152 pilot announced his intention for a straight-in approach to ZZZ runway XX. Communicated directly with that PIC and told him that we would slow down to distance behind him on my own straight-in approach to ZZZ runway XX, since he already had a 25+ mph speed advantage. Within 2 minutes, the Cessna 152 had passed us by on our left side and descended ahead of us to line up for Runway XX. In the process, I lost visual contact with that aircraft, and since there was no other traffic in the area, and ForeFlight did not show a blip for its position, I decided to perform a slight S-turn to the left to further delay our landing until the 152 announced he was clear of Runway XX. At approximately 4 nm from the threshold, with our speed down to 62 mph (58 mph Ground Speed), the Cessna 152 PIC announced 'clear of Runway XX ZZZ', after which I immediately announced a straight-in approach for Runway XX ZZZ and began to adjust our speed and trim to line up with the two VASI lights on the glide path. At approximately 2 nm, we were high (two white lights) but gradually settled to a nominal (white/red) glide slope on the final approach. We completed visual and verbal cockpit checks and I glanced outboard at the right Flaperon position (there being no flap setting indicator in this CH750 STOL, and no stall warning annunciation), but did not notice anything incorrect, even though I had earlier made a mental note that we would be making a flaps-up, standard landing instead of the full-flaps, STOL landings I usually make. We settled slightly low of nominal (two red lights) as we approached the threshold and at that moment, I made a mental 'flip' or attitude adjustment that we were about to land STOL, and I decreased power for a short-field landing. Our sink rate increased, but mentally, I still had confidence that the STOL nose-up attitude was safe, and did not add power but instead retarded it to idle as we crossed the threshold of Runway XX. Without flaps, our stall speed was 48 mph instead of 42 mph, and we stalled out at approximately 12' above the numbers and fell in a slightly nose-high attitude until impacting on the main and then nose gear. The aircraft bounced up and then impacted slightly nose-down, collapsing the nose strut, blowing out the nose tire, and stopping the engine as the fiberglass prop blades impacted and flexibly shattered.We immediately checked for fuel leaks even though the aircraft came to rest tail-high. I switched off the ignition and removed the key, exited the cockpit, checked again for fuel leaks (none), then shut down the avionics manually with the master switch, and turned the Fuel Selector valve to OFF. After ascertaining that the aircraft was not an immediate hazard and that both Pilot and Passenger were able to move about without difficulty, we called other airport residents, and cleared the CH750 from Runway XX.Conclusion: In summation, distracted flying due to traffic avoidance caused energy mismanagement resulting in a stall upon landing flare with flaps retracted and subsequent nose gear collapse without injuries.
ASRS:1786864.s: The pilot of a CH750 STOL with one passenger stalled during a flaps-up landing at ZZZ after distraction from traffic avoidance caused energy mismanagement. The aircraft impacted the runway, collapsing the nose gear and shattering the propeller, but both occupants escaped without injury.

ASRS:1786873.n: I was providing instruction on new avionics for a client in Aircraft X. An IFR flight plan was filed by my client on his certificate. I briefed prior to engine start that he was PIC and that I was there to provide insight on the use of his new GTN 750. He had flown previously with this equipment, based on what he had told me. This was our first flight together in his aircraft.Prior to taxi, I reviewed with him how to load and activate approaches in his new GTN 750. He seemed familiar with its use and only asked a couple questions prior to departure. His knowledge of the features was adequate when I queried him on the unit.After takeoff from ZZZ Runway XXR, we were given a left turn to a heading of 070 and a climb to 3,000 feet. He engaged the autopilot at about 1,000 feet AGL. My client requested from ZZZ Approach the RNAV Y XXR but asked for a non-standard transition. He stated that he wanted the RNAV Y XXR to ZZZ 'via the ZZZZZ transition.' This is not a published transition and not what we briefed prior to departure. We had briefed previously that he would ask for vectors for the approach and he would repeat that same approach three times to increase familiarity with the equipment and its use in the approach environment. A short time later, we were given the instruction to climb to 3,000 feet and after that, to 'turn left direct ZZZZZ.' The autopilot began turning the aircraft to the right, presumably because he had switched from HDG mode to NAV mode without my knowledge. ATC queried and he once again read back the left turn. By the time I caught the erroneous turn direction and autopilot setting, the aircraft was well into the right turn. ATC then requested that we continue the right turn 'since we were already turning right and I have to keep you away from other traffic.'My client did as instructed and I queried ATC to confirm that we would overfly the ZZZZZ waypoint, then proceed outbound for the full approach. I apologized for the error on that same radio call. ATC responded in the affirmative, then cleared us for the approach. No further communication about the incorrect turn direction was made and the rest of the flight proceeded without incident.My client and I debriefed this issue and shared the lessons we learned. We both looked at this with an eye toward learning and future improvement.First, I reminded him of the importance of flying what we brief and that we will commit to always do so in the future. Second, as his flight instructor, it was my responsibility to catch the turn error and take control -- an effort I began but could not finish before ATC requested that he continue the right turn. Third, reliance on the autopilot worked against us and I suspect he switched from HDG to NAV mode without my noticing, initiating the right turn direct to ZZZZZ. Finally, business has been slow due to COVID and I have not been instructing as much as I normally would. I feel this last point is perhaps the most important one. As the pandemic has continued for nearly a year now, its effect on skills as pilots and flight instructors is being felt industry-wide.
ASRS:1786873.s: A flight instructor and client in Aircraft X experienced an autopilot mode error during climb after takeoff, causing an unintended right turn instead of the cleared left turn. The instructor attributed the incident to the client switching from HDG to NAV mode without notice and the instructor's reduced proficiency due to pandemic-related inactivity.

ASRS:1786898.n: On the downwind landing at ZZZ, I was #2 in the pattern when abeam the touchdown point. The plane that was #1 had just touched down, and around the same time my engine began stuttering and soon after failed. At that point, I had begun my descent and was at [approximately] 800 ft. AGL. I began to attempt to restart the engine and was unable to do so. I then decided to execute a power off 180 degree turn and land on the runway. Perhaps as a result of attempting to restart my engine and triggering the master on/off, I lost communication with ZZZ Tower (I had been previously communicating with them). The plane that was previously #1 was already quite far down the runway and not a factor. I ultimately ended up landing safely, although never received clear to land instructions from Tower due to communications failure. I attempted to advise ATC when the engine failed, however I don't believe this was communicated.Upon landing, I noticed that both of the fuel selector valves were turned off. I am not sure if these were inadvertently disabled when I was attempting to restart the engine, or perhaps I had accidentally turned both of them off before engine failure. I am skeptical that this would be the case, as I remember ensuring that they were both enabled as part of my descent checklist ~15 minutes before the engine failed. It is indeed possible that I may have turned both to the 'off' position accidentally during the descent checklist, but I do not believe the engine would have continued to operate for this long were they to be off.I do not have a clear recollection of what actions I took to restart the engine in the air as it is frankly quite a blur. After being on the ground, I enabled both fuel selector valves and attempted to restart my engine without success. I tried a second time, and it started and I taxied off the runway (at that point 2 fire trucks and a police car had arrived, and I taxied off in convoy with them).A takeaway for me is that, regardless of the cause of the engine failure, my previous flights had been in another model of airplane, and while I was very familiar with Aircraft X, I would say that I should have spent more time familiarizing myself with the emergency procedures checklist. Also, earlier in the day while pre-flighting, there were some irregularities with the communications systems in the plane, and also it was very difficult to start the engine. I did not feel that these issues were enough to warrant aborting the flight, but in hindsight perhaps I should not have flown that plane that day and had it serviced instead.
ASRS:1786898.s: The pilot of Aircraft X experienced an engine failure at 800 ft AGL on downwind at ZZZ, likely caused by inadvertently turning both fuel selector valves off. After losing radio contact, the pilot executed a power-off 180-degree turn and landed safely without clearance, later attributing the incident to unfamiliarity with emergency procedures and pre-existing mechanical irregularities.

ASRS:1786903.n: Landing Runway 26 Using Visual approach guidance from GTN 650(Garmin Navigation/Display). No glideslope guidance was provided by the GTN. I crossed what appeared to be the threshold with very faded marking in significant turbulence. I taxied to the ramp without incident. Only after reviewing the track log from foreflight on google earth did I realize I may have actually landed on the displaced threshold. I believe better markings on the displaced threshold would help prevent this in the future. In addition, a more positive identification of runway markings on my part and a go around would have prevented this event. Contributing was a runway change from our planned arrival to Runway 35R due to changing winds.
ASRS:1786903.s: The pilot landed on a displaced threshold at Runway 26 during a visual approach in turbulence, aided by a GTN 650 without glideslope. The event resulted from faded markings and a last-minute runway change, though the aircraft taxied to the ramp without incident.

ASRS:1786905.n: While departing ZZZ1 for a direct flight to ZZZ2, I inadvertently climbed into ZZZ Class C airspace while heading 280. My plan called for climbing to 3,500 feet for the short flight. I completely forgot about the Class C airspace floor. Contributing Factors include:- Not being VFR current due to winter weather, Coronavirus limitations.- The autopilot on the plane was placarded 'INOP'. I typically set the altitude on the autopilot to 2,000 feet (100 feet below the floor) as a reminder for the airspace floor.- Air temperature was -X degrees C, which makes for great airplane climb performance. The last time I had flown was October, and the weather was much warmer. I was distracted by the great visibility and great climb rate.- This plane is part of a local flying club. Planes are at X different local airports, only one of which is under the Class C veil. It's sometimes hard to remember all the different nuances when you are flying different planes from different airports, and don't do it regularly.- I sometimes fly IFR. This provides additional protection from this type of excursion because you are talking to ATC continuously.I just have to be more focused about airspace limitations when flying VFR from this airport.
ASRS:1786905.s: A pilot inadvertently entered ZZZ Class C airspace while departing ZZZ1 for ZZZ2 on a VFR flight, climbing to 3,500 feet. The excursion resulted from forgetting the airspace floor due to inexperience, a placarded INOP autopilot, and distraction from excellent climb performance.

ASRS:1786916.n: This was my first time flying from PAO in this particular aircraft, and I had only been there twice before, in more modern aircraft. Aircraft Y got clearance for a 'Right Dumbarton' departure, just ahead of me. The Controller explained the 'Dumbarton' departure to me and subsequently gave me clearance for a 'Left Dumbarton' departure, right behind Aircraft Y. Just after takeoff, as I was climbing out on runway heading, I noticed I was gaining quickly on the Aircraft Y, but I wasn't worried because I knew he would be turning right at the bridge. Instead, he (or she) turned left instead of right. I also turned left, and the Controller asked me if I had the traffic. I informed him that I did. I was getting close to him but figured I would out-climb him and go above. My focus was on keeping Aircraft Y in my sight and avoiding the traffic. I continued to climb.At the point we felt he was no longer a factor, I looked at my iPad screen and realized that something was wrong, and I could not figure out where I was. I spent several seconds trying to assess the problem, all the while still climbing. I had full control of the aircraft, and I knew where I was visually, but I could not figure out where I was on the moving chart display, so that I could avoid airspace I shouldn't be in.Pretty quickly I figured out how to adjust my screen so that I knew my position, and at that point realized I had climbed into Class B airspace, or at least I think I did. I had received no hand-off from PAO Tower and was so overwhelmed by that time, along with being very concerned about climbing into Bravo, I simply immediately put the nose down and descended below Bravo airspace.Here are the factors that precipitated this event: 1. I was flying an older aircraft with only one radio and an iPad with EFB for navigation. I was not as familiar with it as I am with the other aircraft I fly, which has a modern EFIS. I had not studied the airspace in my departure path from PAO, I thought I could rely on the iPad. This was a mistake I'll not make again! 2. I've never flown in or out of an airport as busy as PAO. I was very anxious about doing everything right, I wanted to be safe and not cause any issues or problems with the flow of traffic and the controllers. The Aircraft Y's unexpected left turn and my focus on avoiding it became distracting factor that took me 'off my game'.In the future, I'm committed to more fully plan my flights, especially in congested airspace, and I will become more proficient in the use of my electronic flight aids.
ASRS:1786916.s: A pilot departing PAO in an older aircraft with an iPad EFB entered Class B airspace after becoming distracted by a preceding aircraft's unexpected left turn. The pilot attributed the incursion to unfamiliarity with the aircraft's navigation display, lack of airspace study, and anxiety in congested traffic, subsequently descending to exit the airspace.

ASRS:1786917.n: On a flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 in my TBM 700 (Aircraft X), I experienced moderate icing and severe turbulence and wind shear. On the approach to ZZZ1 moderate icing was reported to ATC which allowed me to descend to 2,000 ft. MSL. This got me out of IMC temporarily. I visually flew directly over ZZZ2. Shortly after I reentered IMC and experienced severe turbulence and wind shear. I had difficulty maintaining heading and altitude. It also caused me to be disoriented. I got heading and altitude warnings from ATC. I reported the severe turbulence and requested a vector twice. The second time registered and by then I was in moderate turbulence, icing and intermediate wind shear. ATC suggested an immediate landing at ZZZ2. I wanted no part of going close to whatever I had just passed thru and proceeded to ZZZ1. The airport came into view and I landed hot with one notch of flaps because of the wind shear and the fact that the plane was iced up. ATC was very helpful.
ASRS:1786917.s: The TBM 700 pilot encountered moderate icing, severe turbulence, and wind shear during approach to ZZZ1, causing disorientation and ATC warnings. Despite an ATC suggestion to land at ZZZ2, the pilot continued to ZZZ1 and executed a hot landing with one notch of flaps due to the adverse weather conditions.

ASRS:1786924.n: I took off from ZZZ using Runway 18 with my destination to the north. I turned left crosswind then downwind, intending to depart from the area by maintaining a downwind heading until clear of the traffic pattern. During downwind abeam the runway, I continued to climb above traffic pattern altitude but did not announce the climb over CTAF.During upwind or crosswind, a Cessna (Aircraft Y) announced he was west of the airport and would be crossing midfield and entering into a downwind for [Runway] 18. He did not announce his altitude. I assumed he was at traffic pattern altitude and would be turning left and entering into the downwind. By midfield in the downwind myself, I was at about 1,800 ft. AGL and climbing. I did not see the Cessna until he was approximately 300 ft. directly ahead of me and 200 ft. above. I nosed over briefly to arrest my climb.I have since reviewed the AIM and AC 90-66B. I believe the Cessna intended to perform a descending teardrop turn to enter the downwind. This is a standard pattern entry. My own departure was nonstandard.I will use this experience to better judge traffic conflict and miscommunication risks.
ASRS:1786924.s: The pilot departed Runway 18 at ZZZ and climbed to 1,800 ft AGL without announcing, while a Cessna entered downwind without stating altitude. The pilot discovered the Cessna 300 ft ahead and 200 ft above, attributing the conflict to nonstandard departure procedures and miscommunication regarding the Cessna's descending teardrop entry.

ASRS:1786930.n: Flying from ZZZ to ZZZ1. Calculated fuel reserve on the ground and confirmed as we watched the tanks at 60 minutes of fuel left at the time of the incident. We started our descent into ZZZ1 talking to TRACON when the engine momentarily lost full power, but quickly regained it. My student and I both noticed it, and verbalized the anomaly. We had mentioned a few minutes previous ZZZ2 passing off our left wing, but noted that it was uncontrolled and closed, with unconfirmed runway condition information. When we felt the engine shudder a second time, my student and I [advised ATC] and began heading for ZZZ2. They advised us it was closed, and we were tempted to go an additional 5 miles to ZZZ3 with better services and a guaranteed cleared runway, but the engine slipped again, and we confirmed with TRACON that we were going to ZZZ2, closed or not. We copied down the TRACON phone number to reach them on the ground. The engine then maintained full power all the way down to the runway and to the fuel farm. As it is a Tailwheel, the tanks tip back when on the ground and both tanks read empty, while in the air during our power issues they read just under 1/4 on each side, which should have been just under an hour of fuel to go for the remaining 10 mins ETA to ZZZ1. Once clear of the runway, I tried TRACON again, and [another] airplane relayed our safe message to TRACON as we were too low to reach them.Once parked and shut down, I called TRACON and confirmed we were safe on the ground. We elected to divert to the uncontrolled, closed airport out of an abundance of caution to avoid flying over populated areas with a questionable engine. Once on the ground, we decided to drain the rest of the tanks' contents fully and have a mechanic inspect the aircraft before we attempted to fly again. We are on the ground waiting for the mechanic as I write this report.
ASRS:1786930.s: A pilot and student flying a tailwheel aircraft diverted to a closed, uncontrolled airport after experiencing repeated engine power loss during descent. The crew elected to land out of caution regarding the questionable engine and are awaiting a mechanic's inspection.

ASRS:1786934.n: While heading in to land at ZZZ, a black object was spotted approximately 1 mile from our nose at our altitude of 2,400 ft. Initial thought of both pilots was that it was a bird, then after noticing that it did not appear to be moving I determined it was most likely a drone that was heading straight toward us or hovering, so averted to the right at which point the drone flew past our left wing in the opposite direction approximately 500 to 750 ft. horizontal from our left wing at coaltitude (2,400 ft. AGL). The drone was determined to be a black quadcopter, approximately the size of a soccer ball, with a possible camera mounted underneath. ATC was notified, queried us for further information, and announced to all aircraft on frequency of drone activity in the vicinity of the airspace.
ASRS:1786934.s: Pilots approaching ZZZ at 2,400 ft spotted a stationary black quadcopter drone and averted right to avoid a collision. The drone passed 500 to 750 ft left of the aircraft at coaltitude, prompting ATC to notify all traffic of the activity.

ASRS:1786936.n: Initially, cruised at 7,000 ft. From ZZZ to about the ZZZZZ intersection on V185, I was between layers. ATC requested that I change altitude to an even thousand because I was now westward bound and gave me a choice of up or down. Up would have put me in the clouds. So, I requested down to 4,000 ft. because I knew that should be below the freezing level and below the ceiling as I progressed. Upon reaching 6,000 ft., I requested to stay at that altitude because I was still between layers and 4,000 ft. would have put me in the clouds for some time before reaching the higher ceilings. Eventually, the layers merged and I was in the clouds at 6,000 ft. A short time later, rime ice began to form. In about a minute, I lost my airspeed indicator. Just prior to a red X appearing over the G5's airspeed partition, the G5's airspeed tape quickly unwound and a stall indication began flashing. Also, the GFC 500 autopilot had disengaged. I told ATC I was in icing and received clearance to descend.The stall indication did not make sense. But, I was confused by what was happening and pushed forward on the yoke so as to not take any chances. A recovery from a rapid descent and 180 degree turn was executed as I realized a stall was not happening and the auto pilot had disengaged. ATC offered a 2,000 ft. altitude to get out of the clouds and in warmer temperatures. I had turned on the pitot heat and the airspeed was functioning on both the airspeed steam gauge and the G5. The plane was iced but flying without difficulty and the ice was melting rapidly. I turned back on course and continued without further incident below the clouds. In retrospect, I should have descended to 4,000 ft. instead of stopping at 6,000 ft. This would have put me in the clouds for awhile, but beneath the freezing level.
ASRS:1786936.s: The pilot encountered rime ice at 6,000 ft, causing airspeed indicator failure and autopilot disengagement. After descending to 2,000 ft with pitot heat on, instruments recovered and the ice melted, allowing a safe continuation below the clouds.

ASRS:1786953.n: The 10-9, 10-9B, and the sign entering the ramp in BNA all say to monitor frequency 122.95 for ramp advisories. Our station procedures instructions state that the Nashville Ops frequency must be monitored for all ramp movement. Which is the correct frequency to monitor? We can't monitor both since we must also be on the Ground frequency, especially for taxiing out when we are in the alleyway.
ASRS:1786953.s: A pilot reported conflicting ramp advisory instructions at BNA, where signage and station procedures specify different frequencies (122.95 versus Nashville Ops). The crew cannot monitor both required frequencies simultaneously while also maintaining contact with Ground control during taxi operations.

ASRS:1786962.n: This narrative highlights two incorrect published crossing altitudes on two different arrivals that can lead to altitude deviations and aircraft overspeeds. The first is the PASLY 4 (10-2C) arrival to BNA at GROAT intersection. The crossing is depicted to cross GROAT at or below FL 230. It is always 1000 out of 1000 times given to cross GROAT at FL 220 usually by Memphis Center and has been for at least five years. Sometimes this occurs very late. This can lead to a situation where the aircraft was on the path, is now high, and the aircraft then pitches down at the last minute to meet the unpublished altitude of 22,000 ft. This pitchdown can lead to an overspeed and a situation that still does not meet the crossing. The second instance is on the ENDEE 6 Arrival into MDW (10-2). The fix in particular is KAMBL and the published crossing is between FL 270-FL 240. The unpublished crossing that is given, very late, is to cross KAMBL at 24,000 ft. Now the aircraft is in the same situation as the PASLY 4 Arrival, only you may have a 100 plus kt. tailwind to deal with as well. Both these situations persist but are preventable by simply changing the published altitude. Finally, there are several Pilots who are rusty from not flying, due to low utilization, whose situational awareness and lack of currency make this situation even more grave. Please fix these easy to remedy issues and trap the known errors. Thank you. We did not have a deviation. I am only reporting to highlight these issues.
ASRS:1786962.s: A pilot reported potential altitude deviations and overspeeds on PASLY 4 and ENDEE 6 arrivals due to late unpublished crossing altitudes conflicting with published charts. The reporter noted that low utilization affecting pilot currency exacerbates these risks, though no actual deviation occurred during the flights.

ASRS:1786996.n: On final [Runway] XXL ZZZ we were paired up with traffic on another runway in visual conditions. I thought the FO had selected TA on the transponder. After debriefing on the ground he told me that he was telling me to set TA on the transponder, but what I heard was transponder is set to TA. Inside ZZZZZ [Intersection] at about 1,200 feet we got an RA Climb. I verbalized 'We got to go.' I surmised that the TCAS RA would be followed by a go-around. My communication was unclear. The traffic was in sight throughout the approach. The FO continued the approach and landed uneventfully. We should have gone around, but after debriefing I understood that the FO thought it might be unsafe to climb and go-around with the other traffic so close. With the A.P. and A.T. off, I was P.F. on the visual approach to Runway XX. ATC calls out traffic at our 2 o'clock that will be close to us for another runway. We call the Aircraft Y traffic in sight and proceed inbound. Both the Captain and I are wearing masks (COVID), which I believe muffled my request to 'Set to TA only.' The Captain later said he thought I said 'We're set to TA only.' The approach continued normally with us going to managed speed, gear down, as we started down the glide slope inside the FAF. Just after I called for flaps 3 around 1,400 feet AGL, I noted the Aircraft Y a little above us and the appropriate distance to the right joining up with us. I was still slowing the aircraft at that moment, and the RA went off 'Climb, Climb.' I asked the Captain 'We are not in TA only?' He responded 'Well we are going to have to go.' I momentarily considered going around, but thought continuing the approach was actually the safest course of action when the RA immediately stopped. We continued the approach and landed uneventfully. The RA happened the moment the Aircraft Y was joining the other localizer course. What I should have done is gone around. Following the RA is the right thing to do unless it is unsafe to do so.
ASRS:1786996.s: During a visual approach to Runway XX, the crew received a TCAS "Climb" RA due to miscommunication about transponder settings caused by face masks. Although the First Officer considered a go-around, they continued the approach and landed uneventfully after the RA ceased, later acknowledging they should have executed the maneuver.

ASRS:1787029.n: On short final into SDF RWY 17R I noticed a shiny object slightly below and to the left of the aircraft on final. It was not directly in the flight path but close enough to be noticed. I noted that aircraft was 3 miles from the runway and 600 feet AGL. The drone was slightly below us (estimate 400 feet) and East of the extended centerline (estimate 2,500 feet). At first, I thought it might be a balloon, but recognized it as a drone as it passed abeam and behind us. The FO (First Officer) was flying and given the phase of flight and that I did not feel that it was an immediate threat, I elected to wait until we were clear of the runway to inform the FO and Ground Control.
ASRS:1787029.s: The pilot observed a drone approximately 400 feet AGL and 2,500 feet east of the extended centerline while on short final to SDF RWY 17R at 600 feet AGL. Deeming it not an immediate threat, the pilot delayed notifying the First Officer and Ground Control until after clearing the runway.

ASRS:1787034.n: We were on our way to hangar to pickup a plane, driving on Taxi way 1 driving empty tug with instruction clear all the way to the hangar via Zulu X, as we were approaching Yankee Y intersection, we heard a tower giving instruction to a plane just landed on runways XYC-YXC to take Yankee Z, Yankee short of taxiway Alpha, but that corporate jet enter on Yankee Y and took Zulu, I had to immediately take sharp right turn to a grass area to clear the taxiway Zulu to avoid a collusion, FAA was reported and was asked if we are OK and so we continue on Zulu to the hangar.
ASRS:1787034.s: A ground crew member driving an empty tug on Taxiway 1 avoided a collision with a corporate jet that incorrectly entered Taxiway Y and took Zulu instead of the cleared route. The driver turned onto a grass area to clear the path, reported the incident to the FAA, and continued to the hangar.

ASRS:1787048.n: We were on the ILS 09R at PHL approximately 15 DME when the Localizer exhibited erratic deviations on both the Captain and First Officers Primary Flight Displays. The Flight Director and Auto Pilot was engaged and attempted to 'chase' the course which started to worsen the situation. ATC advised us that we appeared to be about a mile south of the localizer course, slightly less than 1/2 dot deflection at this point. The First Officer disengaged the autopilot and hand-flew the approach with no further issue. The deviation appeared to subside as we got closer to the field and we were within stable approach parameters from the Final Approach Fix until touchdown. Also, the NAVAID had been positively tuned/identified per company SOP prior to commencing the approach. Course deviation on the HSI followed by ATC advising us that we were right of course. Unreliable Localizer signal at PHL which is apparently a known issue.The First Officer disconnected the autopilot and hand flew. I notified maintenance and was told by multiple maintenance personnel both on the phone and in person at the aircraft that this was a known issue with runway 09R, it happens all the time, and that there's a NOTAM in effect regarding the issue. I searched all of the NOTAMs and could not find anything remotely related to unreliable LOC/ILS on 09R. I do not believe that the FAA would allow a malfunctioning NAVAID to remain in service and do not think there is any merit in the maintenance department's claim that this is a known problem that we should just accept and learn to deal with. However, if there is a known problem with this or any other NAVAID that necessitates a procedure change, then the company should disseminate that information to the pilot group with an FIL, etc.
ASRS:1787048.s: During an ILS 09R approach at PHL, the crew experienced erratic localizer deviations that caused the autopilot to chase the course. The First Officer disengaged the autopilot and hand-flew the approach to a safe landing, while maintenance claimed the issue was a known problem despite the pilot finding no supporting NOTAM.

ASRS:1787050.n: While on approach to ZZZ in day VMC conditions, crew was instructed to fly direct 'ZZZZZ' - the FAF for ILS XX - for a visual approach to [Runway] XX. The crew had been left high by both Center and Approach, but was able to reach the 5,000 ft. and slow prior to intercept. The PIC/PF (Pilot Flying) briefed the SIC/PM (Pilot Monitoring) on speed/energy management and airspeed 'windows' prior to the approach. After reporting runway in sight and receiving the approach clearance, the PF initiated descent to 4,500 ft. (the FAF altitude) and began to lessen the intercept angle, and PM prompted gear down and flaps 22. Aircraft still slightly overshot the localizer but was able to capture both LOC and GS which happened simultaneously. 4,500 ft. is within 1,300 ft. AGL of field elevation, and due to the short distance both vertically to the runway and laterally (just outside 4 miles), the PM/PIC anticipated an unstable approach and called a go around. The PF pressed the TOGA (Takeoff Go-Around), disconnected the autopilot, and called 'check thrust flaps nine' and the PM set flaps 9 and checked the thrust to discover the PF had not yet increased thrust to detents. Concurrently with the 'check thrust flaps 9 actions', and 'Sink Rate' EGPWS warning occurred, and momentary hesitation by PF prompted PM/PIC to take control and initiate the immediate action in response to the 'sink rate' AURAL as required for the EGPWS escape, with a 'Pull Up' Aural warning occurring concurrently with the initiation of the EGPWS escape procedure. (At the time of initiation the EGPWS escape, PIC noted an 1,800 fpm descent rate). Upon reaching a safe altitude, the aircraft configuration was cleaned up in line as normal, and flight continued back for ILS without further incident. One error was made during EGPWS escape, which was PIC only increasing thrust to detents and not to max. Upon completion of the flight, crew debriefed on a number of key items. These included energy management and the approach profile in the AOM, go around procedure and ensuring power is set concurrently with pitch and callout when conducting a missed, and the EGPWS escape maneuver.Crews should act very early to mitigate unstable approach situations, including in a situation like this requesting a lower altitude earlier and a vector out to the IAF in lieu of the FAF, this can alleviate the chances of an unstable approach long before the issue manifests. Missed approaches should be initiated immediately upon identification of an unstable approach. In the event of a missed approach, crews should ensure the action is taken decisively including the increase of power, and both pilots should remain involved in the process. Should a GPWS warning be received, decisive, immediate action should be taken - as per the AOM - superseding normal missed approach actions due to the time critical nature of high vertical speed close to the ground. Captains especially should keep a close eye on FOs conducting operations at outstations - in this situation, having approach offer a better vector to join or taking an actual ILS clearance may have prevented the situation from manifesting at all.
ASRS:1787050.s: The crew, left high on a visual approach to ZZZ, initiated a go-around due to an unstable approach, triggering EGPWS warnings when thrust was not immediately set to detents. The Pilot Monitoring took control to execute the escape maneuver, and the aircraft returned for a safe ILS landing after a debrief on energy management and missed approach procedures.

ASRS:1787070.n: During preflight in bitterly cold ZZZ, the FO (First Officer) completed the walk around as snow began to fall. The flaps were full down from the previous flight. She came to the cockpit and informed me that the flaps were clear of debris and asked if we should retract them for the deicing we would need after start. I agreed we should, and we did. Unbeknownst to us, the fueling of the aircraft began during this time and we didn't notice as we retracted the flaps. Just before pushback, ramp informed us that Maintenance was checking the refueling door on the wing, as it was damaged. This was our first indication that we may have damaged the door during flap retraction. Later on, maintenance personnel came to the flight deck and told us of the problem and that we would be swapping aircraft due to this.Cold weather operations, delayed fueling, miscommunication and worsening weather all contributed to this event.Don't touch the flap handle until all preflight items are complete before pushback regardless of weather conditions.
ASRS:1787070.s: The First Officer retracted flaps during preflight in cold weather while fueling was underway, damaging the refueling door. This caused an aircraft swap due to miscommunication and delayed fueling, highlighting the need to complete all preflight items before moving flap controls.

ASRS:1787076.n: During preflight, the crew noticed the Hazmat paperwork showed 15300 pounds of Lithium in position 15L. This Lithium was in an AAD can. This can only weighted 2800 pounds. As the Captain, I asked for the Dangerous Goods [DG] specialist to explain what we were seeing. I asked the ramp agent what the weight of the can was and that is when I found out it was around 2800 pound. Clearly there was a problem. First problem is that the two systems do not talk and crosscheck the weights. Secondly, the DG system does not know the max weight of a can and therefore can't check to see that the maximum can weight is not violated. Third, did I have a CG issue? Fourth, how does the system generate paperwork that has such gross errors?I believe the cause is the systems for DG and W&B do not talk and the DG system Allows Lithium to be declared way above the maximum AAD can weight. Also, the W&B system does not catch such gross errors.My suggestion is to ensure the DG paperwork system and Weight and Balance system learn how to crosstalk. There should be no way for the system to produce paperwork that has gross errors. The DG paperwork system must know and be able to verify the max can weight is not violated. Further, the actual can weight must be known by the DG paperwork system as another crosscheck. It should never be able to have more Lithium declared in the can than the can weights.
ASRS:1787076.s: During preflight, the flight crew discovered a discrepancy where Hazmat paperwork listed 15,300 pounds of Lithium in a can weighing only 2,800 pounds. The reporter attributed this gross error to a lack of data integration between the Dangerous Goods and Weight and Balance systems, which failed to cross-check maximum can weights.

ASRS:1787089.n: Upon departing ZZZ early in the morning, both the PF and PNF flight directors failed shortly after takeoff, prompting the PNF to quickly reference the QRH after several attempts to rectify the situation. After the completion of checklists, during the climb out and initial cruise, it was discovered that the FMC had also frozen up, not allowing any keypad inputs for route modifications. Shortly after leveling off at our cruise altitude, the PNF continued to troubleshoot the problem and was eventually successful at restoring both flight directors and FMC's back to normal. Meanwhile, during descent into ZZZ1, ARTCC advised us of a crossing restriction that was not complied with. We immediately stopped our descent and apologized. ARTCC then handed us off to ZZZ1 approach, after which, the flight continued on without further incident. It is suspected that the electronic malfunction of both the flight directors and FMC's, may have deleted or affected the altitude crossing restrictions, or, ARTCC may have linguistically confused the pronunciation of ZZZZZ with the ZZZZZ1 arrival into ZZZ1, as our flight plan indicated. Per SOP (Standard Operating Procedure), maintenance was notified of the situation but unable to determine cause or reproduce the fault.As for the electronic equipment malfunction, both the PF and the PNF became aware of the flight director failures shortly after takeoff when trying to engage VNAV. The FMC was determined to have failed during climb out. As for the altitude deviation, this issue was brought to our attention by ARTCC after crossing the fix below the published crossing altitude.The cause of the electrical/ electronic failure involving the flight directors and FMC's was undetermined by maintenance and could not be reproduced. The failure to comply with altitude crossing restrictions at a fix, may have been due to ARTCC assuming we were given the ZZZZZ1 arrival instead of the ZZZZZ arrival, which was listed on our flight release and selected in our FMC. My reaction was calm but assertive in continuing to fly the aircraft as the PNF, troubleshot the problem.As for the electronic equipment malfunctions, these failures are unpredictable. As for the crossing restriction compliance, our flight planning documents indicate that the correct arrival procedure was selected in the FMC but ARTCC thought different. In the future, I will be a little bit more willing to question, and/ or, verify an ATC challenge rather than assume their always right!
ASRS:1787089.s: The flight crew experienced flight director and FMC failures shortly after takeoff from ZZZ, which were later restored, but subsequently failed to comply with an altitude crossing restriction during descent into ZZZ1. Maintenance could not determine the cause of the electronic faults, while the altitude deviation was attributed to a potential communication misunderstanding regarding the arrival procedure.

ASRS:1787125.n: Both jumpseats at cross aisle 1 are not positioned safely for the Flight Attendants. The FA (Flight Attendant) cannot sit in a protective brace position, due to the proximity to the bulkhead wall. Keep in mind, 2 FA's cannot sit side by side if one has to spread their legs apart to be seated there.
ASRS:1787125.s: Flight Attendants reported that both jumpseats at cross aisle 1 are unsafe because proximity to the bulkhead wall prevents a protective brace position. Consequently, two Flight Attendants cannot sit side by side if one must spread their legs to be seated.

ASRS:1787137.n: While instructing a student in the pattern at ZZZ, just before turning onto our base leg, we were advised to make a wide left 360 and re enter the pattern on the right downwind for Runway XX. As we began our turn to the left we noticed an incoming airplane on a left downwind flying at same altitude in our path. I took controls from my student and we rapidly began to descend. If wasn't for our quick reaction it surely would have been a mid air collision. The incoming traffic began a climb in order to avoid our path. The incoming traffic was out of our line of sight but ATC still made the call giving us clearance to turn after I voiced that we did not have the traffic behind us insight. This event was noticed by another controller and he promptly relieved his coworker and handled the situation. This controller has been known around flight schools operating at ZZZ to decrease safety in the sky. I felt it was imperative to report this event.
ASRS:1787137.s: A flight instructor and student in a training aircraft at ZZZ avoided a mid-air collision by descending when ATC cleared them to turn despite conflicting traffic. A second controller intervened after the initial controller issued the clearance without confirming the traffic was in sight.

ASRS:1787156.n: I received the second dose of vaccine against SARS-CoV-2 (virus that causes COVID). The vaccine is highly safe and effective, but clinical data show that many people have minor side effects like fatigue, muscle pains, headache, and flu-like symptoms. The FAA requires a 48 hour waiting period after administration of this vaccine for that reason.I had not reviewed the FAA circular. I concluded that it would take longer than the flight I had planned for any potential side effects to develop, so I launched on a 4 hour flight. Towards the end of this flight, I made an unscheduled fuel stop and started to develop a mild headache. Recognizing that these might be symptoms related to the vaccination, I grounded myself. Later that evening, I developed symptoms that were severe enough that they would have presented a safety issue, had I been operating an airplane.I neglected to review the FAA circular in advance of this flight. A 48 hour delay after vaccination would have prevented the possibility of experiencing symptoms that could present a danger during flight.
ASRS:1787156.s: The pilot flew a four-hour trip shortly after receiving a second COVID-19 vaccine, neglecting the FAA's required 48-hour waiting period. The pilot grounded themselves after developing a headache, later experiencing severe symptoms that would have compromised flight safety.

ASRS:1787169.n: While flying from ZZZ to ZZZ1 I experienced light rhyme icing at 6,000 ft., -10C about 125 miles SE of ZZZ2. I could see the sun above and tried to climb above the deck to get above it. I went up to 11,000 ft., -20C, but was still IMC and now picking up Rhyme. I descended back to 6,000 ft. and it got worse. I descending to 4,000 ft., -10C, and now had about 1.5 inches of ice on all leading edges and the wind screen. ATC recommended several airports 20 miles off my nose, but these were smaller airports, shorter runways, and no ATC. I elected to fly 65 miles west to ZZZ2 due to longer runway, ATC, and ground support (including emergency vehicles). I never [advised ATC], but I began to lose power and had a difficult time maintaining 4,000 ft., ZZZ2 Approach provided priority handling for me and I was unaware. I flew the ILS to Runway XX (VFR conditions) because I could not see out my wind screen. I carried an extra 30 kts. on final and delayed lowering the landing gear until 1 nm landing with approach flaps only. I was able to land safely but had to flare out the side windows. ZZZ2 approach and tower were outstanding. My flight planning showed I'd be well west of the forecast icing, but several aircraft were reporting icing in my area from 6-10,000 ft. I landed without incident, terminated the priority handling, and had no damage to aircraft.
ASRS:1787169.s: A pilot flying from ZZZ to ZZZ1 encountered severe rime icing between 4,000 and 11,000 ft, causing power loss and windshield obstruction. The pilot diverted to ZZZ2 for priority handling, landed safely with approach flaps only, and reported no aircraft damage despite the unexpected icing.

ASRS:1787174.n: Departed ZZZ1 and was given XXY.A departure frequency and after the fact it was XXY.B. I maintained VFR the whole time and was told I may have violated the Class Bravo airspace. Tower was closed at ZZZ1 due to COVID-19. A lot of confusion on the ground and with traffic in the air. I was VFR the whole time and contacted ATC when I landed in ZZZ2. Talked with Controller and explained my situation and filled out this report. No evasive action was taken.
ASRS:1787174.s: A pilot departing ZZZ1 received an incorrect departure frequency while operating VFR in closed tower conditions, potentially violating Class Bravo airspace. The pilot contacted ATC upon landing at ZZZ2 to explain the confusion, and no evasive action was required.

ASRS:1787188.n: Just prior to pushback on our flight from ZZZ-ZZZ1 (within five minutes or so of scheduled departure time), we received an ACARS message that Dispatch was aware of HAZMAT on board--with Zulu time and initials. This confused me because: 1) I had not seen Dispatch do this before for HAZMAT, and 2) at the time, we had seen no HAZMAT paperwork. I turned around to query the Ops Agent, and just then, she handed me the NOTAC with a single line item regarding [radioactive] HAZMAT material and told me that she had just received it. I read the paperwork, signed both copies, and indicated that I had done so in a replay message to Dispatch. We then departed. After that leg was over, now flying from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2, I found my copy of the NOTAC--and was about to throw it away--when I started to think that I may have missed something. Sure enough, on further review, the first step for this type of NOTAC, as directed at [Section] of the FOM, requires the Captain to ensure that the Dispatch Release has been amended (if needed) to include a note regarding the presence of HAZMAT cargo. Our Dispatch Release did not have any such remark. Presumably, the Zulu time and the Dispatcher's initials should be included in the note that I should have added as a pen-and-ink change.
ASRS:1787188.s: The Captain received a late HAZMAT NOTAC before pushback but failed to amend the Dispatch Release as required by the FOM. Upon later review, the Captain realized the release lacked the mandatory note regarding the radioactive cargo, despite having signed the NOTAC.

ASRS:1787240.n: Arriving into ZZZ the altimeter setting was showing 0996 mb, so during our arrival brief we covered the VNAV limitation for altimeters lower than 29.70/1006 and put special emphasis on using FLCH (Flight Level Change) when transitioning. Transition level was FL070. ATC began descending us in small steps, they gave us a descend to FL070 but when we were passing FL080 they gave us a descend to 6,000 ft. then further lower to 5,000 ft., during those step downs I missed switching the altimeter setting to the local 0996mb. Then when we leveled at 5,000 ft. ATC verified the altimeter setting stating that we were 400 ft. lower than we should have. I immediately realized my mistake, set the correct altimeter setting, took corrective action and called for the approach checklist. Since the airplane wasn't reacting as fast as I wanted, I disconnected the auto pilot, corrected the altitude and continued manual flying all the way until we landed. There is no excuse for missing an altimeter setting during transition. There were many factors/distractions that took place for this to happen and they all came pretty close together: long duty day, our bells to the flight attendants, re-route to a point not in our route, use of wing and Engine anti-ice, heavy rain during descent so continuous ignition was set, multiple small step downs from ATC, VNAV limitation, all of them occurring often simultaneously. We, as crew, came together and managed all threats that were thrown at us as best we could to bring the airplane safely to the ground.I will, from now on, better prioritize on the stuff that I delegate and ask my crew to keep an eye on me and remind me of things that could make us incur a deviation like this one. Even though we all had our hands full, I should have asked someone for some sort of reminder about the transition level. At the conclusion of a long duty day and the second flight leg of the day, I was PM (Pilot Monitoring) en-route. This was my second leg as PM (6th leg as flight crew) in an international theater in nearly 3 years. Prior to descent and during the approach briefing as well as once the relief pilots entered the cockpit, we discussed the lower altimeter setting of 0996mb and the associated procedure per Company limitations from not using VNAV when transitioning from QNH (Height Above Sea Level) to QNE or QNE to QNH when below 1006mb. We felt very prepared for the arrival and descent into ZZZ. The transition altitude of 7,000 ft. was also briefed however as we proceeded, we encountered winter weather requiring extra vigilance (icing conditions and heavy precipitation). ATC descended us in multiple small increments below 10,000 ft. but the last prior to this event was a descent to 5,000 ft. With the added attention to the weather and ensuring proper use of FLCH instead of VNAV during what should have been the transition, both the pilot flying, and the pilot monitoring did not switch the altimeters at the proper time to the local setting of 0996mb. Upon level-off at 5,000 ft., ATC came over the radio to verify local altimeter of 996mb and stating the observation of being 400 ft. low. I quickly realized my altimeter was incorrect and took corrective action and confirmed the pilot flying did so as well both with the altimeter and the flight path. One of the observer pilots also confirmed and stated the MSA for situational awareness. The pilot flying disconnected the auto pilot and continued to intercept the localizer path while returning to the cleared altitude. The aircraft was hand flown to landing with no further incident.Multiple links in the chain led up to this event and while we thought we had sufficiently briefed the several unique environments (low altimeter/Company limitation, winter weather) we also were distracted by being vectored to a point not on an arrival or the approach expected. It only goes to show that even with the best preparation and briefing that events can change and compound quickly and while attention to detail is most crucial during all phases of flight, extra vigilance is needed for approach and arrival, especially in areas that have not been flown to in recent months or years. Ultimately, the crew worked together to safely return the aircraft to the desired state and ensured a lesson learned for the future when operating in areas with differing transition altitudes.
ASRS:1787240.s: During arrival into ZZZ, the crew failed to switch altimeters to 0996 mb during step-downs to 5,000 ft, causing a 400 ft low deviation attributed to distractions from weather, re-routing, and fatigue. The pilots corrected the altitude, disconnected the autopilot, and hand-flew the aircraft to a safe landing.

ASRS:1787245.n: At 10,000 ft. cleared direct ZZZZZ and cleared visual RWY XXL ZZZ. We both agreed 8,000 ft. was a safe altitude due to terrain then 7,000 ft. after clearing the hills. Flying pilot, FO (First Officer), set 8,000 ft. then 7,000 ft. in the altitude window. It seemed we were high since we delayed the descent so we were trying to get down. I did not notice the altitude was set to 6,000 ft. Approaching ZZZZZ I realized we were low and told the FO to stop the descent. We climbed slightly and joined the Glideslope to continue the approach. We did not get any terrain warnings but it was concerning that we descended lower than anticipated at night into a high altitude airport.The FO was low time in the airplane and had just came back from a 5 year absence. I did not realize he was behind a bit on the automation. While I was trying to figure out what he was doing I lost situational awareness even though we had discussed safe altitudes. It was also the third leg we had flown that day so we were both tired.I was overly depending on the automation to help reduce the work load for both of us. The automation will only help if it is programed correctly so a person has to be very careful to cross check all available information. From now on I think it is best to request an instrument approach when it's dark going into airports you're not 100 percent familiar with. From now on I will at the very least request to join the visual further out on the instrument approach course in order to get more stabilized.
ASRS:1787245.s: The Captain and a low-time First Officer descended below the agreed 8,000 ft altitude to 6,000 ft at night due to an incorrect automation setting and fatigue. The Captain stopped the descent, climbed to join the glideslope, and noted the incident resulted from over-reliance on automation and lost situational awareness.

ASRS:1787266.n: Performed a go-around on [Runway] 30R at MSP. We queried controller that we saw an aircraft sitting on runway while we were on short final approximately 900 feet. He told us to go around which we did - then thanked us for the query due to him being distracted or involved with a disabled aircraft on Runway 30L, this occurred during VFR conditions at night.
ASRS:1787266.s: Pilots on short final at 900 feet over MSP Runway 30R queried a controller about an aircraft on the runway. The controller instructed a go-around, attributing the oversight to distraction by a disabled aircraft on Runway 30L during night VFR conditions.

ASRS:1787272.n: While on final approach into Seattle on a visual approach to [Runway] 16R, after Capturing glide path with the auto pilot, we were configuring the last of our flaps through 1,000 ft. and the Captain called for below the line, while running the checklist the Captain made the remark we were looking low. As I came up the plane was in the flight director, however for some reason the auto pilot had gotten knocked out of GS mode and defaulted to pitch hold. As the Captain started to correct back to the PAPIs we received a low alt alert from Tower, along with a glide slope warning from EGPWS. The Tower saw us correcting during the call however and noted disregard. As we were able to re established on glide path and were stable before 500 ft. we continued the approach to land. Not sure why the flight director disconnected from the glide slope and defaulted to pitch hold, and if was something we did while configuring, or if it was a fault of the plane or ground equipment.I was distracted by the running of the checklist and did not see the entities deviation from glide path, more why the autopilot changed modes. After returning to the displays I was getting conflicting information from the flight director and the glide slope indication. It would have been easier to just look outside and get the indications from the PAPI as to our current airplane state. ILS [Runway] 16R into Seattle, visual conditions, LOC and GS captured with autopilot engaged. After aircraft configuration complete I felt like we were low. I saw that we were now in pitch hold and below glide path. LOC was still captured. I disconnected autopilot and leveled off, heard 'Glide-slope' as well. ATC was informing us about low altitude alert, then immediately said disregard. I regained glide-slope utilizing PAPI.Not sure why the GS disconnected, if it was something we did wrong or if it was a fluke or something to do with the system. I talked to the Captain taking the airplane about the event and suggested to use the ILS. Lesson learned, at all times monitor glide path and lat/vertical modes. The transition from GS to pitch hold was very subtle.
ASRS:1787272.s: During a visual approach to Seattle Runway 16R, the autopilot unexpectedly switched from glide slope to pitch hold while configuring flaps, causing a low altitude alert and EGPWS warning. The crew manually re-established the glide path using PAPIs and landed safely, though the cause of the mode change remains unknown.

ASRS:1787280.n: Accelerated to 250 knots while climbing on the TECKY3 departure out of San Jose while in the Class C airspace but believe we went below the Class B shelf. First Officer was Pilot Flying and as Pilot Monitoring I hesitated momentarily before telling the First Officer to slow down while I checked our position in Jeppesen charts. As we were slowing back to 200 knots we entered the Class B airspace from below. No comments from ATC and continued on our way. Began accelerating to 250 knots above 2500 feet per setting in FMS Departure Limit page. We had discussed the SID and the propensity for aircrews to encounter non-normal issues during our preflight threats briefing. We had also discussed maintaining 200 knots during climbs away from intended course to destination on a flight leg earlier that day. I recall seeing the 200 knots below Class B note. The First Officer briefed the FMS Departure Limit page set at 2500 feet and I missed the chance to change it. I thought from previous experience we would remain outside of the Class B shelf. I can only surmise this was a momentary lapse in the preflight setup. Perhaps I got distracted by some Captain's duty during briefing. The First Officer said that seeing the 230 knots restriction in the SID led him to believe 200 knots wasn't a necessary restriction. That's a reasonable assumption and acceleration to 250 knots isn't prohibited if remaining outside Class B shelf. We debriefed the event thoroughly and had a chance to redo the departure the next day with proper speed settings. Departed [Runway] 30R at SJC via the TECKY3 Departure, speed restriction at MLPTS of 230 was met, however the speed on FMS went to 250 shortly after MLPTS. This created a possible speed violation below the Class B shelf. Set the appropriate speed and altitude in the departure limit page on FMS. Include the note in the departure briefing. The [airport] chart for SJC does include the speed limit note of 200 KIAS while under the SFO Class B.
ASRS:1787280.s: The Pilot Monitoring and First Officer accelerated to 250 knots below the Class B shelf during the TECKY3 departure from San Jose due to an incorrect FMS Departure Limit setting. The crew corrected the speed to 200 knots upon entering Class B airspace, attributing the error to a preflight setup lapse and misinterpretation of SID restrictions.

ASRS:1787286.n: Climbing out of ZZZ around 11,000 feet or so we received an aural warning and master warning light. Noticed the #2 engine oil pressure gauge fluctuating wildly from normal pressure down to the red line and back and forth. Emergency checklist had us reduce power to idle and condition levers to start feather. Pushed the alt feather switch and engine did not feather. NP was above requirements to shut the engine down so we left it operating in accordance with the checklist. I notified ATC before that with the assumption we would have to shut it down. We completed the checklist with the condition levers to max and the engine still producing power and I held a conservative airspeed around 180 kts all the way down the approach. I flew the visual approach to [Runway] XXL without incident and taxied to the gate. After turning the aircraft over to Maintenance we received a new plane and flew our last leg safety getting our passengers to their destination. The emergency checklist directed us to not shutdown the engine and we diverted back to ZZZ since we were only about 30 miles out. The oil pressure gauge continued to wildly fluctuate with the aural chime all the way back to Seattle. After parking and deplaning, Maintenance notified me the engine was covered in oil. Once we landed, Maintenance informed us the engine was leaking oil and when they opened the nacelle they discovered oil covering the engine was covered in oil. One of my senior flight attendants remarked she liked the fact I made the announcement to the passengers and let them know that emergency vehicles would be meeting the aircraft and following us to the gate.
ASRS:1787286.s: The crew experienced fluctuating #2 engine oil pressure and a failed feather attempt during climb from ZZZ. Following the emergency checklist, they diverted back to ZZZ, landed safely, and discovered the engine was leaking oil and covered in fluid.

ASRS:1787299.n: During climb out from ZZZ en route to ZZZ1, we got a chime that quickly went away but then continued to happen. We noticed that the [Engine] #2 oil pressure was fluctuating between the normal indication of about 67 PSI to below 31 PSI. We confirmed the chimes came from the #2 oil pressure warning. We ran the #2 oil pressure warning checklist which later asked if the NP was below 300. It showed 364 and then asked if the NH was below 64%. It was showing between 67% to 69%. We turned back to ZZZ and through out the descent and approach the chime would continue.Causes: Upon landing Maintenance notified us that the #2 Engine was leaking oil and when they opened the nacelle they noticed it had oil all inside the nacelle.
ASRS:1787299.s: During climb out from ZZZ to ZZZ1, the crew experienced fluctuating #2 engine oil pressure and warning chimes. They returned to ZZZ, where maintenance found the #2 engine was leaking oil inside the nacelle.

ASRS:1787320.n: We discussed as a crew that in the future when we get pressured by time constraints and environmental pressures (i.e. raining hard during the walk around) that we won't allow ourselves to be hurried and in a rush. That is when things get missed.I missed the cowl latch key left in the Number One Engine on the preflight walk around. It was dark and raining hard and we were running a little bit late due to an excessively long line at the KCM (Known Crewmember) checkpoint. We discussed as a crew that in the future give us more time to get to the airplane in ZZZ with the long train ride and busy departure time. And no matter never get caught rushing any procedure. Get down on your knees and check those cowl keys! Long line at KCM (Known Crewmember) Checkpoint and we were rushing to get the flight out on time. Rainy cloudy morning in ZZZ FO (First Officer) missed cowl latch key during walk around. Proper keys and pins located on the [Aircraft] during our interior cockpit preflight. Only informed of our mistake by the outbound crew in ZZZ1. Captain called Crew Scheduling to get my number.
ASRS:1787320.s: The First Officer missed a cowl latch key on Engine One during a rainy preflight walk around at ZZZ while rushing due to delays at the KCM checkpoint. The error was discovered by the outbound crew, who found the key inside the aircraft during their interior preflight.

ASRS:1787327.n: All crews should be informed and knowledgeable about emergency procedures in order to be prepared for such unexpected events in flight.After an uneventful preflight preparation and exterior inspection we departed ZZZ, myself as Pilot Flying and the Captain as Pilot Monitoring. We climbed to planned cruise altitude without issue. Shortly after reaching cruise and just south of ZZZ1, an ECAM message and associated chime presented on the lower ECAM screen indicating 'ENG 1 SYSTEM FAULT'. We worked through the indicated actions and referenced the COM procedures. As the engine was reduced to idle thrust only, we began a descent and began diversion planning as it became clear that we could not continue to ZZZ2 with this issue at the lower altitude required on a single engine at ZZZ3. Initially ZZZ was selected, but while I was flying and communicating with ATC the Captain in consultation with the dispatcher elected to divert instead to ZZZ4. With plenty of time to prepare we did all necessary tasks for the diversion and proceeded to an uneventful landing on ZZZ's longest runway, XXR, with fire/rescue services on standby. After landing with no issues we taxied to the assigned gate and shut down the aircraft without issue.
ASRS:1787327.s: The crew diverted from ZZZ2 to ZZZ4 after an 'ENG 1 SYSTEM FAULT' ECAM message at cruise altitude required reducing Engine 1 to idle. They completed an uneventful landing on runway XXR with fire services on standby, citing the need for crew knowledge of emergency procedures.

ASRS:1787345.n: [Cabin fumes event] causing irritation to throat and lungs.
ASRS:1787345.s: Cabin crew reported a fumes event causing throat and lung irritation. The narrative does not specify the aircraft, flight phase, or the cause of the fumes.

ASRS:1787366.n: Upon reaching clearance for ILS XX circle Runway XY at ZZZ from Approach, we were switched over to ZZZ Tower frequency. Established on the approach between the IAF and FAF, I keyed the mic to establish contact with Tower inbound. The entire avionics turned off completely, losing intercom, transponder, GPS/Nav/Comm 1, and Nav/Comm 2. ZZZ was currently under IFR due to 2SM visibility, but we were in visual conditions on the approach course. I broke off from the approach and turned to the south, since we were no longer receiving navigational guidance along the approach, and I had no communications to contact Tower or Approach. I knew the weather towards the south was looking clearer so the plan was to continue south towards ZZZ1 or ZZZ2. We troubleshot the avionics, checking circuit breakers and cycling the avionics switch to no avail. No indications of ammeter discharge or low voltage illuminated, and the turn coordinator was still operable as well as engine instruments, so I presumed that the failure was based solely on avionics and not complete electrical failure. We descended lower, maintaining VFR so that we could receive cell signal, and I contacted ZZZ Tower via cellphone, since they gave us instructors their phone number another time when they had an ATC/instructor meeting. I told them we were okay, and had complete avionics failure. I asked for the phone number for ZZZ1 Tower so I could communicate with them if I decided to continue south to ZZZ1. At that time, the visibility and clouds around ZZZ began to clear up and we could start to see towards ZZZ. I asked ZZZ Tower if the field was still IFR, and they replied that it just went VFR. We proceeded inbound toward ZZZ, maintaining VFR, and were able to receive landing and taxi clearances for our aircraft through the cell phone. The aircraft was repaired, with the problem being a short-circuited avionics switch.
ASRS:1787366.s: During an ILS approach to ZZZ, the pilot experienced a total avionics failure caused by a short-circuited switch, losing all navigation and radio communications. The crew maintained VFR, contacted Tower via cellphone for clearances, and landed safely after the weather improved.

ASRS:1787389.n: I had been delayed 1 day while performing a conditional inspection due to weather at the departure airport. Once in the air, I transited through the congested ZZZ1 airspace to return to my home airport. I contacted the ZZZ Control Tower once I exited the ZZZ1 airspace and read back instructions to make a downwind entry. I monitored the radio for other traffic in the airspace and flew the pattern. Once on the ground, I realized I might not have read back a landing clearance.Due to Coronavirus, I have been making limited flights, basically only to maintain currency. Because of this, I pay more attention to flying the airplane, while radio work is handled habitually, and I wasn't letting each radio transaction sink in, nor ensuring I make all the necessary calls. This leads to diminished piloting skills, and more practice is necessary to operate in congested airspace.
ASRS:1787389.s: The pilot, flying a limited schedule to maintain currency, entered the traffic pattern at ZZZ airport but realized after landing they might not have read back a landing clearance. The pilot attributed this to habitual radio handling and diminished skills due to infrequent flying in congested airspace.

ASRS:1787396.n: Based on unfamiliarity with the FAA's COVID relief policy regarding medical duration's, I acted as PIC between ZZZ and ZZZ1 on date in a type aircraft with an unknowingly expired 2nd class medical (issued date). The unfamiliarity came from reading headlines in several industry publication emails about the FAA extending medical certificate duration's during COVID. I failed to follow up on these headlines to determine the extent of the extensions and therefore performed this flight under the assumption that medicals were extended indefinitely until COVID was over.I discovered my mistake after my coworker (in ground school) asked me about medical duration's in preparation for his private pilot written exam. I proceeded to search for his answer, and in the meantime recalled the COVID medical certification extension news. Upon finding and reading FAA orders describing the extension details, I discovered my certificate was subject to a two-month extension and expired date. Immediately I visited the FAA's AME directory and called several AME's because my AME has since closed their practice. I found several AME's (including my previous AME) to be no longer practicing FAA exams (some for several years), however they were still listed in the FAA directory. I finally found someone still in business and am in the process of scheduling an appointment with them at the earliest convenience.I have a flight today to/from ZZZ2 where I will sit the in the right seat only to provide an extra set of trained eyes and ears for the safety of the flight while not acting as PIC or SIC until my medical is renewed.
ASRS:1787396.s: The pilot acted as PIC on a flight between ZZZ and ZZZ1 with an unknowingly expired second-class medical certificate due to misinterpreting FAA COVID relief headlines. Upon discovering the error, the pilot ceased acting as PIC or SIC and is currently scheduling a medical renewal while flying only as a non-operating observer.

ASRS:1787397.n: This was my third solo XC (Cross Country). Flight planning was approved by the instructor. Weather and NOTAMs were reviewed by both myself and instructor and flight was deemed safe to proceed. There were no NOTAMs or field condition reports for the destination airport. One pattern was flown at departure airport with an instructor to update currency prior to departure of solo flight. Takeoff, climb, en route, and descent were uneventful. During a visual approach to Runway 02 at the uncontrolled airport, I noticed patchy snow on the runway. I noticed other aircraft had landed recently. I was expecting a normal landing to a touch and go. ASOS indicated the winds were from the northwest at 8 kts. I touched down on centerline at 67 kts. Before I set the nose down, the aircraft started veering to the left. I made the attempt to correct and the airplane continued to slide to the left. I believe due to the unresponsiveness of my control inputs, I was on ice. I made the decision to full stop and applied brakes. The aircraft continued to slide on the icy portion of the runway with no response to my braking or control inputs. The aircraft struck a snow bank on the left side of the runway. The aircraft tipped forward and to the right, resulting in damage to the propeller and the right wingtip. I'm not sure if this is a reportable incident/accident at this time. The following day, a NOTAM was issued for 30 PCT patchy snow and ice. I believe I landed on a patch of ice. There were no NOTAMs published at the time of my departure. Had a NOTAM been published for wintery conditions, I would not have attempted a solo XC to this airport. I have not yet been trained to land in wintery conditions. Based on previous landing markings on the snow in the runway, I assumed it was safe to land. My relative inexperience resulted in not recognizing the ice under the snow. I should've gone around. In the future, I will take a harder look at my experience level and the conditions present in order to make a better decision. I have learned a valuable lesson to always err on the side of caution.
ASRS:1787397.s: A student pilot on a solo cross-country flight landed on an uncontrolled runway with patchy snow, unknowingly encountering ice that caused loss of directional control and braking. The aircraft struck a snowbank and tipped, damaging the propeller and wingtip, due to the pilot's inexperience and lack of NOTAMs regarding winter conditions.

ASRS:1787414.n: The single-engine taxi restriction from EWR Taxiway RG began around [Date] and I have observed minimal awareness and compliance since then. I believe a significant contributing factor to this un-intentional non-compliance is that the caution is located on the EWR 10-9D at the bottom in plain text. The ORD 10-7 for the same caution is significantly more visible immediately after the Safety Alert boxes and is in bold type.
ASRS:1787414.s: A pilot reported minimal awareness and compliance with the single-engine taxi restriction at EWR Taxiway RG. The reporter attributed this non-compliance to the caution's low visibility in plain text at the bottom of the EWR 10-9D chart compared to the bold, prominent placement in the ORD 10-7.
