ASRS:1787423.n: After arrival [at] ORD Flight Attendant advises door 2L has been disarmed but the slide armed light was still illuminated. ELB report of write up was sent and maintenance was verbally advised. Station operations and ramp control advised of irregular door situation. Jet bridge was unsuccessfully re-positioned to remove passengers via door 1L. Idea to taxi aircraft to [gate] was rejected after Captain consulted maintenance and MRD was broken therefore pushback unauthorized. Move team was called to tow aircraft. Duty Manager was contacted for authorization. Move team plugged headset into aircraft and plan was discussed on towing aircraft to [gate]. Pilots ran all normal checklists and consulted QRH tow in supplementary procedure. Move team advised pilots he would be providing all Ramp and ATC communications. He also stated that after he commanded the pilots to release parking brake he would need to disconnect headset with no further communications available until reaching [gate]. After parking aircraft at [gate] he would re plug in headset and advise pilot to set parking brake. As aircraft approached [gate] ramp area was covered with ice and snow. Digital sign read slippery conditions. Braking action appeared to be poor. Aircraft was brought to a stop. Captain was unsure if towing was complete, tug was sliding in slippery conditions or another white tug that was parked in front of aircraft was an obstruction. After a few seconds aircraft began to move forward again at the same feel, rate and speed as under tow. Soon mechanics were seen on both sides of the aircraft frantically giving the set parking brake signal. Both Captain and First Officer immediately and simultaneously pushed down brake pedals. Captain then set parking brake. Move team plugged in headset. Captain asked the question what happened? Move team replied they followed their correct procedures which was to chock main tires, disconnect tug, and they were in the process of chocking nose gear and plugging in headset when the aircraft jumped the main chocks and began uncommanded aircraft movement towards the terminal of approximately 10 ft forward lasting several seconds. Weight of aircraft was approximately 217,000 lbs. Aircraft made no contact with any person, jet bridge or equipment.
ASRS:1787423.s: At ORD, a Boeing aircraft with a broken MRD was towed to a gate on icy ramps. The tug disconnected and chocked the main gear, but the aircraft jumped the chocks and moved forward 10 feet before the crew applied brakes, causing no damage.

ASRS:1787426.n: Enroute ZZZ-San Salvador at FL390 we were able to ascertain through ATC Control that Runway 25 was in use and that we could expect to proceed via CAT VOR and execute the ILS Y 25. The FO (First Officer) was the Pilot Flying and thoroughly briefed the approach and his expectations for altitudes, automation modes and aircraft configuration throughout the approach. We were turned over to San Salvador Approach approximately 70 miles from the airport descending to FL200. San Salvador Approach cleared us direct CAT VOR, cross VOR above 5,000 [ft.] cleared ILS Y Runway 25. Both pilots confirmed clearance, altitudes and automation as we proceeded. As we neared CAT we were around 8,000 [ft.] at 240 kts., still on the VNAV path. Although the FMC appeared to like the profile we both agreed it was time to slow down to meet the briefed approach profile. The FO selected vertical speed and dialed the speed back in the MCP window. With the selected vertical speed we weren't slowing down so I recommended Level Change. We slowed, configured and continued the approach passing CAT VOR. I set 2,500 [ft.] in the altitude window to fly outbound from the VOR as we completed the landing checklist. Once crossing the fix at [8.0 nm] we turned inbound via LNAV and set the FAF crossing altitude of 1,600 [ft.], approach mode selected. We were in VFR conditions with the airport in sight on my side of the aircraft. As we turned towards the airport and descended I noticed we seemed low since we were more than 8 miles away and below the glide path. I looked back at the FMC and noticed fix [7.8 nm] with a crossing altitude of 2,500 [ft]. Shortly afterwards ATC asked what our altitude was and I replied 1,600 [ft.]. At that point both the FO and I realized we had missed [7.8 nm] on the procedure and should have crossed it at 2,500 [ft.]. [7.8 nm] is not clearly depicted on the approach plate with a crossing altitude nor is there an altitude depicted for the turn inbound. Also, we flew the procedure properly if the automation was in VNAV, but it wasn't. Although it was nighttime we were in VFR conditions with the airport in sight throughout the procedure. No GPWS cautions. At no time did I feel the procedure unsafe. I was the PF. CENAMER approach cleared us to descend out of FL390 to FL 200. We were expecting the ILSY Rwy 25. We briefed the approach thoroughly and I explained I would stay in VNAV until lined up on final approach where I would select APP for the ILS. Well above FL200, we were handed off to ElSal approach. They told us to proceed to CAT VOR and cleared us for a full approach ILS Y Rwy 25 approach with procedure turn. HOWEVER, we were high before arriving at CAT so I selected to use vertical speed and open the speed window to control speed. The CAPT suggested I use LVL CHG instead since it would do a better job getting down and controlling speed. I did so, while flaps and gear helped slow us. I was still well above 3500', over the VOR beginning the procedure turn outbound to D8.0. Still in LVL CHG, We were able to fully configure and be on the VNAV PATH at 2500' at D8.0. We completed the LANDING CHECKLIST. At this point we had the airport in sight and never lost contact the whole time. We were both using TERR MODE for obstacle clearance. After passing D8.0 I asked the CAPT to select the next lower altitude of 1600' as depicted on the approach chart, and he did so. In my haste to get at the correct altitude, slow down and configure for landing, I did not realize I had not reselected VNAV. The autopilot descended us to 1600' as we turned toward final. We crossed D7.8 at 1600' vice 2500'.. There was no GPWS warning and we had the airport in sight the whole time. On final approach I selected APP and we noticed we looked low and at the same time, the control tower queried us about our altitude. That was when we noticed our error but were already capturing the glideslope at that time. We continued the approach, landed safely and taxied to our gate without further incident.
ASRS:1787426.s: The Captain and First Officer flew an ILS approach to Runway 25 at San Salvador. While in Level Change mode, they descended to 1,600 feet at the 7.8 nm fix instead of the required 2,500 feet, but landed safely with no GPWS warnings.

ASRS:1787431.n: [Aircraft X] was a ZZZ1 flight and the ramp had already planned the loading and was ready to load. I checked the loading to see if the Hazmat was loaded correctly. There were a total of 3 pieces all planned in Pit 3. I noticed that two of the pieces, Items 3 and 5 can not go into the same pit they needed to be separated. One piece was Hazmat Class 5.1 and the other Hazmat Class 3. I contacted ZZZ Ops and advised them of it and to have the ramp lead call me. He called and Item 3 was held off due to not enough bags (15 bag minimum) to separate and load it into another pit. He also advised that Item 3 item did not have a bar code on the package to scan.
ASRS:1787431.s: A ramp agent discovered incompatible Hazmat Class 5.1 and Class 3 items planned for the same pit on ZZZ1. The agent contacted ZZZ Ops, resulting in Item 3 being held off due to insufficient baggage for separation and a missing barcode.

ASRS:1787440.n: We arrived at ZZZ after receiving minimum rest due to weather delays the previous duty period. Normal preflight, startup and taxi to Runway XX intersection X1 for takeoff. At approximately 90 knots, airspeed stagnation was noted and then airspeed increased. On climbout, we received the IAS Disagree caution. The Captain advised ATC. We leveled initially at 4,000 feet and the Captain took over the Pilot Flying role. I became Pilot Monitoring and worked with the jumpseater, who was an experienced B757 Captain, to run the checklists. Once checklists were completed and power settings were calculated. We requested vectors to the ILS at ZZZ. Approach vectored us and a successful landing was made. Upon return to the ramp, it was discovered that all four pitot covers were still installed.
ASRS:1787440.s: The flight crew experienced airspeed stagnation and an IAS Disagree caution during climbout after takeoff from Runway XX. The issue was caused by all four pitot covers remaining installed, but the crew successfully landed at ZZZ after consulting checklists with a jumpseat captain.

ASRS:1787457.n: Cleared for Visual Runway 24 in UNV we descended to 3,400 feet. We were straight and level at 3,400 feet crossing the highest obstacle (approximately 2,400 feet MSL) to the southeast of the field. We got the 'terrain, terrain, too low pull up' GPWS warning.[We] climbed to 3,800 feet [and] leveled off, once passed terrain continued approach and landed uneventfully.
ASRS:1787457.s: The flight crew received a GPWS "terrain, terrain, too low pull up" warning while descending to 3,400 feet on a visual approach to Runway 24 at UNV. They climbed to 3,800 feet, passed the terrain, and completed an uneventful landing.

ASRS:1787473.n: During the crew briefing prior to commencing descent we discussed runway turnoff closures as listed in the NOTAMS and on the JFK ATIS. During the landing roll we noted that the green turnoff lights were illuminated for Taxiway WW, which was closed. After clearing the runway at Taxiway V we asked the Ground Controller if this was normal and she stated they had no control over individual turnoff lights. At other airports I have seen the taxiway lights turned off for closed exits and feel that pilots are expecting to see turnoff lights illuminated only for available taxiways. Since we had briefed the closures we had no issues exiting at the proper turnoff. I could see fatigue, poor visibility, and/or snow obstructed signs causing an incident. I feel that instituting individual runway lighting controls for the controllers at JFK would enhance safety.
ASRS:1787473.s: The flight crew noted illuminated green turnoff lights for closed Taxiway WW during landing at JFK, despite briefing NOTAMs. The Ground Controller stated they lack control over individual lights, prompting the pilot to recommend individual lighting controls to prevent potential incidents caused by fatigue or poor visibility.

ASRS:1787476.n: Cleared RNP 22 at MHLM. After landing Runway 22 and exiting at Taxiway B, Tower instructed us to taxi left (west) on Taxiway A, enter Runway 04 and backtrack down runway to Taxiway D. I advised Tower that we were entering runway at Taxiway A, whereupon tower instructed us to hold short of runway. I advised Tower that we had crossed the hold short line. Tower reiterated hold short instruction, 'For traffic.' CA (Captain) told the tower that an aircraft should not land on runway with us in our position. Tower said that aircraft was only doing a touch and go. After CA protested again, saying that it was unsafe for an aircraft to land on the runway, Tower said that aircraft would turn at the SAP VOR, which is on the approach (east) end of Runway 22. The aircraft, a yellow light twin engine, callsign Aircraft Y, completed its approach and made a low pass, flying the full length of the runway at 50 ft., and passed in front of our nose. Tower then cleared us to backtrack on runway to Taxiway D. Remainder of flight without incident.Language, use of non-standard phraseology by ATC, lack of safety awareness (Tower).The tower seemed to think it was ok for an aircraft to land with another aircraft over the hold-short line.
ASRS:1787476.s: Tower instructed the crew to backtrack Runway 04 while another aircraft performed a low pass at 50 ft. The incident resulted from ATC's lack of safety awareness and non-standard phraseology, allowing an aircraft to fly the full runway length while the crew was positioned over the hold-short line.

ASRS:1787499.n: During the boarding of [Aircraft X] ZZZ - ZZZ1, I noticed a message on [Software] from the gate agent to station operations to inform the ramp personnel that there was a 'motorized wheelchair' on the jet bridge to be loaded onto the aircraft. I made a note to make sure we were provided notification of the wheel chair and when it did not come through the automated weight and balance data I asked the ramp lead. He just told me that it was 'very light' so he scanned it as a normal bag. I asked him if it was electric and if it had a battery and he said he did not know. He did not understand why I needed to know so after explaining that it was Dangerous Goods and required notification, he went to check it. I decided to go down with him to the cargo bin to make sure he knew what we needed. When he went in the cargo bin there was not a belt loader available so I was not able to also get in, and it was surrounded by bags so I was not able to see the base of it myself. He looked for several minutes, then informed me that it was 'not electric' and had 'no battery or electric parts' at all. I clarified this with him multiple times, both while standing at the cargo bin and also over the headset in the cockpit. After the flight was complete, we saw the agents in ZZZ1 unload it and the passenger get on it. I asked her if it was motorized and she said that it was. I asked her what type of battery it had and she said it was lithium ion and it was removable. She also showed me exactly where the battery was and how it could be removed. She also said that someone, it was unclear who and whether or not it was a [Company] employee, told her not to 'give too much information' during her check in process or she might have trouble flying with it. She couldn't remember if she had told the agent if it was a lithium ion battery. Regardless, multiple employees should have been able to figure out along the chain that it was motorized somehow, which meant it had to be electric.The cause was the ramp's misunderstanding of our DG (Dangerous Goods) policies and not being able to identify DG loaded on the aircraft, as well as possibly the passenger not reporting it as DG during check in.This is now the second time I have had an undeclared lithium ion wheelchair carried in the cargo bin in the past year and a half, which is indicative that this may be a larger issue than just one single missed item. Also, given that the ramp lead had no idea that electric wheelchair batteries had to be declared, it is impossible to know how many other events have happened where we simply didn't see the passenger after the flight.
ASRS:1787499.s: During boarding of Aircraft X, a ramp lead incorrectly loaded an undeclared lithium-ion motorized wheelchair as a normal bag due to a misunderstanding of Dangerous Goods policies. The pilot confirmed the battery's presence post-flight, noting the error stemmed from the ramp's inability to identify the item and the passenger's failure to declare it.

ASRS:1787539.n: While taxiing on Alpha Taxiway at a slower than usual rate for departure on Runway 33 and attempting to turn onto Alpha 1 to enter the runway, the aircraft continued sliding forward on Taxiway A. The right quartering tailwind combined with the icy taxiway caused the aircraft to depart the paved taxiway surface where the left main gear and nosewheel slipped off the paved surface onto the frozen ground. The right main gear remained on the paved surface. With the aircraft stopped we shut down the aircraft and arrangements were made with airport ground crews and maintenance personnel to have the airplane towed back onto the taxiway to the hangar where an inspection was made. No damage was found and the aircraft was deemed safe to fly. In addition no damage occurred to airport property.
ASRS:1787539.s: During departure taxi on Alpha Taxiway, a right quartering tailwind and icy conditions caused the aircraft to slide off the pavement, with the left main gear and nosewheel slipping onto frozen ground. The aircraft was towed for inspection, which found no damage to the airplane or airport property, deeming it safe to fly.

ASRS:1787575.n: While flying a cross-country, I encountered strong mountain-wave action, making altitude difficult to hold. I asked for and received a 'block altitude'. The conditions were VMC all the way to the surface. The aircraft was on autopilot with altitude hold engaged. The autopilot called for 'trim up;' as the aircraft was descending I added power. I asked the other pilot to give it nose-up trim as he had done several times before. (The aircraft only has manual trim.) Suddenly, the aircraft nosed over. I immediately hit the autopilot disconnect button and pulled the circuit breaker. I noticed that the aircraft was very nose-heavy and I struggled to keep it from pitching down further. I called for more nose-up trim, but the problem got worse and I could barely slow the pitch-over even by pulling with both hands.During our descent, the controller queried us about our rapid descent. Given that I was extremely busy, I advised ATC. Finally, I told the other pilot to help me pull the nose up, whereupon the aircraft responded and I began adding nose-up trim and climbing back to altitude. We arrested the descent and leveled off and then I began the climb back to cruise altitude.I checked the aircraft for any control difficulties and determined that there were none, I advised ATC that I was climbing back to cruise altitude. Upon discussion with the other pilot, we determined that instead of adding nose-up trim, he was inadvertently adding nose-down. Because the autopilot had been engaged, we did not notice the wrong direction trim. We continued to our destination to get clear of the AIRMET for turbulence. Upon landing, an A&P inspected the aircraft and found no evidence of over-stressing the aircraft.
ASRS:1787575.s: Two pilots flying a cross-country encountered mountain waves and requested a block altitude. The aircraft nosed over when the second pilot inadvertently applied nose-down trim while the autopilot was engaged, causing a rapid descent that was arrested after the error was identified and corrected.

ASRS:1787596.n: On reposition flight to ZZZ1, climbing through FL250, had Amber CABIN ALT CAS message followed shortly thereafter with Red CABIN ALT message. (Checked Pressurization gauges and abnormal checklist while descending). Leveled off and requested immediate descent which was approved. Rapid descent to 13,000 feet followed by return to ZZZ for maintenance on this aircraft. (Center provided priority handling, but we said it wasn't necessary).
ASRS:1787596.s: During a reposition flight climbing through FL250, the crew received Amber and Red CABIN ALT messages. They executed a rapid descent to 13,000 feet and returned to ZZZ for maintenance after receiving priority handling from Center.

ASRS:1787604.n: While approaching MCO Gate XXX to park the aircraft, we noticed that the Marshaller had two wands that were flickering on/off. A wand that is flickering on/off is not a properly working lighted wand. The Marshaller needed to bang the wands individually to get them to operate. Neither the left and right Wing Walker's had lighted wands. I stopped the aircraft, set the parking brake, made a radio call to MCO Operations asking for six lighted wands (two for the Marshaller, two for the left Wing Walker, and two for the right Wing Walker). We waited about 10 minutes while waiting for the MCO Ramp Supervisors to find six working wands from the surrounding gates. One of the supervisors saw that the wands being used by the Marshaller were flickering on/off. One of the Ramp Supervisors took one of the inoperative wands from the Marshaller and discarded it by throwing it across the ramp I spoke to the two Ramp Supervisors, and they explained the following:1. This situation happens all the time in MCO where the safety equipment (lighted wands) do not work properly at night.2. If we go to an adjacent gate to obtain wands, there is a 50/50 chance that we will find lighted wands that work (all the time, not just tonight).3. There is no manager on duty tonight. All managers left for home earlier in the evening. The managers do not preflight the equipment to ensure it is working properly and ensure that we have adequate numbers of lighted wands before the managers go home for the night (ongoing issue). 4. We have communicated the problems about the safety equipment not operating properly many times to our managers, and nothing ever happens to fix the problem.5. Other pilots have mentioned the same concern about lack of operating safety equipment to MCO Leadership and still nothing improves.6. One Ramp Supervisor explained that he has worked at four different (Company) Stations. He said that MCO is by far the least prepared with ramp equipment, safety equipment, etc. The (Company) VP of Ground Operations needs to ensure that all stations have adequate safety equipment and that it is used consistently when required. The MCO Station Manager needs to get involved and ensure his/her (Company) Ground Operations Team has an adequate amount of properly working lighted wands every evening before the Ramp and Operations Managers retire for the evening. The ramp agents need to be trained that the use of the lighted wands is mandatory to ensure the aircraft arriving at night can be safely parked in the safety zone. No exceptions!
ASRS:1787604.s: The pilot stopped the aircraft at MCO during night parking because the marshaller and wing walkers had flickering or non-functional lighted wands. Ramp supervisors confirmed this is a recurring issue caused by inadequate equipment preflighting and lack of management oversight, requiring a 10-minute delay to locate working wands.

ASRS:1787634.n: Air Carrier requested [taxi clearance] to deice [pad] after push to get the [Release] for this flight. After they deiced, Ramp Tower got a call concerning HAZMAT packing. The flight is now returning to the gate to deal with the HAZMAT.
ASRS:1787634.s: The Air Carrier requested taxi clearance to deice after pushback but was recalled to the gate. Ramp Tower received a call regarding HAZMAT packing issues, causing the flight to return to the gate to address the problem.

ASRS:1787641.n: Ground ops and takeoff were all nominal. During the climb phase passing approximately 18,000 feet MSL, we noticed a strong smoke odor with visible smoke and haze emanating from the courier area. The burning, smokey, smell was increasing. We requested priority handling with ZZZ center and stated the nature of our priority and our request to begin an immediate descent into ZZZ for Runway XXR. We ran the Smoke/Fumes checklist. The procedure cleared the smoke very quickly. An expeditious approach was conducted to ZZZ XXR. Crash/Fire/Rescue inspected the ac and followed us to parking without any further issues. Captain was PM, First Officer was PF: Preflight, engine start, taxi and take off were all normal. Climbing through roughly FL180 I noticed a slight burning smell which seemed to be intensifying in both smell and irritation level to eyes/throat. Took a look behind me and noticed the light in the ceiling by the cockpit door shining down on a dense hazy smoke. Mentioned to the Captain to take a look behind him and he noticed it as well. We requested priority handling with ZZZ Center and requested an immediate return to ZZZ for a visual backed up by the ILS to Runway XXR. As we began the turn and descent back towards ZZZ, the Captain ran the 'Non-Alert' Smoke/Fumes Removal Checklist. At some point, approach control was notified of our intentions to be high speed below 10,000 feet. After descending below 10,000 feet, the cabin was depressurized via the QRH procedure and the smoke/smell dissipated relatively quickly. Flight Control was notified via Sat Phone of our intentions to return to ZZZ. Approach and landing went smoothly. After landing, we vacated the runway and came to a stop on the parallel taxiway so Airport Fire and Rescue services could take a look around at the exterior of the aircraft. After getting the all-clear, we taxied back to the ramp and met with maintenance and eventually with EMS to get checked out.
ASRS:1787641.s: During climb through FL180, the flight crew detected smoke and a burning odor from the courier area. They executed the Smoke/Fumes checklist and depressurized the cabin below 10,000 feet, which cleared the smoke, allowing for a safe return to ZZZ for a Fire/Rescue inspection.

ASRS:1787756.n: On an ILS approach to Runway 16L at HEF, at approximately 300-400 ft AGL, while scanning for approach lights, the crew observed two bright white steady burning lights located to the northwest of the approach lights to Runway 16L creating a momentary impression of REIL lights for Runway 16R. The lights were shining directly into the approach path. Crew continued the approach on localizer and glideslope, identified the MALSR for Runway 16L and landed normally.
ASRS:1787756.s: During an ILS approach to Runway 16L at HEF, the crew observed two bright white lights northwest of the approach lights that momentarily resembled Runway 16R REIL lights. The crew continued the approach, identified the correct MALSR, and landed normally.

ASRS:1787759.n: I departed ZZZ after topping off my aircraft fuel tanks. I flew VFR in VMC conditions to PDK. The traffic pattern very congested so much so that several aircraft had difficulty obtaining clearance to enter the controlled airspace at PDK. After monitoring the tower frequency, I elected to call ATL Approach to request a VFR ILS to PDK for a full stop landing. This would help me to practice a VFR approach, setting up the approach, capturing the localizer and glide-slope, Because I was solo I remained alert to visually remain clear of all aircraft nearby.I contacted ATL Approach and received a discreet transponder code as well as VFR vectors for the approach, I was vectored through the ILS localizer for sequencing and then cleared for the approach just outside of the FAF CHAMB and was transferred to the PDK tower frequency.The radio traffic was so heavy that I was not able to transmit before the tower called my call sign and cleared me for landing number 2 behind jet traffic. Because I was cleared to land #2 behind the jet, this contributed to my understanding I would land on Runway 21L, the longer runway used by Jets. The parallel Runway 21R is shorter and primarily used by piston and training aircraft.I continued on approach on the Localizer and Glide slope until short final. When I was approximately over the Runway 21 L approach end I observed Aircraft Y fly over head at approximately 75 ft. at a faster speed. I immediately called the tower and reported the aircraft overhead while side stepping to the right to go around. The tower sequenced me to land on the parallel Runway 21R and I continue to a safe landingThe issue was I was cleared for the ILS by ATL approach and expected to land on Runway 21L. Also I was cleared initially by the tower to land #2 behind Jet traffic However, the tower said that they cleared me to land on [Runway] 21R.I have been flying from this airport for over XX years and I as well as many other pilots regularly receive runway landing changes often on short final. In this case I may have misunderstood or did not hear correctly the landing clearance and as a result had a near miss with another aircraft.Contributing factors was the radio frequency congestion as well as the high volume of aircraft in the airspace, and my expectation to land on the longer runway behind jet traffic. Also the Aircraft Y pilot did not see me as he approached from above and behind my aircraft, which also contributed to the near miss. I have on board Aircraft X an L3 active TCAS as well as ADSB traffic advisory. I do not believe I heard or saw a traffic alert on my avionics.
ASRS:1787759.s: A solo pilot flying Aircraft X experienced a near miss with Aircraft Y while on a VFR ILS approach to PDK. The incident resulted from runway clearance confusion due to radio congestion and the pilot's expectation to land on Runway 21L, requiring a go-around and landing on Runway 21R.

ASRS:1787763.n: We departed ZZZ on a part 91 day VFR local pleasure flight with one adult passenger in this 1979 Cessna 172N aircraft flying approximately east south east. The weather appeared to be six plus miles visibility with some cirrus clouds, winds under 10 kts. with what seemed to be an occasional thermal. Approximately ten to fifteen minutes into the flight, was at about 1,800 ft. and began a gradual turn to the right.As the yoke was first being moved clockwise, or perhaps shortly thereafter, a pop was felt, the yoke then had no resistance whatsoever with the control yoke ending up being all but fully deflected to the right where it remained at that moment. A vibration in the airframe began. It was a light though consistent somewhat disconcerting vibration. Even with the yoke as it was (all but fully clockwise at that time, in other words, the yoke was about 90 degrees clockwise from level) the aircraft was not banking right. The left rudder pedal may have been instinctively depressed to pick up the right wing after the snap occurred, but uncertain. The aircraft now appeared to not be entirely controllable as the yoke and inputs to it did not seem to be having the effect which they should have.Thereafter, if the yoke was moved counterclockwise, especially if moved past neutral to the left, a distinct buffet of unknown nature was felt, and the yoke was immediately returned to the position which resulted in the least vibration, about ninety degrees clockwise. Not being a mechanic there was significant uncertainty as to what actually was broken and what effect it could have on the flight characteristics of the aircraft. When a shallow climb was introduced or the pitch was increased, a distinct buffet of unknown nature was felt and the climb with the associated pitch and power increase was immediately discontinued and not attempted again. When a very shallow descent was introduced the ongoing vibration seemed to decrease or cease. When the engine rpm was decreased slightly the ongoing vibration also seemed to decrease. That said, no further attempts were made to bank or turn left or climb or increase the pitch or power. All turns thereafter, which were slight with little bank, to the right, were accomplished with slight rudder pressure.7700 was squawked and ATC was advised on guard. Center responded promptly to the call. Due to the limited and questionable control problem, along with the ongoing vibration and buffeting issues, the best course of action at the time appeared to be not to continue the flight back to the closest and seemingly most prudent airport as it would have required a flight directly over a densely populated area. The next closest airport considered potentially usable in the situation appeared to be ZZZ1. However, ZZZ1 was much further than ZZZ (about 18 NM vs. about 10 NM), although few homes along the route it required a flight over water which would have necessitated a climb and a left turn. Due to the buffet experienced during the prior attempted climb, local knowledge of many times there being turbulence where the water meets the land, the distance (would something else happen during that longer travel time?) and the buffet experienced when a left turn was attempted previously, ZZZ1 did not seem to be a good choice at that time.There was an acceptable looking farmer's field which required a slight turn to the right and was just prior to the populated area of ZZZ2 and ZZZ2, it seemed to be the best choice. The aircraft was maneuvered slightly right using slight rudder pressure. After the turn was completed a gradual descent at reduced power was begun. Communication with Center was lost due to the descent although an airliner relayed our communications with Center.During the descent at reduced airspeed a very minimal amount of flaps were introduced to see if any negative effect was experienced. No negative effect was experienced. The descent continued, doors were propped opened, fuel was turned off;mixture to idle cutoff, mags and master switch off which all then culminated in an uneventful though spirited landing on a farmer's field. The airplane came to rest seemingly undamaged. Aircraft was exited normally and moments later Center called to my cell phone in order to check status and get information. FSDO's and local law enforcement were notified and responded accordingly.
ASRS:1787763.s: A pilot flying a 1979 Cessna 172N on a VFR pleasure flight experienced a sudden loss of yoke resistance and airframe vibration at 1,800 feet, likely due to a control system failure. The pilot squawked 7700, avoided populated areas, and executed an uneventful off-airport landing in a farmer's field with the aircraft undamaged.

ASRS:1787819.n: On the arrival into DCA, we experienced icing starting at 15,000 ft. Within 2 minutes it built up rapidly. Upon seeing the thickness on the window and judging how quickly it built, we immediately contacted center for a lower altitude and declared sever icing. Descending though about 10-11,000 ft., we exited out of icing conditions. However, it took another 15 minutes for the ice to clear off the windshield due to the thickness and amount. We proceeded to cancel the next flight to ZZZ as we expected to encounter more icing along our route of flight and altitude. When we landed, there was still ice on the plane and at least a quarter inch thick of ice covering a 5-6 ft. spread on both sides of the radome. The ice was thick, coarse, and bumpy.Ensure the ice protection system is working properly.
ASRS:1787819.s: The crew encountered severe icing at 15,000 ft during arrival into DCA, descending to 10,000–11,000 ft to exit the conditions. They canceled the next flight due to residual ice on the radome and windshield, recommending an inspection of the ice protection system.

ASRS:1787821.n: While on approach into CHO we were being vectored by Potomac Approach on frequency 126.4. We were on a right downwind being vectored for the ILS Runway 03. It was IMC conditions with light to moderate rime ice accumulating on the aircraft. At 3,000 ft. MSL we were given a right turn, a base turn, toward the final for Runway 03. We were just outside, south of the fix WULDU. I noticed were getting close to the localizer course for the final approach, and Potomac had not issued a turn for us to intercept the approach. I prompted Potomac approach and tried to establish communication. There was no answer on 126.4. I prompted again, and still there was no answer from Potomac. At this time we crossed over the localizer course without a turn to intercept given from Potomac. I had guard (121.5) already tuned in on comm 2. I heard Potomac approach trying to hail us on 121.5 on guard and advised us to switch to frequency 132.85. I switched to 132.85 and they gave us an immediate turn to the right to reestablish us on the localizer course. The coverage on 126.4 for the area was lost and I confirmed that with Potomac that we were trying to contact them. Apparently a Learjet overheard us trying to transmit on 126.4 and relayed it to Potomac. Once we re-established communication, Potomac gave us that right turn to intercept but it was 'too late', The aircraft GPWS detected terrain and gave us a 'Terrain, Terrain' 'PULL UP' audio warning. I directed the First Officer to Climb the aircraft and disregard the instruction from Potomac Approach. We climbed up to 3,500 ft. MSL and got the aircraft clear of the terrain. I advise Potomac what had happened and that we were unable to intercept the approach from the vector that they gave us. Potomac than gave us more vectors to get re-established on the approach. From there we landed with no further issues. I conversed with Potomac about the drop in radio coverage on frequency 126.4. They agreed and confirmed that they could not hear us and we could not hear them on 126.4.[Problem was identified by] flight crew scan. No communication from ATC have prompting them several times. Having Guard (121.5) on comm 2 and have our audio on to re-establish communication. Being aware of the terrain in the area and seeing the aircraft GPS position on The Jepp charts. [Cause was] loss of two-way communication on 126.4 between our aircraft and Potomac approach lead us to not receiving an instruction to intercept the localizer course. Without that instruction we continued on our heading and had to re-establish communication via guard and switch to a different frequency that has radio coverage in the area. All of this lead to vectors in an area with terrain and caused us to be in a position where the aircraft GPWS was activated. [We] contacted ATC. Followed the aircraft GWPS system and climbed to avoid terrain. Advised ATC that we were responding to a GWPS annunciation. [Suggest] better radio coverage equipment is needed for the area around CHO. Suggest the importance of ALWAYS monitoring 121.5 on Comm 2 for flight crews.
ASRS:1787821.s: The flight crew lost two-way communication with Potomac Approach on 126.4 while approaching CHO in IMC, causing them to cross the localizer without an intercept turn. This resulted in a GPWS terrain warning, prompting the crew to climb to 3,500 ft to avoid terrain before re-establishing contact and landing safely.

ASRS:1787833.n: Upon entering the ramp (Taxiway Delta to Foxtrot) both of us noted that the Foxtrot taxiway centerline on the ramp and perpendicular to the gate centerline seemed too close to the southern edge of the taxiway on the ramp next to the grass. Recommend a site survey be conducted for heavy aircraft arriving/departing San Salvador to better understand how close taxiing on the Taxiway Foxtrot centerline will place the main wheels to the grass and edge of the taxiway. It appeared that taxiing on the Taxiway Foxtrot centerline would put our wheels very close to the grass or in it. We elected to deviate from centerline to keep us away from the edge of the grass and edge of the ramp taxiway. It is possible that taxiway Foxtrot was measured and painted for B757 and smaller aircraft. Conduct a site survey of MSLP to determine if the taxiway centerline is measured and painted for larger aircraft like Aircraft X. Publish guidance on the -7 pages describing the need for deviating from taxiway centerline on Taxiway F if it is found to be of sufficient distance from the edge.
ASRS:1787833.s: Pilots taxiing Aircraft X on Taxiway Foxtrot at San Salvador deviated from the centerline to avoid the grass edge, suspecting the markings were designed for smaller aircraft. They recommended a site survey to verify clearance for heavy aircraft and publish guidance on centerline deviations.

ASRS:1787859.n: During the preflight brief by the Captain, specially as he completed the 'T' Brief, I observed the CYAN WX-A on his nav display, indicating that his radar was on. I quickly looked to see if my radar was on also, it was not. I know for certain his radar was not on prior to this as I cross checked altimeters and field elevation during my cockpit preflight and glanced at his Nav Display. I am constantly looking to assure that the CYN WX-A is not displayed on the NDs this issue a big pet peeve of mine. I believe this event occurred during the power transfer from GPU to APU as it occurred shortly prior to push and shortly after starting the APU and is a well known anomaly on the LDS (large display system) 767. Further, on this day, the airplane had a bird strike on the nose cone which I noticed on the preflight. The mechanic was working directly in front of the nose cone. I'm glad that the radar didn't power on while he was inspecting the nose cone. I have no reasonable assurance that a scenario like that can't happen as the radar powers on at various times when there is a power transfer. As a matter of fact and ironically, I had that exact thought earlier as I completed my preflight and saw the mechanic on a ladder in front of the nose cone. I can't tell you how relieved I am to know that the radar didn't power on with the mechanic in front of it. A known anomaly on the LDS Boeing 767 [is] the radar powers on at various times, which the technician believes is predominately tied to power transfers. Further, the issue appears to be tied to whether or not the parking brake is set or not. The design assumption of the radar assumes the parking brake is going to be set at the gate. If the brake is set, supposedly the radar will not power on. However, at my company, that is not the case as we release the parking brake once the airplane chocks are in place. There is a belief by those in Flight Management that the Flight Manual has addressed this issue with a change to the Interior Safety Check and Power Application. The change in the flight manual was a note stating that this power on anomaly can occur and the Captains should be looking for it. However, the problem with that is that the radar powers on at various times. I have seen it occur with a simple power transfer from GPU to APU, when the IRS selectors are moved from Off to Align with the APU already running and no power transfer occurring by the flight crew and I've seen the issue occur during a pushback following a pneumatic ground start as the generators come online. I've also seen the Cyan WX-A displayed on one ND and not the other, and sometimes it is displayed on both NDs. Further and a separate issue entirely, I'm not entirely certain the WXR button location isn't an issue itself. It is a very easy button to toggle on/off. The location is also very poor and is in a position that could be accidentally bumped by those installing the sun shades in the summer, those cleaning the windshields and by someone getting into or out of the seat.This anomaly needs to be corrected as soon as possible. I've been on the 767 for nearly X years and this issue has been on going. I have had discussions regarding this issue with many people over the course of several years, Standards, LCAs and most recently Fleet Captains. There is a fix, LDS Software Update, which will correct the issue. However, unfortunately, they are looking at a need to do a wiring change and at present time it appears that that will take 2 years to complete. To make matters worse however, I have noticed this phenomenon is occurring on brand new 767s that we have just taken from the factory, like [another] aircraft which is a very new airplane. It is unacceptable that we are taking new airplanes from the factory with this issue, knowing that the fix will not take place until Heavy Checks. I feel this is irresponsible to all people on the ramp who are exposed to a radar in operation while parked at a gate. We have pilots, crew bus drivers, ramp load teams, mechanics, fuelers, caters, lavatory service techs all being exposed to an operating radar when this event occurs. I can't tell you how frustrating it is to complete the walk around, sit down in my seat and see the radar has been on because the Captain missed it or it occurred at sometime that he wasn't aware of. This needs to be fixed quicker than a few years and some sort of procedure needs to be established soon to provide a safe/healthy work environment to all those I previously listed. This really is not OK.
ASRS:1787859.s: A First Officer on a Boeing 767 observed the weather radar unexpectedly activating during a GPU-to-APU power transfer while a mechanic inspected the nose cone. The reporter attributes this known Large Display System anomaly to power transfers and parking brake status, noting it exposes ground personnel to radar radiation until a future software and wiring fix is implemented.

ASRS:1787877.n: On the ZZZZZ6 we were told to level at 7,000 feet for traffic. This was my 3rd trip on IOE and was practicing hand flying the departure. It was turbulent and we were in and out of IMC. Since we were extremely light due to light loads we were climbing at an extremely fast vertical speed. Passing through 6,000 I announced that I was going to use TCS to reduce the rate of climb to about 1,000 since there was traffic above and I wanted to avoid a RA. I corrected the VS to about 1,000 ft/min. I was not quick enough to override and reduce the autothrottles to avoid increasing airspeed. The airspeed quickly and momentarily increased to 270 knots as we were leveling at 7,000 feet. I reduced the autothrottles too late and while reducing them altitude deviated by 140 feet high. Both deviations were short and immediately corrected. Nothing was mentioned by ATC. We were later given higher once the traffic passed. The combination of hand flying in turbulent conditions in IMC and leveling at a low altitude with light loads was a recipe for distraction and error to occur. I could have eliminated some of these variables by engaging autopilot earlier or reducing autothrottles quicker. The CA and I debriefed and talked through what led to the event and how to prevent it in the future.I learned that when possible reduce extra variables that could lead to an error. I am new to flying with the company and new procedures, was hand flying in turbulent conditions and IMC, light loads with good performance, and was given a low level off. That is a lot of variables at once and the ones that I could control are the earlier use of automation to help alleviation some of the task saturation. Hand flying in turbulent conditions and maintaining altitude can be difficult and the autopilot can alleviate and sometimes do a better job to avoid deviations. Additionally I learned not to lag on overriding the autothrottles when using in FLCH mode. From this experience I feel that I can better identify and evaluate a handful of risks in a certain situation and will take prompt action to reduce these risks in a timely manner. The CA and I had a productive debrief and agreed on what variables led to the deviation and how to prevent in the future. Upon departure we exceeded the 250 knot speed limit in class B while leveling off. We sped to 265 knots for about 15 seconds while leveling off at 7000 feet. Aircraft was very light and a great deal of convective weather in our vicinity.This was a training flight with a new first officer who was hand flying the departure. The rapid climb rate and early level off instructions caught the First Officer off guard. The First Officer recognized the issue and overrode the auto throttles to get the aircraft slowed to 250 knots.
ASRS:1787877.s: A new First Officer hand-flying a light ZZZZZ6 departure in turbulence and IMC exceeded 250 knots and deviated 140 feet high while leveling at 7,000 feet due to delayed autothrottle override. The Captain and First Officer debriefed the event, attributing the deviations to task saturation from multiple variables and agreeing to use automation earlier to mitigate risks.

ASRS:1787885.n: When we arrived and the door was opened we started to deplane the aircraft, a full flight, just as the first three first class passengers were deplaning , the cleaning crew started to enter asking if they could board to clean first class to start. The first class wasn't even deplaned. Only three people had deplaned while others were trying to get their bag down and deplane. I said no not at this point, which in turn the first cleaner gave me serious attitude. The Gate Agent came down, no mask on, with an attitude about us not letting the cleaners enter to clean. They had 12 people to clean, usually they have a shortage of cleaners. But we hadn't even had first class passengers cleared and they started coming on. I asked not yet, let the passengers deplane and this flight is a full flight. This is becoming a serious issue at times and passengers getting upset they can't deplane and usually the cleaners keep cleaning and not moving in so they can deplane. Understand at this time with COVID the importance of cleaning but passengers complain at me about cleaners not clearing so the could deplane. It's stressful enough with all we are dealing with no food drinks and upset passengers about what they can't have. Our passengers were moving quick and not stalling getting off. When they were off we couldn't get our bags and personal items together. The flight deck wasn't able to exit. I understand there is time a limit and all but this rushing is going to seriously cause problems with safety of crew and passengers. I was wrong possibly and maybe for which i will follow these memo's I forgot about from now on. Just trying to give our paying passengers a pleasant and safe flight including safe deplaning.
ASRS:1787885.s: Cabin crew reported that cleaning staff and a gate agent attempted to board a full aircraft before first-class passengers finished deplaning, causing congestion and preventing crew from retrieving bags or exiting the flight deck. The reporter stated this rushing created safety risks and passenger complaints, though they acknowledged they may have been wrong to deny entry.

ASRS:1787904.n: During taxi to Runway 31L, ground control told us to hold short of the approach end of Runway 22 at Taxiway Z. As another aircraft was landing, ground told us to cross Runway 22 In front of the aircraft on landing roll and told that aircraft to give way to us. As we began to cross in front of the aircraft on landing roll, there was no indication that the aircraft was slowing down to give way to us. So I stopped our aircraft and the aircraft on landing roll passed in front of us. Ground said that we shouldn't have stopped.This event was caused by ground control setting up a disaster scenario by wanting us to cross in front of the aircraft on landing roll. If anything went wrong, like brake failure of the landing aircraft, then there would have been a potentially catastrophic aircraft accident.In the future, ground shouldn't cross aircraft in front of other aircraft on landing roll unless they are positive that the aircraft on landing roll has slowed down sufficiently to be safe. We were instructed to taxi from FBO to '[Runway] 31L via Zulu, hold short approach end [Runway] 22 at Zulu'. We exited the FBO ramp onto Zulu, turned left towards [Runway] 22 and noticed that [Taxiway] Zulu terminates before the approach end of [Runway] 22, and it becomes [Taxiway] Yankee. We discussed this on the flight deck that the taxi instructions should have been clearer because you can't really hold short of [Runway] 22 on Zulu, you would actually either hold short of [Runway] 22 approach on Yankee, or hold short of Yankee on Zulu. In any case, the Captain as PF (Pilot Flying) exercised some good judgement and decided to stop a bit back from Yankee, at least from the sign anyways. It's hard to figure where Zulu actually ended. That way we could respond to Ground if they modified their instructions to hold back further. Whatever is the case with Zulu or Yankee, we stopped and awaited further instructions. We noticed a bizjet (Aircraft Y) landing on [Runway] 4 so we suspected we were being held from crossing the approach end of [Runway] 22 (same as rollout end of [Runway] 4) due to the landing traffic. After a short wait, we heard ground instruct Aircraft Y which was now rolling out to 'give way to Aircraft X, he will be crossing at the end of the runway in front of you'. I cannot recall if the other aircraft acknowledged. The next thing we both heard was 'Aircraft X, cross Runway 22 and continue via Kilo'. I turned all the lights on and the Captain started to move forward. I looked right to clear and noticed the landing Aircraft Y was very close, it seemed to me he was past Bravo and Kilo 2 where I presumed he would have turned off, that his reversers were still deployed, and he was rolling very fast for so close to the end of the runway. I said 'STOP, we're not clear' or words to that effect and the Captain immediately stopped as he was now seeing Aircraft Y appear large in my windshield. It may have been hidden beside my windshield side pillar previously. We both agreed it would not have been pretty had we gone across the runway as it clearly appeared Aircraft Y was landing fast and rolling out long, and more importantly, evidently not giving way to us. After just a few seconds, Ground said 'Aircraft X, you're not moving' and we responded that it was not safe to do so. Ground replied, 'Aircraft Y is giving way to you' or words to that effect, and we replied that wasn't the case. After a few more seconds Aircraft Y exited onto Kilo in front of us, and Ground then instructed us to cross the runway and continue onto Kilo on our taxi to [Runway] 31L. Ground and Tower frequencies were combined per ATIS onto tower frequency 118.7, we were always using it, but when Aircraft Y cleared in front of us and we followed him until we turned left onto Charlie, we never heard him. Our subsequent taxi and departure was uneventful.The confusing or incorrect taxi instructions provided (i.e., is it Zulu or Yankee to hold short) started us off with noticing ATC peculiarities as we spoke to Ground. The other aircraft not giving way to us, or appearing to do so, was the major cause of this averted conflict. Combining Tower and Ground on one frequency may also have caused some confusion, because the tower cab can hear everything but in the aircraft we can only actively hear the frequency we're currently using.First off, I think our alertness was the link in the chain that prevented an incident (or worse). I think that ATC made a procedural error in directing us to cross in front of the landing traffic without adequate time/distance to do so. I recommend [Company] request an official copy of the tape from the FAA if possible for review and development of lessons learned.
ASRS:1787904.s: Pilots of Aircraft X averted a runway incursion during taxi to Runway 31L by stopping when instructed by Ground to cross Runway 22 in front of a landing aircraft that failed to yield. The reporter attributed the near-miss to Ground's unsafe clearance and confusing taxi instructions, noting that the landing aircraft passed in front of them before they could safely cross.

ASRS:1787908.n: Cleared to descend via the ZZZZZ2 arrival except maintain 10,000 feet. Initially high, changed descent mode from managed to open and selected 300 knots to get to path with speed protection. However, due to distractions, failed to manage descent appropriately. A few miles from ZZZZZ with a constraint of 12,000 feet from FL190 I noticed we were approaching 12,000 feet rapidly. I asked the FO to request descent to 10,000 feet. We leveled off, but not in time and crossed ZZZZZ several hundred feet below 12,000 feet. ATC did not say anything however this was not safe and not professional airmanship.Distracted with conversation related to COVID and job security instead of flying the aircraft more attentively. Switched descent modes without alerting the PM. Failed to recheck altitude constraint early enough to discover error. Discontinue involved conversations prior to phase of flight changes.
ASRS:1787908.s: The flight crew descended via the ZZZZZ2 arrival but crossed the ZZZZZ waypoint several hundred feet below the 12,000-foot constraint. The pilot attributed this error to distractions regarding COVID and job security, switching descent modes without alerting the First Officer and failing to monitor altitude early enough.

ASRS:1787988.n: Our flight departed from ZZZ enroute to EWY. Clearance was issued as follows: 'CLEARED TO EYW AIRPORT [via SID] FLY TOWER ASSIGNED HEADING THEN AS FILED MAINT 3000FT (ZZZ..ZZZZZ..MTH..EYW..KEYW)'. Established level at our cruise altitude of 14,000 ft. and on our cleared route we were handed off to MIA Center (ZMA). ZMA cleared us Direct to EYW and we proceeded on the new route. During our descent ZMA issued the cross a fix not on our route at 10,000 ft. We believed we heard GINGA as the controller pronunciation had the hard G sound. Looking at the chart the closest intersection with this sound was GIGIH. However, as we now know the fix was JANKA to the South. We requested clarification of the intersection 4 times from ZMA and received no response. Believing the clearance was to a GIGIH we started out turn to the West and continued our decent to meet the restriction. ZMA asked if we wanted to arrive from the North to EYW and we responded we had no preference. ZMA then issued at turn to heading 180 and we continued our descent to 10,000 ft. ZMA handed us off to Navy Key West Approach and the flight continued without incident. Upon landing and researching the charts in more detail we discovered the similar sounding intersections of GIGIH and JANKA in the EYW area, neither of which were on our flight plan. It is my opinion no violations occurred, and all altitude restriction were accomplished as published, however, the Safety of Flight is highest priority at our company and the crew felt this issue should be submitted as an ASAP report to further pilot education and professionalism. Similar sounding intersection names not on our flight plan. Controller pronunciation and being unable to confirm the waypoint.The ability to confirm the proper waypoint spelling with ATC.
ASRS:1787988.s: The flight crew descended from 14,000 ft to 10,000 ft after misinterpreting a MIA Center clearance for fix JANKA as GIGIH due to similar pronunciation. Despite four requests for clarification receiving no response, the crew turned west to meet the restriction before being redirected by ATC, with no incident occurring.

ASRS:1788038.n: After departing [Runway] XXR from ZZZ [airport] on the ZZZZZX SID, began to accelerate through 9,000 feet MSL using speed mode. This caused the aircraft to level off around 9,300 feet MSL as it was speeding up from 250 KIAS. Captain was talking with ATC regarding our climb clearance when the acceleration began. ATC did not acknowledge the increased speed. After finishing the clearance readback the Captain noticed the increasing speed and changed to vertical speed mode to reduce airspeed. As pilot flying I reduced the thrust as well. Upon reaching 10,000 MSL we resumed normal profile climb.Limited experience taking off with wing and cowl anti-ice on. Normally upon reaching ZZZZZ1 intersection we have reached 10,000 MSL and can begin to accelerate. Because of the reduction in climb performance using the anti-ice system we were 1,000 feet lower than normal. The use of cowl and wing and anti-ice also caused the aircraft to use a lower angle of attack to reach entered airspeed resulting in a reduced climb performance. Because of reduced loads from COVID-19 we have normally not encountered a problem reaching 10,000 MSL before the west bound turn resulting in a habit of increasing speed at ZZZZZ1 or west/east bound turn.
ASRS:1788038.s: The pilot flying and captain experienced an unintended level-off near 9,300 feet MSL after accelerating through 9,000 feet while using wing and cowl anti-ice. Reduced climb performance from the anti-ice system and a habit of early acceleration caused the aircraft to exceed 250 KIAS before reaching 10,000 feet.

ASRS:1788042.n: Descending into ZZZ my First Officer (FO) and I noticed there was an unusual sound but we couldn't tell where it was coming from, I called the flight attendant and asked her if she could hear anything and she said no everything sounded normal to her in the back. We then pulled up the engine page and looked at the engine system followed by checking the electrical page but we couldn't see anything abnormal. We continued our descent and started our approach, it was visual conditions so we were on a visual approach to Runway XX, we had already canceled IFR. I called for flaps 12 and the FO put flaps 12 in, we noticed that the sound had changed a little so we again went through the engine instruments and everything still seemed normal. As we continued to add flaps we noticed the sound would get a little louder each time and when we went flaps 32 we could feel a small vibration coming through our feet. We checked the hydraulic page and everything looked fine, we then checked the flight control page and everything still looked normal. I was hand flying and did not notice any change to the handling of the aircraft, the only thing we noticed was the sound and then the small vibration. We continued to land with no issues, just a normal landing. After parking the aircraft and deplaning, I asked my First Officer to take a little extra time with his post flight to see if he could see anything that would have made the noise and vibration on the approach. After his postflight he came in and said he couldn't see anything unusual outside. I finished up my tasks and then decided to walk around the aircraft myself. When I got to the left side I noticed something sticking up on top of the wing maybe a foot or two from the fuselage. I grabbed a ladder and climbed up to look at it, I found that the trailing edge of the flap was cracked right next to the fuselage and then again about a foot or two away there was another crack. The top trailing edge of the flap had a piece that had come off and was sticking up. I took pictures and called the mechanic on call. I sent him the pictures and he called me back with a plan to send a mechanic down on a different aircraft that night. I went off duty at that point and when I got back to the airport the next morning my aircraft had been swapped out with a different aircraft for us to continue our day.
ASRS:1788042.s: During a visual approach to Runway XX, the Captain and First Officer heard an unusual sound and felt vibrations that increased with flap extension, though no instrument anomalies were detected. Post-flight inspection revealed a cracked left flap trailing edge with a detached piece, causing the aircraft to be swapped for the next day's operations.

ASRS:1788048.n: On a descent into DEN, we were cleared to descend via the CLASH 3 Arrival. I confirmed that the final altitude was 9,000 ft. and selected it in the altitude window. About 10 miles from EVRLY, we experienced wake turbulence for about five seconds, and then experienced it again. I selected Vertical Speed and leveled off the descent to get above the wake turbulence. After we were clear of the wake turbulence, I selected a 2,000 FPM descent to get back on my vertical path. At that time, we were told to switch to Denver Approach. Upon checking in with Denver Approach they changed our runway to 35L. At this point I was concerned about changing the approach in the FMC. I forgot to re-engage the VNAV. Because I forgot to re-engage the VNAV, the aircraft did not slow down to 250 kts for EVRLY. The aircraft also continued a descent below 12,000 feet., which was the lowest altitude at TWNSN. The aircraft continue to descend until I notice the deviation. By this time I was leveling at 10,000 feet. and was below the 11,000 feet. altitude required for PNBAL. ATC advised me to slow the 210 knots, and gave me a vector for the final approach to Runway 35L. They also gave me a descent to 9,000 feet. The rest of the arrival went as planned.
ASRS:1788048.s: During a descent into Denver on the CLASH 3 Arrival, the pilot forgot to re-engage VNAV after avoiding wake turbulence, causing the aircraft to descend below required altitudes and fail to slow for EVRLY. ATC subsequently vectored the aircraft, issued speed restrictions, and cleared a descent to 9,000 feet for Runway 35L.

ASRS:1788087.n: The deicing crew at ZZZ briefed myself and the First Officer (F/O) where the deicing was going to take place and we requested FULL AIRCRAFT DEICE with Type 1 and WINGS AND TAIL ANTI ICE with Type 4. After we pushed back and parking brake was set, the QRH was complied with for configuring the airplane for deicing as instructed by the deicing crew. The ice-truck drove past the nose to the left side and disappeared. Approximately, 15 minutes later, the truck rolled up from the right side and told us over the radio that the deicing was completed without giving us the pertinent data that we need like the type of fluid used for the deice and anti-ice. Moreover, we were not given the start time for the anti-icing. The first officer had to ask them for the information even to the point of getting clarification for the type 4 used in the anti-icing. This baffled us! As we tried to figure out what was going on, I asked my F/O if he had heard the sound of the spraying on the fuselage. He said no he really didn't hear it and I didn't hear it. So just to make sure, I asked the F/O to verbally ask if Type 1 was WHOLE FUSELAGE and TYPE 4 FOR WINGS AND TAIL, iceman said YES! So we got the holdover time, and stated to taxi out but I had my doubt on what was done. As I was telling the F/O that we will need to pullover and do a pre-takeoff check by going in to the cabin to inspect at least the wings, we got a call from the flight attendants telling us that the windows were still glazed over with ice.I decided to return to the gate to do another walk around inspection. When we arrived at the gate at my F/O did the second walk around inspection, he came back angry and furious, and rightly so because the airplane was still ENCASED IN ICE! I too was very angry with the UNSAFE Job the iceman did for us and LIED about it. And please note that there was NO precipitation since we arrived at the airport. During the night in ZZZ they had gotten freezing rain, so when we got to the airplane (10 minutes before departure due to the road conditions) we already knew that we had to deice, which my walk around affirmed that. At this point everything was pretty normal except for the fact we were late, (we did not rush nor did I feel rushed) and we had to deice. We ran all checklists and pushed back, we ran the QRH for de-icing and called OPS for deicing/ anti icing, and my exact verbiage was 'parking brake set aircraft configured for de-icing full body wings and tail Type I and wings and tail Type IV' when they were done which looking back, it didn't seem to have taken the usual amount of time, it was way shorter! We finished up with the QRH, started the engines, ran the checklists and started to taxi, to which we may have taxied 100 yards when the FAs (Flight Attendants) called and said that the windows in the back were covered in ice, the CA (Captain) was also listening to this, I than told ground that we needed to stop and work a problem, he stopped the airplane and we discussed the issue and both determined we CANNOT takeoff with ice on the airplane, we both made the decision to gate return and inspect the airplane, we got to the gate ran the parking checklist and they brought up the Jetway, I exited the airplane to do another walk around and discovered the airplane still covered in ice! When I returned to the Jetway the CA was talking to the station manager, I shared what I had seen on the walk around and returned to the flight deck and re-repaired the aircraft for departure, I was not part of the discussion with the station manager or the Chief Pilot, I was briefed by the CA as to what each had said, and the thing that gets me the most is that the Chief Pilot was making excuses for ZZZ Operations, as they 'don't do it very often'! Come to find out the person spraying our aircraft was the stations de-icing trainer!! After all the decisions and a call to dispatch for a new flight plan we pushed back again ran checklists, got property de-iced ( we think and hope) and departed about two and a half hours late for a uneventful rest of the flight.
ASRS:1788087.s: The flight crew requested full deicing at ZZZ, but the deicing trainer failed to apply fluid and falsely reported completion. The crew discovered the aircraft remained encased in ice during taxi, returned to the gate for a proper inspection and re-deicing, and departed 2.5 hours late.

ASRS:1788092.n: We were being vectored from the northwest to the ILS approach and descending to 2,000 ft. when Tower asked if we had the airport in sight. This was my first time in ZZZ and although I thought I saw the airport I was not in a hurry to call it in sight, just to be sure. I verbalized that with the First Officer but he had been there before and was comfortable calling the airport in sight, so I did. Our initial vector would have taken us just outside the Final Approach Fix. However, when Tower issued clearance for the Visual Approach, the First Officer turned to a heading that would take us inside the Final Approach Fix. At the same time, he continued to descend while configuring with flaps (I think at either 10 or 15) and landing gear, and the speed brake extended. As the descent continued, Tower issued an 'Altitude Alert' and instructed us to adjust immediately. I cannot remember the exact verbiage, but there was a mention of our altitude being 1,200 ft. and perhaps something about 'minimum vectoring altitude.' The First Officer immediately adjusted his attitude to level off at around 1,200 ft. and continued to fly towards the runway center line. We were approximately abeam the Final Approach Fix at this point. He then asked for more flaps, ultimately Flaps 30, for the landing. I realized at about that point that he still had the speed brake extended and told him. He immediately stowed the speed brake and intercepted the visual glide path to the runway. I think he asked me at about that point if I was okay to continue. He was on the glide path and stabilized, so I said 'yes.'On landing rollout I noticed what sounded like an open microphone on the Tower frequency. Since there didn't seem to be any other aircraft on the frequency, I suspected it was coming from our aircraft. The Tower made a broadcast to all stations on the frequency that they were broadcasting on an active ATC radio frequency, and that they should cease immediately. When I made the '80 kts.' call out on landing roll, I heard myself over the radio. That confirmed that the First Officer was holding down the microphone button in his grip on the yoke. As soon as he loosened his grip, the transmission stopped. I was the pilot flying. Based on the weather reported we briefed the RNAV Arrival to be followed by the ILS Approach. We made special note that we were not to utilize the Autothrottle for the approach due to MEL(Minimum Equipment List) restriction. The arrival went as planned until we were given a vector off the arrival and then direct to the Final Approach Fix and a descent to 2,000 ft. As we were a bit high and fast, the speed brake was being utilized to expedite descent. While proceeding to the Final Approach Fix, the weather was acceptable to proceed visually so we reported field in sight and were cleared for the Visual Approach. Due to the high intercept angle to the Final Approach Fix I turned to establish a more acceptable intercept angle to capture the localizer. My perception looking outside was that we were quite high so asked the Pilot Monitoring to set Touchdown Zone Elevation. I failed to engage Vertical Nav for better situational awareness in relation to my vertical path and relied solely on the visual sight picture until on final. While on a dogleg to final we received an ATC Altitude warning alert telling us that we were below the sector altitude. We were approximately 1,100 ft. just abeam of the Final Approach Fix on a dogleg to final. I then stopped the descent until approaching final approach course and engaging Approach mode for glideslope capture. Continued the Visual Approach to a landing.
ASRS:1788092.s: The Pilot Flying and First Officer descended below minimum vectoring altitude during a visual approach at ZZZ due to aggressive descent and failure to engage Vertical Nav. Additionally, the First Officer inadvertently keyed the radio during landing rollout by holding the microphone button on the yoke.

ASRS:1788110.n: Not realizing we were planning dangerous goods I requested pushback and in fact began the pushback without the final manifest.
ASRS:1788110.s: The pilot requested and began pushback without the final manifest, failing to realize the aircraft was carrying dangerous goods. This procedural error occurred because the crew did not verify the cargo status before initiating the pushback.

ASRS:1788176.n: We had been vectored off of the WAZKO1 RNAV Arrival toward the final approach course for the RNAV Runway 4 at ELP. We broke out of the overcast around 9,000 ft. and were approaching KANTR at 7,500 feet. There was a lot of ambient light from the city below and the reflection of that light from the overcast above as well as the fresh layer of snow on the surface. Approach cleared us for the approach and gave us 'Direct KANTR, Maintain 7,200 ft. until KANTR;' which I read back, with an emphasis on the '200'. The FO (PF) selected vertical speed mode after I set 7,200 ft. in the altitude preselector and called '7,200 ft. set!'. The published altitude at KANTR is 7,500 feet, which is located above terrain at 5,851 ft. We leveled at 7,200 ft. and she called for Flaps 18, and we joined the final approach course with the runway, and the terrain below in sight since descending out of 9,000 ft. Just then the GPWS System chimed in with 'Terrain! Pull Up!'. The FO dutifully disconnected the autopilot and I told her NOT to go around, as we were on a published segment of the final approach in good VMC (ELP was reporting 10 SM Vis) and I had the terrain in sight the whole time. We were not descending, and we had been level for some time. We landed without incident and taxied to our gate. Upon docking, I asked Ground for the phone number to the folks at approach control. The fellow who answered offered that he was indeed the Controller. I told him what had happened and he said that it was not at all uncommon, and that 7,200 ft. was their Minimum Vectoring Altitude in that sector. I told him that I would be filing a report with respect to the incident, for his own information.If there are other similar incidents here a communique should be distributed to the pilot group.
ASRS:1788176.s: During an RNAV approach to Runway 4 at ELP, the crew descended to 7,200 ft per ATC clearance, triggering a GPWS "Terrain! Pull Up!" alert despite visual contact with terrain. The controller later confirmed 7,200 ft was the Minimum Vectoring Altitude, and the flight landed safely without incident.

ASRS:1788189.n: After deicing the aircraft we taxied to [Runway] 35L. Upon completion of all of our checklists we requested time on the runway to do a 30 second engine run-up for the A319. [Runway] 35L had just been plowed of snow before our taxi onto the runway. The Captain was the Pilot Flying and began to increase the thrust. At about 55% N1 the airplane began to slide and point away from centerline. The Captain tried to steer the airplane using the tiller with great difficulty. The aircraft rolled forward about 1,000-1,500 ft. I called Tower and notified them that we had a steering problem and requested to exit the runway. We decided to return to the gate to have the aircraft nose wheel inspected. The runway, although recently plowed, played a significant factor in our situation. Also, the recommended 70% N1 engine run-up per our [Operating Manual] is a lot of power to control in icing conditions on the ground. I think that the engine run-up procedure approved by Airbus can lead to very problem when operating on surfaces during icing conditions. After deicing we were cleared to lineup and wait on 35L and to conduct our engine run up. I ran up both engines symmetrically to 70% N1 [following the SOP]. It was then that the right main gear lost traction and the aircraft turned aggressively to the left. I immediately retarded both throttles to idle and used nose wheel steering to regain the centerline. There was nose wheel scrubbing felt. I then cleared the runway and returned to the gate for a maintenance inspection of the nose wheel. The factors were the unprecedented DFW weather. Although the runway was freshly cleaned and we were the first aircraft to use it. There was obviously ice in spots that were hard to see at night. The light takeoff weight of 116,000 lbs coupled with the high power setting for the run up played roles in the incident. Although I had operated two previous flight in and out of DFW that day the runway conditions changed rapidly. I felt that the runway had been freshly cleaned moments before I took to the runway and that it would be suitable for the run up. I will continue to be vigilant in inclement weather conditions. I have gained a newer understanding for the power of the engine on an A319.
ASRS:1788189.s: The crew of an A319 lost directional control during a 70% N1 engine run-up on a recently plowed, icy Runway 35L at night. The aircraft slid off centerline due to hidden ice and high power, requiring a return to the gate for a nose wheel inspection.

ASRS:1788209.n: Significant freezing rain event the day of this flight led to 1/4 to 1/2 inch clear ice covering the entire aircraft. There was no attempt to de-ice the aircraft prior to the crew arriving for preflight. The engine inlets needed to be de-iced prior to block out so that we could start the engines after block out. This de-icing of the inlets took a considerable amount of time due to the significant accumulation of ice in the bottom of the fan section of both engines. By the time we were able to block out (2h 39min late) and taxi to the remote de-ice pad A, a short distance from our ramp, the de-ice trucks had run out of fluid and trucks needed to also be refueled. Another significant delay ensued. Almost an hour after block out, de-icing began. The entire airplane was de-iced with Type I fluid since there was no precipitation falling. Aircraft was fully de-iced and inspected by the de-ice team. We then proceeded to our departure runway and prepared for takeoff. The reason for this safety report became clear as soon as we began the initial climb segment immediately after takeoff. We began shedding ice from the entire fuselage and this shedding continued through 12,000 ft., approximately 7-10 minutes after takeoff. All four crew members could hear the ice departing the aircraft and felt the airframe vibrations as large chunks of ice tumbled down the length of the fuselage. All four crew members each have 20-30 years of aviation experience, and no one had ever experienced anything like it. In my 30 plus years of heavy transport category aircraft operation I have never experienced this kind of ice shedding event. I believe that the de-ice procedure was completely ineffective for this amount of clear ice that covered the entire aircraft. With that amount ice being shed from the aircraft for that long, we had a significant amount of Ice still adhering to the airframe when we took off. The engine vibration was well within limits even during the climb out and so the crew chose to continue the flight. I was concerned about airframe damage from that amount of ice departing the aircraft, and because of that concern, I recorded an AML entry asking that the aircraft be inspected for damage after arrival in ZZZZ. [Cause was] inadequate de-icing for the amount of clear ice that was adhering to the airframe. Also the de-ice crew was possibly unable to see the ice after de-icing, since it was clear ice and fully covering the aircraft, and the airplane was still wet from the de-icing fluid used. [Suggest] re-evaluate the process of de-icing when so much clear ice is adhering to the airframe.
