ASRS:1788209.s: The flight crew reported that inadequate de-icing of significant clear ice on the aircraft led to large ice chunks shedding from the fuselage during climb to 12,000 ft. The pilot attributed this to ineffective procedures for the ice accumulation and requested a post-flight inspection for potential airframe damage.

ASRS:1788228.n: We took off from ZZZ in normal conditions. At approximately 1,600 ft., the pilot flying had problems with the controllability of the aircraft. The PIC took control of the aircraft and confirmed the actual problem - the aircraft was turning left by itself, without any reason. To maintain heading it was necessary to use abnormal force to the right with the aileron controls. The rudder pedals apparently were stuck. To maintain 2,000 ft. that was required, we asked for radar vectors to returned to ZZZ. ATC gave us vectors to downwind for Runway XX and cleared us for visual approach. Speed was 170 kts. We made an early turn to base leg making us too close to Runway XX, so we decided to ask for vectors for an ILS to Runway XX. Vectors were given to us and we performed an ILS, with a safe landing. The conditions with the flight controls were present till our landing. After we left the runway, we stopped and then were followed by the fire truck. When we started to taxi in again, the rudder pedals were apparently with normal deflection, so we continued to the ramp.
ASRS:1788228.s: The crew experienced uncommanded left turns and stuck rudder pedals shortly after takeoff from ZZZ, requiring abnormal aileron force to maintain heading. They returned for a safe ILS landing with the flight control issue persisting until after touchdown, when the rudder pedals reportedly normalized during taxi.

ASRS:1788313.n: Upon completion of work on the aircraft, we boxed up our three pieces of tooling with no HAZMAT to return with us on the first ZZZ1 flight. We attached the SLI (Shipper's Letter of Instructions) labels as required and moved them to the far left of the baggage cart that we were provided. We then moved the three hard containers with visible HAZMAT labels and no return paperwork on them to the far right of the baggage cart. We then took our escort over to the baggage cart and showed her the form and explained to her that the three boxes on the left of the cart with our tools and the SLI labels needed to be sent on the first ZZZ1 flight in the morning, and the three hard containers on the right side of the cart were labeled HAZMAT and needed to be sent through the freight house for HAZMAT shipping. We then asked her if we needed to move the cart to a secure area and she said to leave it where it was. We again, reiterated the importance of making sure the HAZMAT items were not shipped with our tooling, and asked her to make sure and leave a turnover if she was not going to be available in the morning. We still had to scan paperwork to Maintenance Control, and I failed to give her a copy of step 3A after confirmation from Maintenance Control that they received all documents. After going through security in the morning we asked the Operations Agent on the ZZZ1 flight to confirm that our three boxes of tooling and only our three boxes of tooling were on the plane. Due to TSA requirements, we are unable to go down to the ramp to confirm or review shipping procedures once we have been screened.
ASRS:1788313.s: Maintenance personnel instructed a baggage escort to separate non-HAZMAT tooling from HAZMAT containers for the ZZZ1 flight, but failed to provide a required paperwork copy. The crew later confirmed with the Operations Agent that only the tooling was loaded, as TSA restrictions prevented them from verifying ramp procedures personally.

ASRS:1788331.n: We came to land at ZZZ airport, executed ILS Runway XX to approach to it even the weather conditions where completely Visual. Everything was normal, we touched down and begun our landing roll, lowered the nose of the aircraft to the ground, deployed reverse thrust and applied brakes, suddenly master warning illuminated indicating a failure, I was not able to determine the source of the failure at that very moment, I have increased progressively the pressure on the brakes and reverse thrust, aircraft begin to decelerate rapidly and begin to veer slightly to the left side, condition I counteracted with differential braking and thrust reverse power reduction, reached for the steering wheel to continue counteracting the veering tendency and steering wheel was stiff and locked unable to move it, I mention to my First Officer we have lost steering control, continued counteracting with rudder pedal and differential braking, but rudder aerodynamic capability diminish with speed reduction, I mention again to my First Officer that we had lost steering control and felt diminish braking action, airplane slowly overrun into the grass to the left side and lost braking action, I went to and transfer to emergency braking and recover partial control of the aircraft finally stopping on the grass.Executed passenger evacuation checklist to secure aircraft, passengers and crew evacuated through main door, no injury occurred to any one onboard, airplane is in good condition, we called FSS to advise of our incident during landing.
ASRS:1788331.s: The flight crew landed an aircraft at ZZZ airport on Runway XX under visual conditions when a master warning illuminated and nose wheel steering locked. The crew used differential braking and rudder to counteract veering, but the aircraft overran onto the grass before stopping safely with no injuries.

ASRS:1788339.n: As I was setting up cruise at 11,500 ft. I noticed my speed was not what it should be with a bit of a tailwind and the plane was yawing severely to the right. I used a fair amount of left rudder to keep the ball centered for the whole flight. I tried to figure out what could be wrong with the plane to cause this, but could not come up with a plausible explanation. Checked the trim, looked at the flaps, ailerons, elevator where visible and could see nothing. [On a previous flight] there was pretty substantial turbulence and I thought maybe something happened to the rudder that I missed on the preflight. Other than being slow and requiring the constant pressure on the left rudder pedal, the flight was uneventful. Approach cleared me through the Bravo airspace utilizing the west transition to get to the south side of the Bravo airspace. Once clear of Bravo, they terminated VFR Flight Following and I contacted Tower about 10 miles west and indicated inbound for landing with ATIS. I believe Tower had me #2 with a 2 mile final. I had nice stable approach utilizing a fair amount of left rudder to align with the center line at a 90 kt. approach. I crossed the numbers at about 84 kts. and mains touched down at about 76 kts. When the nose gear settled, the aircraft immediately shot straight right off the side of the runway. I worked the left rudder pedal and brake to try and regain control and got the plane back on the runway fairly quickly. Tower asked if I needed assistance and I told them no. I tried to explain what happened but really did not know. Tower said to contact ground. I did so and they said the pilot waiting to depart said my nose wheel was canted 45 degrees to the right as I came by them. That would explain the yaw and the plane shooting off to the right on landing. I contacted a mechanic and he will be looking at the plane to [determine] what the issue is and what it will take to repair that issue. The mechanic said there is a pin on the strut that can break and cause this issue. He said I was very fortunate to have regained control and the nose gear released and was able to track again. He said when that pin breaks, very often the nose gear will not release and allow straight forward movement. I had no idea that this is a not uncommon occurrence with these aircraft. I had googled a description of what happened and got nothing coming up that would explain what the mechanic told me.
ASRS:1788339.s: The pilot experienced severe right yaw and slow cruise speeds due to a broken nose gear strut pin, requiring constant left rudder input. Upon landing, the aircraft veered off the runway but was recovered; ground personnel confirmed the nose wheel was canted 45 degrees right.

ASRS:1788343.n: This airport's rotating beacon is located 1.4 nm NE of the airport, well outside the airport boundary. Though very non-standard, it is not mentioned in the Flight Information Publication (FLIP) or depicted on the IPP plates. Even the Green Bay sectional could show the correct position, instead of the standard symbology which implies the beacon would be found on the airport.Only the Jeppesen instrument charts depict it accurately.This secret non-standard placement could result in disorientation and worse, at least give pilots a chance by publishing it.
ASRS:1788343.s: A pilot reported that an airport's rotating beacon is located 1.4 nm NE of the boundary, a non-standard position omitted from FLIP and IPP plates. The reporter stated this undocumented placement, shown only on Jeppesen charts, could cause pilot disorientation.

ASRS:1788349.n: I was flying with a student practicing approaches. We were flying an ILS approach when we were given a traffic advisory regarding another aircraft. I saw this aircraft from several miles away and kept an eye on it. This aircraft was flying laterally through the approach corridor at altitudes published on the ILS approach we were flying. The aircraft did not deviate from its path and continued towards us. I took controls from my student (then using a view limiting device) when the aircraft was close enough to warrant evasive action, which resulted in a 300 foot climb. I advised approach that I was climbing to avoid the traffic. I looked down and saw the aircraft at the altitude that we had just vacated with little to no lateral separation from where we just were. I believed that this aircraft would see where we were given that I saw them, however this aircraft either did not see us, or did not choose to deviate from their current trajectory despite having seen us. I should have deviated sooner to avoid this aircraft and prevent what ultimately turned into a near miss.
ASRS:1788349.s: A pilot flying an ILS approach with a student took control to climb 300 feet after a traffic advisory, avoiding a near miss with an aircraft crossing the approach corridor at published altitudes. The reporter attributed the incident to the other aircraft's failure to deviate and admitted they should have maneuvered sooner.

ASRS:1788356.n: There are currently no NOTAMs published for N40.Upon landing I see that the runway is not plowed full width, and there are large snow piles on either side of the runway that could result in an impact with low wing aircraft. The taxi way snow piles are high enough that low wing aircraft will strike their wing on them.Also the AWOS-3 has been INOP for at least a year and I've never seen a NOTAM.Someone could easily strike a wing or flap on the snow piles during takeoff or landing and end up in an accident. The problem is caused by the airport management's ongoing failure to publish NOTAMs. N40 has forty (40) separate owners. which may lead to a 'if everyone is in charge, no one is in charge' situation. To prevent this in the future someone needs to tell N40 airport management to keep their NOTAMs up to date. If there are no plans to fix the AWOS then it needs to be removed from the chart.
ASRS:1788356.s: A pilot reported that upon landing at N40, the runway was not fully plowed and high snow piles posed a strike hazard to low-wing aircraft. The pilot attributed the risk to airport management's failure to publish NOTAMs regarding these conditions and an inoperative AWOS-3.

ASRS:1788363.n: There were snow drifts on the taxiway and runway. Due to the snow, upon climb out, pilots side landing gear door would not close completely. I cycled the gear several times to try and clear the snow to allow the gear to close fully. We were unsuccessful getting the gear to close, so I decided to land and see if we could resolve the issue. Feeling the departure airport was unsafe due to the runway conditions, I decided to divert to ZZZ1 to assess the situation. I am familiar with the airport and they have a Tower and other facilities. Roughly 20-30 minutes after ATC gave us our clearance to ZZZ1 (while we were at FL270), there was an explosion like sound and all cabin pressure immediately departed. This blow out knocked off all of our headsets. Understanding that we had a cabin de-presserization, I immediately pulled the power back to idle, dropped the landing gear and nosed the plane over for rapid descent. Once we were going down, I changed our squawk to 7700 (knowing that this was our only form of communication with the outside world), set the autopilot to level off at 12,500 feet and re-engaged the autopilot in case I were to black out. I didn't grab for my oxygen mask because at the time we were already coming down at a rate of over 8,000 ft/min and the wind/cold and just chaotic nature of the cabin, I didn't feel comfortable taking my hands off of the controls. I also didn't go for my headset for similar reasons, as well as there being so much noise, I knew there would be no way for me to hear ATC let alone they be able to hear me. After we were able to level off at 12,500 feet, I looked for the closest airport (ZZZ2), brought up their weather and loaded the approach we wanted and turned to the appropriate heading. I opened the inertial separator, turned on our landing and wigwag lights and decided to leave the gear down for the remainder of the flight. I didn't want to accidentally add any other complications to our situation. After what seemed like the longest approach in history, we finally touched down safely at ZZZ2, where I taxied the plane to the already waiting emergency vehicles.
ASRS:1788363.s: Pilots diverted to ZZZ1 due to snow preventing landing gear door closure, but suffered a sudden cabin depressurization at FL270. The crew executed an emergency descent to 12,500 feet, squawked 7700, and landed safely at ZZZ2 with gear down.

ASRS:1788368.n: Aircraft is non-electrical with no starter, and based at a private airpark home. Aircraft was tied down at tail and triple chocked. Preflighted and prepared for a normal start and flight. Normal start, but as I was walking around wing to the cockpit engine power increased more quickly than expected after start. I was unable to reach the cockpit to shut the engine down before the chocks gave way followed by the tiedown stake pulling out of the ground. Aircraft traveled unoccupied down sloping yard and hit a ditch coming to rest on the taxiway, resulting in landing gear damage and propeller striking ground and pavement and engine shutdown. No injuries or property damage occurred. In retrospect I have always been careful to secure the aircraft for start correctly with triple chocks and tie down. It's possible, on this start, I may not have tightened the throttle friction lock fully which may have allowed the throttle position to travel partially forward after start. The chocks in front of all three tires started to strain, then failed and the aircraft rolled forward as I was moving around the wing. The last available restraint was a tiedown at the tailwheel position. Momentum and some slack in the tie down rope caused the tiedown stake to pull loose from the ground as the slack was taken up. The downhill slope of the yard added to the acceleration before impact with the ditch. I should have double checked the throttle setting and friction lock to make sure that throttle position would not change. The increase in power would not have happened.
ASRS:1788368.s: The pilot of a non-electrical aircraft at a private airpark experienced unexpected power increase after start, likely due to an unsecured throttle friction lock. The aircraft broke free from chocks and a tail tie-down, rolled down a slope, and struck a ditch, causing landing gear and propeller damage with no injuries.

ASRS:1788373.n: I am a CFI and I was flying a training mission with my client who is a licensed private pilot working on transition training to a new model aircraft (Aircraft X). This was my client's first flight in a Aircraft X. The lesson started with a detailed preflight, followed by a similarly detailed run-up. Once ready, we departed Palo Alto Airport for a familiarization flight in a practice area south and west of the airport. During our time in the practice area we maintained visual separation from another aircraft in the training area (each trying to stay in our own section of the training area, while we also maintained appropriate distances from scattered clouds in the area, and staying below the Bravo which starts at 4,000 in that area. During this time, we stayed in contact with the Tower having asked them for advisories during our training mission.After approximately 1 hour of Hobbs time (including the taxi and detailed run-up), we copied ATIS Quebec and informed the Tower that we would like to return to the field for the option, and closed traffic. We were instructed to fly over Stanford and enter the pattern for left traffic for Runway 31. We made our way as instructed and entered the left downwind for Runway 31. The Tower then told us that we were number 4 cleared to land, and that the traffic that we were following was roughly abeam us in the opposite downwind. We acknowledged the instruction and reported negative contact with the traffic to follow. Meanwhile, the Tower was very busy with numerous other traffic entering, leaving, and in the pattern. We were then told to extend our downwind, that we had extensive extensions into Moffett Field's airspace (it is very common for Palo Alto to have and use extensions into Moffett's airspace - this extension was even further than usual) and that the Tower would call our base. While extending, we saw our traffic to follow turn base and then final. But we continued downwind since the Tower said that they would call our base.Moments later, the Tower instructed us to fly 'straight towards the 31 numbers' which was a bit strange since we were so far from the runway (probably at least 3 miles at this point). But the frequency was very busy and it didn't seem to make sense (or even possible) to ask to verify the instruction. We turned left onto a long final and proceeded towards the runway. We were holding approximately 1,000 feet (+/- since my student was flying and this was their first time in the aircraft) this entire time on downwind, base and long final.Not too long after we turned long final, the Tower told us to climb 500 feet immediately for traffic. I immediately took the controls of the plane, quickly (re)checked nearby traffic on the G1000 MFD (with ADS-B traffic) and did a visual scan for traffic as I went full forward on the throttle, prop, and mixture and pitched the nose back for the climb. The quick scan of traffic (visual and ADS-B) did not indicate any traffic below or next to us, but it did indicate one aircraft above our altitude but not in the immediate vicinity. None-the-less, we tried to visually acquire the above traffic as we climbed.Moments later, the tower told us to stop our climb immediately and to turn right and fly directly towards Leslie Salt. Again, we immediately complied with the Tower's instructions as we continued to try to acquire and track any immediate threats visually. Just then, we saw another aircraft pass directly above us, slightly off to our left side, in very close proximity to our aircraft. The Tower then instructed us to make a right turn back to final for landing.I've been flying at PAO for nearly XX years, so I am familiar with how busy it can get. But even with that experience, it was particularly busy at this time. One of the things that I think was a factor in this situation was a partial callsign conflict. Our aircraft callsign ended in [--] while the callsign of another aircraft on frequency at the time ended in [--]. In fact, it is possible that the aircraft above us when we were instructed to climb, and the one that nearly collided with moments later, was the aircraft ending in [--]. My theory is that the instruction to climb was actually intended for Aircraft Y and not Aircraft X, and that the controller tried to stop our climb as soon as he noticed the error. Unfortunately, these problems were all compounded by the heavy radio traffic making it virtually impossible to verify instructions, especially in a timely fashion.My client and I replayed this whole incident both while still in the air, and during debrief on the ground, and we are both quite certain that we responded to our correct callsign and that this wasn't a case of us improperly (and unintentionally) responding to someone else's callsign. I wanted to use the G1000 PLAYback feature to check/verify the radio call, but, unfortunately, the radio traffic was so heavy that there was no way to use the replay feature successfully. I have replayed this entire situation a number of times trying to analyze what I could have / should have done differently to avoid getting this close to another aircraft. Unfortunately, I haven't really come up with a good answer given the details of the situation.Given that the only nearby traffic that I could observe at the time was the one above us, I could have held my attitude of 1,000 feet, in defiance of the Tower Controller's instruction, until I could verify that the climb instruction was for us, or until I could verify another nearby traffic threat. But this seems like a very bad idea. I have always operated that when ATC gives you an immediate traffic avoidance instruction that you follow that instruction immediately. There could have very well been another nearby aircraft that I was unaware of that was an even more of a threat that I was currently unaware of. Hence my immediate response as instructed.I believe that the similar sounding callsigns, heavy radio traffic, and large number of aircraft operating in the class Delta, all contributed to the confusion for all parties. I know that it made our task (mine and my client) much more difficult, and I believe that you could hear that in the voice and instructions of the Tower Controller and the other pilots. After landing, we opted to terminate rather than continue pattern operations. Once back in the flying club, we talked with another CFI and student who was flying (and returning to the airport) at the same time. I asked them if they heard the Tower 'trying kill us' and the CFIs response was 'yeah, the Tower Controller was clearly overwhelmed!' We asked him if he heard any indications that we responded to the wrong callsign. His response was 'no' and that, again, he thought that whole problem was that the Tower Controller was simply overwhelmed by the overall situation.I know that Palo Alto is an FAA Training Tower, and I'm fully understanding and supportive of that. But perhaps in this case maybe there should have been additional oversight of Tower operations, or at least a senior controller stepping in before the controller got too overwhelmed.
ASRS:1788373.s: A CFI and student in Aircraft X experienced a near-miss at Palo Alto Airport while following ATC climb instructions during a busy training pattern. The reporter attributes the incident to controller overload, heavy radio traffic, and similar callsigns, which likely caused the climb clearance intended for another aircraft to be issued to them.

ASRS:1788393.n: Following a flight from ZZZZ to ZZZZ1 arrival at XA:50 local, I parked the aircraft on the north apron and installed all covers for protection.At approximately XF:00 local time, it started snowing lightly around the airport.Upon receiving a message from the passengers to inform me that they would be at the airport at XG:30 local, I went directly to the aircraft to prepare for departure. This involves taking the protection covers away from engines, pitot tubes and static wick dischargers also preforming a check on electrical heated pitot tubes, static sensors and various other checks and tests (pre-flight).The passengers arrived at the aircraft XG:55 local (approx.) and boarded. At this time, it had started snowing more heavily and I instructed [the] FBO to contact company for a Type I de-ice and Type IV anti-ice for the aircraft. The de-icing vehicle arrived shortly after XH:00 (approx.) and I spoke with the de-icing operator and FBO representative for the co-ordination of the de-icing and anti-icing of the aircraft. This involved me explaining exactly which surfaces I wanted to be treated and I showed the de-icing operator a diagram from the aircraft AFM to provide visual explanation.I was informed by the FBO that ZZZZ1 were to close the runway for snow removal from XH:00 - XH:25 local, I therefore requested the de-icing and anti-icing to begin at XH:20 to be finished within a 15-20 mins timescale and to be ready for start and taxi with taking into consideration the 'holdover time' tolerance.I was present on the apron ramp the whole time that the de-icing operator preformed the de-ice and anti-ice procedure and confirm that this was preformed correctly.Once the vehicles and personal had moved away and following a final external visual check of the aircraft, I secured the door from the inside and informed the passengers that we would be on our way shortly.Following a request for start, taxi and departure clearance and after performing all checks and aircraft test required, I started the taxi from the spot on the north apron. This was without event. ATC requested that the aircraft stop and hold short at holding point north apron 1 due to arriving and departing traffic. After a wait at 1 of maybe two minutes, ATC announced that we would not be able to depart, as they were to close the runway for a second snow removal. I informed ATC that we had de-iced and anti-iced, had start, taxi and departure clearance and was able to depart from intersection 1 with 2750 meters available. Cessna performance calculations based upon meteorological conditions at the time of aircraft start showed that 1027 meters was needed to perform and safe departure.After lining up on runway XX and upon receiving ATC clearance for departure, I applied approximately 75% power whilst holding the toe brakes to confirm that the engines were performing correctly following the de-icing and anti-icing. With engine parameters correct, I released the toe brakes, increased power on the engines to take off power (FADEC) and the aircraft started its ground roll. A cross check between the two airspeed indicators (PFD's 1 & 2) at 70 knots confirmed that I could continue the take-off roll. Upon reaching the calculated V1 (91 knots) and VR speed (98 knots), I applied a normal force to the aircraft yoke which moved in the normal manner, but the aircraft did not rotate. A little more the normal force was then used and still the aircraft would not rotate. The aircraft seemed to be 'stuck' to the snow on the runway. A rejected take-off (RTO) was performed without event.A considerable distance was required to stop the aircraft. Once controlled I taxied and exited the aircraft onto taxiway at 2 holding point on the south side. Conversation with ATC informed me that I was to stop and await the fire services who were on their way. Fire services gave the all clear and ATC requested that I was to follow the 'follow me' vehicle to the parking ramp. Once at parking position south side and after all required checks, I shut down the engines and spoke with the fire services about the RTO.Runway XX was now closed as scheduled for a second snow runway removal.I disembarked the passengers and after a visual check of the aircraft to establish if there was any evidence of why the aircraft would not rotate, I re-installed all protection covers and left the aircraft on parking ramp as it was now dark.Upon arrival at the aircraft [the next morning], I completed a thorough visual inspection to establish a possible cause to the rejected take off but could not find anything for explanation.As the anti-icing fluid was covering the aircraft, the aircraft was clean of ice and snow. Following all ground checks and system checks, a normal departure was performed without event.
ASRS:1788393.s: The pilot attempted a takeoff in a Cessna from a snow-covered runway after de-icing but the aircraft failed to rotate, seemingly stuck to the snow, necessitating a rejected takeoff. No mechanical cause was found during subsequent inspections, and the flight departed normally the next morning.

ASRS:1788414.n: I reviewed the weather at approximately XA00 hours, including visibility, winds, and turbulence. When I reviewed this weather, the winds forecast for the ZZZ airport was indicated to be 18-25 knots, and mild turbulence was indicated through both visual and graphical reviews using the ForeFlight products. At 1 1/2 hours later, two passengers and I boarded our SF50 Vision Jet and rechecked the winds at the ZZZ airport. The winds had held steady at the previous levels. We decided that we continue with our planned trip, understanding that the winds were mainly straight down the direction of the runway. We filed for an altitude en-route at 11,000 feet, believing that it would be high enough to prevent any issues that we've encountered on the numerous trips we've flown to ZZZ with respect to turbulence. We've flown over 100 missions into the ZZZ area over the past six months. The takeoff from ZZZ1 was routine and without incident. We climbed up to 11,000 feet without incident and no issues with turbulence. Our issues began when we transferred to the TRACON frequency. Twice during the turbulence, we attempted to review the weather using the GTC 2 system within the aircraft and were having a difficult time stabilizing our inputs with our fingers, even using the bezel to support our hands and use our thumbs to do so was challenging. During one of the larger turbulent events, the autopilot disconnect was engaged by the second pilot in the right seat, which we were immediately able to re-engage as the buttons on the aircraft's autopilot is not electronic but tactile. Once we had the autopilot back engaged, we referred back to the GTC 2 to re-engage the flight plan and selected the approach that was already listed on the display, which was the visual approach to Runway XXL, using the VOR as a descend and entrance point. We had not noticed that the VNAV aspect of the approach had been selected when we re-engaged the auto-pilot, at which point we were now consistently in moderate to severe turbulence. During this period, the TRACON controller called us and simply said 'Why are you descending.' We told them about the visual approach being loaded in and began to describe what our corrective action would be -- however, in that split second, we hit the single most severe turbulence I've ever felt in an aircraft. The turbulence threw the aircraft up, then aggressively left, which then dropped aggressively, throwing everybody to the header of the cabin. My headset (a Bose A20) was broken on the upper hinge, which struck the upper panel and broke loose my supplemental oxygen mask, breaking the clamp. Objects in the cabin flew forward and up. At this point, I immediately placed the aircraft in recovery mode, with full power, level wings and attempted to contact ATC to advise that I needed an emergency descent. In VFR conditions, I noticed that I was over the mountain and switched to [next] frequency, and immediately advised the same and was given the approval to descend to 6,000 feet with a distinct heading. I was then advised other aircraft were experiencing similar issues with turbulence and had gone missed into ZZZ. On the new heading and altitude, I began a full systems check of the aircraft, landing gear cycle, ailerons, flaps and review the fuel system. I advised the TRACON controller that we were fine and that the oxygen masks had been deployed. The controller provided be vectors, then cleared us for the VOR approach into ZZZ. We flew the approach, we decided about three miles from the airport to abandon our approach and return to ZZZ1, in which we were given vectors and an approach back into the ZZZ1 airport without incident. Many things happened on this trip, almost in serial. Without a doubt, the level of forecasted and reported turbulence was well above what we had seen using ForeFlight, or based on our prior experience. When recovering from the several avionics disruptions (auto-pilot switch shut-offs, etc.), we had maintained a fairly vigilant response to restoring our programmed flight activity - until the turbulence began to get violent. In a similar environment, I would ask for a 180-degree turn to remove myself and the aircraft from the events that led to deteriorating events with even lesser conditions. Our corrective action after getting clearance for the emergency descent was sound, but it should have never been necessary if we had more carefully judged the degree of the turbulence, which had caused us not immediately to identify the VNAV programming into the GTC 2. The three of us debriefed the flight in detail, including a review of the ForeFlight products to identify in greater clarity about Airmets (Tango) and how we could set up levels of automation that we could defer in order to maintain more positive control of the aircraft. In reviewing our training materials, we reviewed the SF50 process on how to accept lower levels of automation during events that require higher pilot concentration and how this aids in the better situational awareness in events that we experienced on this date.
ASRS:1788414.s: The pilot and two passengers in an SF50 Vision Jet encountered severe, unforecasted turbulence while attempting a visual approach to ZZZ, causing autopilot disengagement and cabin injuries. The crew executed an emergency descent, diverted back to ZZZ1, and attributed the incident to underestimating turbulence severity and inadvertently activating VNAV.

ASRS:1788429.n: During cruise at FL400, the Pilot Monitoring noted a crack developing across the midpoint of the left windscreen. Approximately 15 seconds later the entirety of the left windscreen outer ply fractured, leading to no forward visibility from the left seat pilot. The Pilot Monitoring initiated the 'cracked windscreen' checklist and followed line items per the LR45 airplane flight manual. Per the manual, a descent was requested to FL250 or below. Upon approval, the crew descended to FL250. Air traffic control was notified of the cracked windscreen. Passengers were made aware of the situation and advised to remain seated and belted. The crew discussed several options and determined that a landing at the intended destination under VFR conditions was the most correct option. Flight controls were transferred to the right seat pilot and pilot monitoring duties were transferred to the left seat pilot. A landing from the right seat was made and the flight concluded with the normal debarcation of passengers on the FBO ramp. As PIC of this flight and performing Pilot Monitoring duties. At approximately XA:45hrs, FL 400, 350 miles SE of VOR. I noticed a brown streak, with bubbles forming through the middle of the left windshield, soon after a loud bang. The outer layer of the windshield shattered resulting in poor visibility from left windshield. The appropriate checklist was completed in accordance with the manufactures QRH. Passengers/cabin were briefed & secured. ATC was notified of the situation and a descent to FL 250 was requested and granted. Weather, NOTAMs and airport conditions at the destination were the most favorable and the decision was made to land there. The landing at ZZZ was uneventful, no assistance for the passengers was required. The Director of Operations and Chief Pilot were immediately notified.
ASRS:1788429.s: During cruise at FL400, the left windscreen outer ply fractured, causing loss of visibility for the left seat pilot. The crew descended to FL250 per the QRH, transferred controls to the right seat, and landed safely at the intended destination.

ASRS:1788436.n: A VFR flight was to be flown from BFL to ZZZ for the purpose of repositioning an aircraft for company business the following day. This flight was operated under Part 91 pursuant to all applicable FAR's and company SOP's. The intended route took the pilot from BFL to ZZZ2 to ZZZZZ to ZZZZZ1 then direct ZZZ at an altitude of 9,500. The pilot obtained a briefing via Foreflight at XA:21 local time for an intended departure time of XA:45. Upon reviewing the briefing, it was decided current conditions would allow for the safe operation of the flight. The pilot departed BFL at XA:45 local time and climbed straight out in VMC conditions to an altitude of 095. Cloud conditions in the valley were broken at various altitudes below 8,000 feet. As the flight progressed towards ZZZ2, the pilot then proceeded direct to ZZZ3. As the pilot approached the ZZZZZ2 intersection, traffic could be viewed on ADSB traveling opposite direction on the V197 (Northwest) at 10,500. This traffic was indicating a ground speed ranging from 50-70 knots confirming the PIC's suspicion of stronger than forecasted winds aloft. As the pilot continued southeast bound, it was apparent that the cloud conditions below and ahead were worsening and the PIC initiated a climb to 11,500 MSL. upon reaching 10,300 MSL just south of ZZZZZ3 intersection, the pilot turned east to avoid building clouds. During this moment, the pilot encountered a 2,000 FPM downdraft which they countered with a pitch up attitude to achieve Vy. Once established at Vy, the rate of descant had slowed to 700 FPM. Knowing conditions improved to the west, the PIC initiated a turn back to BFL and informed ATC of the intentions as well as the conditions. Upon receiving a handoff to BFL Approach, the pilot informed them of their intentions and that it may be necessary to notify ATC. As the ground speed began to drop below 45 knots still in a descent at Vy, the PIC saw a situation where the aircraft would not be able to stay above the cloud layer and safely away from rising terrain to the west. The PIC then informed ATC that they were turning southbound, notified ATC due to weather and squawked 7700. As this decision was made, the PIC was experiencing a severe downdraft where positive control of the aircraft's altitude was difficult to maintain. Upon descending to an altitude of 6,500' MSL, the pilot encountered a large updraft and used this to climb to an altitude of 12;00 MSL which allowed exceptional terrain separation. The pilot flew southbound, where it was visibly better weather and began to request PIREP's from ATC for a VFR field east of the terrain knowing that the area east offered high ceilings and lower terrain. ATC informed the pilot of a large hole in the cloud layer on a 090 heading and suggested the pilot land WJF. ATC then asked the pilot if they were able to accept a 090 heading and it was accepted. The pilot then sighted the large opening, measuring roughly 25-30 nm x. 5 nm and began a decent in VMC conditions. As the pilot descended below the surrounding cloud layer's bases (5,700 feet MSL), they verified ZZZ4 in sight and were given a handoff. Upon assessing the situation, the PIC decided against landing at ZZZ4 and determined an emergency declaration was no longer needed, relayed intentions to ATCT at ZZZ4 and were handed back to Joshua Approach. The declaration was canceled with them and the flight continued to ZZZ1 for a safe landing. Upon landing, the PIC contacted the Director of Safety for the company and informed them of the events that occurred. It was decided that the pilot made appropriate inflight decisions to ensure the maximum safety of flight. Further reviewing the events that took place, the pilot decided to reread the briefing to determine if any significant signs of these conditions were missed. No information was found to be omitted during the PIC's decision to conduct the flight. Numerous other aircraft had flown the same area throughout the day and encountered conditions well within the PIC's comfort, conditions were not reported outside of VFR regulations at departure, or at arrival. The only adverse weather reported was IFR at TSP to the north east of the intended route and winds aloft in that area in excess of 45 Knots. Going forward, the PIC will study material specific to the safe operation of a single engine aircraft over mountainous terrain to better be able to determine when such adverse conditions may be found and what to do differently when they are encountered. An action that could have been utilized by the PIC that was not was to request an IFR clearance east of the position where it encountered the first sign of severe downdrafts and flown via radar vectors to an area that was VMC away from rising terrain.
ASRS:1788436.s: A Part 91 pilot flying a single-engine aircraft VFR from BFL encountered severe downdrafts and worsening clouds while climbing to 11,500 feet, forcing a 7700 emergency declaration. The pilot diverted south, utilized an updraft to regain altitude, and safely landed at ZZZ1 after canceling the emergency.

ASRS:1788464.n: Upon pushback from ZZZ Gate 1, it was soon apparent the Pushback Crew was experiencing a problem. They said nothing but it was increasingly clear the Tug was sliding as well as the aircraft not proceeding in a direction I would expect. I tried asking the Driver if there was a problem but did not receive an answer via wireless headset. When his Tug was starting to jackknife, I decided to use my brakes to stop the aircraft. By this time, the Tug came very close to impacting the aircraft on my side. I later learned that his headset was working, but he was trying to talk to the other Ramp Agents instead and not me. I also believe he was cognitively overwhelmed with the unexpected situation as that same phenomena (not responding to me) continued later when we attempted to another push after re-attaching the tow bar/Tug. The First Officer was also adding his input, which was not helping the situation with communication. It was a communications mess. We called the station to inform them of the situation and eventually a Ramp Supervisor came out and took over. We then discussed the option of attempting to move the aircraft to another part of the ramp where it was known to be less than nil braking. Going back to the same gate would only have been to an area of known poor/nil control. We eventually got to an area where the Ramp Agents could safely walk and feel that the ramp was in better condition and where other aircraft were not experiencing any problems.When I landed approximately an hour prior in a different aircraft, my taxi to Gate 2 took me to an area where I lost all steering and braking control for about five seconds. We immediately notified this on Ops frequency, and at least one other Crew stated they experienced the same. Luckily, we slid to an area where I regained control and then carefully proceeded to the gate when the aircraft performed adequately. I then called Dispatch via my cell phone immediately after block in. He said he would pass it on to the supervisor, but I did not hear any apparent immediate concern. Instead, he said I needed to alert the Station, as it is their job to manage that info (I was really puzzled that our Dispatch gave me that answer). I eventually found the Ops Agent and wanted to make sure the Station had this information, as I was very concerned that others could experience worse.Q1: What does it take for a Pilot to state before any real concern is expressed by those managing our operation? Was poor or nil braking not a big enough concern?Q2: Why had nothing been done to correct the situation or at least alert other Crews that some areas were okay but others were NIL? Or stop the operation?Q3: Why would a Push Crew try to fix this problem without getting any other assistance or guidance? I could see they were guessing and even willing to just leave us there as they told us to try to taxi out of it. They even tried to tow us forward on the re-attempt with our engines running. They were completely overwhelmed, which gave me even greater concern.Q4: As Crews, we have no accurate resources (ZZZ is a joke as it is often old and/or inaccurate) to tell us real time conditions on other parts of the airport other than asking Ground Control (which I did). I was concerned that everything was starting to freeze over, and I did not want to the PIREP stating I was in NIL or off the taxiway later on. Without having routine freezing rain experience, how can I know how quickly conditions can go from good to bad?Q5: What does it take for a pause or stop in our operation? Damage? Injury? Taxiway departure? It seems like we just continue pushing with no apparent oversight. That is not a comforting feeling nor does it give me much confidence our system has mechanisms to protect me before getting in a terrible spot.I would appreciate answers to these questions and would like to know if anyone in Headquarters feels this situation was acceptable or not?
ASRS:1788464.s: The Captain stopped a pushback at ZZZ Gate 1 when the tug jackknifed due to poor ramp braking and communication failures between the crew and ramp agents. A Ramp Supervisor eventually took over, and the aircraft was moved to a safer area after the Captain reported similar braking loss during a prior taxi.

ASRS:1788476.n: Jeppesen plate ILS 5 ORF. Note 3 towards top of page states: Glideslope unusable for coupled approaches below 744 ft. In minimums section box note 1 states: RVR 18 with Flight Director or Autopilot or HUD to DA. How can I use the Autopilot to DA when I'm not allowed to use the autopilot to DA!
ASRS:1788476.s: A pilot reported a contradiction on the Jeppesen ILS 5 ORF plate regarding autopilot use. The chart notes the glideslope is unusable for coupled approaches below 744 ft, yet the minimums section requires the autopilot to reach the decision altitude.

ASRS:1788494.n: We were turning the corner on Taxiway 1 to takeoff on runway XXL, but braking action was nil and the nose gear exited the taxiway.
ASRS:1788494.s: The crew reported that while turning from Taxiway 1 to Runway XXL for takeoff, nil braking action caused the nose gear to exit the taxiway.

ASRS:1788520.n: Pushed away from gate. Started taxing in ZZZ alley when I got a call from #1 Flight Attendant, (FA), that there were First Class, FC, passengers that were not wearing face coverings after being told to wear them by the FAs. Stopped the aircraft and made a very 'To the point' PA that any non-compliance with Flight Attendant instructions, particularly pertaining to facial coverings, would have 'un-favorable' consequences. I had already made it clear that facial coverings were required while on-board during my 'welcome aboard' PA. Conferred with FAs that my second PA was successful, and we continued taxi and takeoff. Once established in cruise, the FAs informed me that they were having problems with FC passengers willfully being non-compliant regarding wearing a facial covering after being advised as such multiple times by at least 2 different FAs. My FAs had even switched working positions in order to try to de-escalate the situation and convince the passengers to comply. I commenced communication with Dispatch and relayed the situation with advisement to contact customer representatives. Shortly thereafter, due not only to non-mask wearing, but also, disruptive behavior by passengers requested to be re-seated in Main Cabin. I further relayed this information to Dispatch. It was at this point the FAs gave the notification of passenger misconduct warning. Shortly thereafter passenger started harassing my FAs with constant cornering them in the FC galley and demanding trivial items. At this point, even after a tremendous amount of patience, de-escalation attempts and warnings by the FAs, and with building harassment and aggressiveness being demonstrated by passengers, I notified Dispatch that we would be diverting to ZZZ1. We landed at ZZZ1 non-eventfully, without being overweight and without declaring an emergency. Passengers were removed from the aircraft. We departed ZZZ1 and arrived in ZZZZ uneventfully. Please allow me to acknowledge my FAs for their display of 'Consummate Professionalism' during this flight. They were tireless in their attempts to de-escalate the situation in hopes of precluding a diversion. I would also like to acknowledge the support of Dispatch and company as reflective of the number of communications that were made prior to our diversion. And last, but certainly not least, I would like to acknowledge the expert airmanship demonstrated by my First Officer during our extremely busy diversion as well as throughout the rest of a very long day. Should you need additional information from me regarding this diversion, please don't hesitate to contact me.
ASRS:1788520.s: The Captain diverted the aircraft to ZZZ1 during cruise due to First Class passengers refusing to wear face coverings and harassing Flight Attendants despite multiple warnings. The disruptive passengers were removed at ZZZ1, allowing the flight to continue to ZZZZ without declaring an emergency.

ASRS:1788524.n: On approach into MCO, the Captain identified a drone off our port side as we were landing [Runway] 18R. I was the pilot flying, had no visual on the drone, but was advised of it.
ASRS:1788524.s: The Captain identified a drone on the port side during the approach to Runway 18R at MCO. The pilot flying had no visual contact with the drone but was advised of its presence by the Captain.

ASRS:1788525.n: A321 TOGA (takeoff/go-around switch) takeoff with APU on. Pouring rain. While climbing through approx 18,000 ft, first one, then other flight attendants called to say they smelled a burning rubber smell in cabin but could not see smoke. Passengers were also complaining. We smelled deice fluid in cockpit (plane had flown from ZZZ1 to ZZZ), but otherwise we kept talking with them to see if it would dissipate. While still discussing a return to ZZZ, first one, then two passengers had trouble breathing and the flight attendants made a PA for a doctor on board. At this point we felt we needed to return to ZZZ for an overweight landing. We notified and coordinated with ATC, Dispatch, and ZZZ OPS to return and have paramedics at the gate. The cause was unknown, but aircraft did have an MEL for avionics cooling extract fan that required it to remain in override. Perhaps this could have contributed to burning smell or a different load on air conditioning. The Captain (CA) and I noticed a smell in the flight deck while in the climb, roughly around 10,000 feet. The FAs (flight attendants) called climbing through flight level 180 stating they smell an odor in the cabin. The FAs also stated some passengers were complaining about the odor. The Captain requested the flight attendants to call back in 10 minutes and state if the smell is dissipating. The FAs call back shortly stating several passengers are having difficulty breathing. At that time the Captain made the decision to return to the ZZZ. I took over as Pilot Flying and ATC communications. I requested to return to the ZZZ and notified ATC for an overweight landing. At that time the aircraft weighed roughly 180,000 lbs. The CA took over Pilot Flying on the arrival shortly before joining the approach to runway. The aircraft weighed approximately 177,000 lbs on landing. When we arrived at the gate paramedics attended to several passengers who were having difficulties breathing. [Possible cause or related issue], we were relatively heavy, had a slight tailwind and the runway was wet. The TPS (takeoff performance system) called for config 2, TOGO, APU OFF. As a measure of safety the CA decided to leave the APU and APU bleeds on. I concurred. The aircraft's extract fan was also MEL'd (MEL 21-05a). The CA and I both felt the odor mostly resembled anti-icing fluid. Though we also discussed the possibly the inoperative extract fan or the APU usage on takeoff was the cause of the odor. But mostly we thought it was anti-icing fluid. Once we realized passengers and the cabin crew were being affected the decision was made to return to ZZZ which resulted in an overweight landing.
ASRS:1788525.s: The crew of an A321 returning to ZZZ due to a burning odor and passenger breathing difficulties during climb. The cause was suspected to be anti-icing fluid, potentially exacerbated by an MEL'd extract fan and APU usage, resulting in an overweight landing and paramedic attendance.

ASRS:1788532.n: At 800 feet AGL, clicked autopilot off for a visual landing. At 500 ft., FO called 'Stable, cleared to land Runway XX Center.' I replied 'Landing.' Between 500 and 400 feet AGL tried to make small lateral correction with aileron but aileron movement was limited. Used a touch of rudder for correction. Clicked autopilot button again and crossed checked then confirmed that 'Flight Director' was displayed in PFD. Landed uneventfully but elevator movement was very heavy in flare. After landing at taxi speed, I tried to move the yoke left and right and there was very limited movement. The First Officer tried as well with the same result. We checked the Flight Control and Hydraulic Displays and both were normal.I considered a go-around but quickly [determined] a go around would be extremely difficult with big power changes and limited flight control capability. The flight path was set up to touch down in the landing zone on speed so I elected to land.Unsure what caused the flight controls to be limited. After landing, I debriefed Maintenance in the cockpit and put a detailed write up in the logbook.
ASRS:1788532.s: The Captain and First Officer experienced limited aileron and heavy elevator control during the final approach and flare of a visual landing. Despite normal hydraulic displays, they elected to land rather than go around due to restricted flight control capability, later reporting the issue to maintenance.

ASRS:1788543.n: On initial climbout of ZZZ off Runway XXC we experienced loss of power shortly after passing 400 feet and received the 'Landing gear' aural warning. I double checked the gear handle and verified gear position, then verified N1 rollback, momentarily thinking we had dual engine failure. FO exclaimed startle, I replied 'fly the plane'. FO disconnected auto throttle, brought the thrust back up to takeoff position. We momentarily lost altitude and airspeed as Startle and surprise delayed our recognition slightly. Timing of the event was before flap retraction so we were near flap over speed during recognition and recovery, I said 'watch the speed pitch up pitch up' until flaps were retracted. FO later indicated his flight director was not giving correct indications for phase of flight. FO was able to recognize and manually control the aircraft, resuming normal climb out. Once the aircraft was under control, auto pilot and auto throttle engaged normally and no further anomalies were experienced.Unknown, weather was stormy, with moderate turbulence and lightning flashes in vicinity, in full IMC.We teach hand on thrust levers at all times during arrival and landing phase, but not during takeoff...had the FO had physical contact with the thrust levers during the climb, the AT retarding would have been instantly detected. I recommend the same procedure is taught for takeoff as is for landing...one hand on the thrust levers. After checking everything was normal we lined up on runway XXC in ZZZ. We verified our automation was in the correct mode including TO, ROLL, and FLCH were verified on our FMA as well as the crosshair flight director was up. As I advanced thrust the auto throttles took and the captain confirmed that ATTCS armed and we had normal TO thrust. at 80 knots while verifying the speed I saw the AT were in their normal HOLD mode. At this point everything was completely normal. When I went to rotate and was transitioning in the instruments I noticed that the FD had switched during the roll to the diamond mode which is supposed to happen at 1000'AGL. (Latter the captain confirmed that there's was normal). I had a normal rotation and pitched towards a normal takeoff attitude disregarding the flight director. At approximately 400 AGL the auto throttles commanded idle thrust suddenly. The startle and surprise nature of this took a second to process where we lost approximately 50 feet. At this point I disconnected the auto throttles and set climb power. The automation was still not working correctly including the flight director. Once we climbed through sterile we turned on the auto-throttles and they worked throughout the flight but we watched them very carefully and called Maintenance writing up the experience on the ground. The cause is unknown. before Takeoff we both verified we were in the correct automation modes. Once in cruise flight we verified all out take-off date and departure limits were set correctly and they were. Contributing factors to the loss of altitude was the thunderstorms in the vicinity, night, and moderate turbulence. More effective startle and surprise training in the sims. We are taught to keep both hands on the yoke throughout departure I think at 400 feet though 10,000 we should be guarding the thrust levers like we do on approach to landing.
ASRS:1788543.s: During initial climbout from ZZZ, the crew experienced an uncommanded auto-throttle rollback to idle at 400 feet AGL, causing a 50-foot altitude loss due to startle and surprise. The cause was unknown, though the pilot attributed the delay in recovery to a lack of hand-on-thrust-lever training during takeoff.

ASRS:1788578.n: I was landing Runway XX at ZZZ. It was a normal centerline approach to landing. As I touched down, the nose gear seemed to touch before it should have, as if the nose gear strut was in an extended rather than a normal (compressed) position. Within moments of touchdown, the aircraft darted quickly to the left of Runway XX, I lost directional control of the aircraft. The aircraft came to an abrupt stop at the side of the runway. No one was injured in this incident.
ASRS:1788578.s: The pilot reported that during landing on Runway XX at ZZZ, the nose gear appeared extended, causing the aircraft to dart left and lose directional control immediately after touchdown. The aircraft stopped abruptly at the runway side with no injuries.

ASRS:1788598.n: We were cleared for takeoff on Runway 31C very close after a B737. He was given a left turn on departure of 250, we were given a left turn to 220. We were given a subsequent level off of 2,000 ft. As we turned left, we encountered significant wake turbulence, which rolled us quickly to 45-50 degrees of bank. We recovered, and reported the incident. We feel the entire event could have been avoided with different takeoff instructions (earlier turn, or different headings).
ASRS:1788598.s: The crew encountered significant wake turbulence from a preceding B737 shortly after takeoff on Runway 31C while turning left to 220 degrees. The aircraft rolled to 45-50 degrees of bank before recovery, which the pilot attributed to insufficient separation or delayed turn instructions.

ASRS:1788601.n: After detailed pre-flight inspection according to manufacturer checklist, we noticed that both fuel tanks are full, samples from each fuel sump and sump under the engine are clear, we checked the color - blue color for 100LL, there was no water or other contaminants, oil level was in the operational limits for our airplane, and we decided that airplane is in the condition to make a safe flight. After listening the ATIS and getting all necessary information about the airport, we contacted Clearance Delivery requesting VFR Flight to NW (northwest) to our practice area, and after that Ground Control for taxi instruction.We completed the runup at the runup area next to Runway XX, as instructed by Ground Control, following every step on the checklist. During the runup we didn't find any issues with the airplane, magneto check was within the manufacturer limits, oil pressure and temperature were ''in green', engine was working and responding normally like any other day. After completing runup, and agreeing that there is nothing wrong with the airplane, we decided to proceed with our flight. After contacting Tower, we departed NW to practice area. Student was flying the airplane and I was monitoring his and the airplane's performance. During takeoff roll we checked engine instruments, everything was normal, and we continued with liftoff and climb. When we arrived at [the] practice area we practiced Steep turns, S-Turns over the road, and turns around the point. During the time from takeoff, climb and during maneuvers, the engine was performing normally as well, without any issues. Once we completed the maneuvers we decided to go back to our airport. After gettingATIS information, [student] contacted the Tower and requested a full stop landing on Runway XY. We were told to proceed directly to the Airport.At that moment we were at around 1,700-1,800 feet and decided to slowly start our descent. Around 20-30 seconds after that we experienced engine roughness, loss of power and the airplane started shaking, and we started losing altitude. I took over the controls from [student] to try to troubleshoot and to find out what exactly could cause the airplane to behave like that. After checking the fuel selector (BOTH), mixture position (FULL RICH), carburetor heat (ON), primer (IN AND LOCKED) and ignition (BOTH), and noticing that everything is in position for normal operation, I started reducing the power to see how airplane will behave. With less power, shaking was reduced, but still present, and altitude losing was increased. After that I advanced power to maximum to see how the airplane will respond, but rough running increased again, shaking increased, and altitude loss was reduced but still present.At that moment we were at around 1,300-1,400 feet and descending, and I decided to contact the Tower again and to try to explain our situation. Tower asked me if we can come back, and after finding out that we are constantly descending regardless of our power setting, I acknowledge them that we are unable to do so. I decided to [follow] the [the] Expressway, to stay away from busy streets and populated areas, and to try to at least maintain the present altitude which was at that moment around 900 feet. They cleared us to land at any runway at any airport around, but not being able to maintain altitude using different power settings, I knew that we were not going to make a safe landing at any airport around, because we were getting too low, and airports were 8-10 NM far from us. At that moment we were at around 700 feet and descending, when I told the Tower that we will probably land somewhere around the Expressway. Having the populated area and narrow streets on our left side, [marsh] on our right side, and low altitude, I decided the best option will be to land on Highway, which, we were lucky, was not too busy. Having the wind from [the south] and traffic flow towards it, landing in the southbound lane was the best choice I could make at that moment. We touched down in the middle lane, and immediately started moving the airplane to the right side so traffic can keep moving. After noticing that we landed safely, without any injuries and damage to other persons and property, we secured and exited the airplane.
ASRS:1788601.s: A pilot and student experienced engine roughness and power loss at 1,700 feet while returning to the airport after VFR maneuvers. Unable to maintain altitude, the pilot executed a forced landing on a highway, resulting in no injuries or property damage.

ASRS:1788602.n: During cruise, a smoke smell was detected. We attempted to trace the smell and quickly found smoke to be coming out of the foot wells. We proceeded to descend to the nearest airport where we found oil spattered inside of the cowling. The local Mechanic traced the leak to the oil filter which was installed by a different Mechanic who we contracted for a pre-buy. The Mechanic in question had used a pair of pliers to torque the oil filter, punching a small hole in the exterior which started leaking in flight and dripping on the heater, creating the smoke. The local Mechanic fixed our issue with a new oil filter and we proceeded to our destination the following day.
ASRS:1788602.s: During cruise, pilots detected smoke from foot wells caused by an oil leak from a filter damaged by pliers during a pre-buy inspection. The crew descended to the nearest airport, where a local mechanic replaced the filter, allowing the flight to continue the next day.

ASRS:1788606.n: While descending on the CLASH Arrival just prior to EVRLY we encountered a wake turbulence event 2x in short succession with roll deviation. Autopilot disconnected, was immediately reconnected by the Captain (PF). He disconnected VNAV and initiated Vertical Speed mode to reset our descent path to be slightly above the previous aircraft path, to prevent a third event. About this time, ATC offered us a runway change from 35R to 35L, additionally they requested us to slow to 210 kts. The Captain went to reprogram the FMS for Runway 35L, I was confirming the Captain inputs at this time. The aircraft was still in Vert Speed rather than VNAV, neither of us noticed this and we descended below the STAR required altitude and did not slow to 210 kts. as directed. A query from ATC as to our speed brought us back to reviewing our flight path, at which point we leveled off and reduced speed. ATC made no further comments as to our flight path deviation and at that point broke us off from the STAR with a vector to intercept the LOC. No loss of ATC separation was reported to us.
ASRS:1788606.s: The flight crew encountered wake turbulence while descending on the CLASH Arrival, causing autopilot disconnect and a mode change to Vertical Speed. This led to an unintentional descent below the STAR altitude and failure to slow to 210 kts until ATC queried their speed, after which they leveled off and were vectored to the localizer.

ASRS:1788632.n: Stores dropped DG (dangerous goods) paperwork to manifest without the freight. The Cargo team refused to manifest as the freight was not present. I received from the Store Supervisor that the team failed to manifest the shipment. I explain to him that we need to be able to check the DG label, checklist prior to manifesting.
ASRS:1788632.s: Stores personnel dropped dangerous goods paperwork without the freight, causing the Cargo team to refuse manifesting. The reporter explained to the Store Supervisor that DG labels and checklists must be verified before manifesting.

ASRS:1788633.n: I was the wing walker. As we were pushing back we noticed two aircraft coming on to the taxiway from another gate area. We got clearance and were already into the push. We passed the vehicle service road and the taxiing aircraft were getting closer. I told our driver to stop. We had wireless headsets, luckily. I tried to get the taxiing aircraft to stop by giving the stop signal with my lighted wands. I walked to the back of our aircraft to see if it would be too close and possibly hit our tail. I told our driver to start pulling back toward the gate. About 20 feet. when we got back to the gate after push was completed we found out the tower had made a mistake. We got clearance from the tower to push. We were just passed the vehicle service road when there were two aircraft taxiing around the corner. Our wing walker gave the aircraft the stop signal and he did not slow. Luckily, we had wireless headsets and the pushback driver was told to stop. As the taxiing aircraft got closer the wing walker told the pushback driver to then start backing up or the taxiing aircraft could clip our tail. I called to inform them and they said the tower admitted it was their fault.
ASRS:1788633.s: The wing walker stopped a pushback and reversed the aircraft after two taxiing planes approached too closely due to a tower clearance error. The wing walker used lighted wands and wireless headsets to coordinate the stop and backup, preventing a tail strike.

ASRS:1788734.n: Once the aircraft door was opened and only a few passengers from first class deplaned, the cleaners were trying to come on. We asked them to wait just a bit, as we had 4 wheelchairs, and our first-class cabin was still getting off. The cleaners told us they are instructed to get on right away. The Captain said No, they needed to wait till most of the aircraft had deplaned. A few of the cleaners were still trying to argue with us, even after the Captain had said they had to wait. There are no quick turns, as our cleaning procedures during this pandemic are totally opposite of the term quick turn. This also is dangerous for the passengers and crew. There is no room for cleaners in the galleys or in the aisle as we safety try to deplaned using the company's policy of social distance, and deplaning a few rows at a time.In addition, the cleaners are getting in the way of the flight crew full filing our FARs responsibilities and safety obligations, post cabin sweeps. This is a safety hazard and needs to be addressed immediately.
ASRS:1788734.s: During post-flight deplaning, cleaners attempted to board immediately despite the Captain's instruction to wait for wheelchair passengers and social distancing procedures. The crew reported this created a safety hazard by obstructing aisles and interfering with mandatory cabin sweep obligations.

ASRS:1788735.n: Before boarding. They [Deice Crew] deiced the plane. Air Packs were open and fumes blew into cabin. Back to front. We waited in gate area for 25 minutes until fumes were somewhat dissipated. Then we boarded passengers. I had a sore throat and cough. During flight and at home.
ASRS:1788735.s: Cabin crew reported that open air packs allowed deicing fumes to enter the cabin before boarding, causing a 25-minute delay. The reporter subsequently experienced a sore throat and cough during the flight and at home.

ASRS:1788747.n: I was enroute to ILM. As I began my descent into the Wilmington terminal area the ATIS and Approach Controller indicated ILS Runway 06Z was the approach in use. Weather was reported as 400 overcast and one mile visibility. Winds 030 degrees at 4 knots. A cold front and convective activity was approaching the airport and I requested a short vector to final. I was cleared for the approach and began my descent. I ended up too high on the approach and executed a missed approach at minimums. As I was being vectored back for another approach I was advised that the aircraft following me also executed a missed approach due to being too high. I looked at the wind vector on my PFD and realized that I had a 50 knot tailwind at 1,500 feet on my last approach. I advised the Controller about the strong winds at altitude and asked if Runway 6 was still the best runway.I also asked the Controller if he had any real time winds on the ground and was reminded that the Tower was closed, he would try to get me an update from the automatic reporting system. I was told that the automatic reporting system still indicated winds out of the NE (northeast) at 11 knots. I continued for a second approach but at 700 feet AGL my wind vector was showing a 50 knot tailwind and my groundspeed confirmed that. I deemed it unsafe to land and executed another missed approach.The Controller suggested ZZZ as an alternate. I began vectors to an approach to RNAV GPS Runway XX. I quickly realized that I would have the same 50 knot tailwind situation at ZZZ and began questioning the Controller about any real time wind information on the ground. He said the only info he had still indicated winds on the ground were out of the NE about 7 knot. He said the convective activity situation at Wilmington was improving and asked if I would like to go back for another approach. I was beginning vectors to another ILS Approach 06Z. I was still seeing the same 50 knot winds at altitude and began doubting the wind reports on the ground. I asked for an approach to Runway 24. I was cleared for the RNAV approach 24. As I was descending on final approach, I had a 50 knot head wind at 1,000 feet.When I reached minimums and began to go visual, I encountered a windshear. I increased power to MCT (Max Continuous Thrust) trying to climb out, but to no avail. As I was continuing to recover from the windshear, my landing gear contacted a treetop about 1/4 mile from the runway. At this point I deemed the safest course of action was to continue to land. I made a normal landing to a full stop, turned off the runway and taxied to the FBO. After exiting the airplane minor damage was noted. At this point the winds on the ground had shifted to the SW (southwest)) and were gusting to 35 kts indicating to me that I had landed during frontal passage.The biggest contributing factor to safety I noted, was the lack of any real time winds on the ground. If I had real time wind data from the Controller as I was conducting my approach, I would have been advised of the wind shift occurring, and might have been able to take preventive action before I encountered the windshear. My recommendation is to not have a system that solely relies on the automatic reporting system which is not real time. I would have each Approach Control have the ability to see and give real time winds just as an operating Tower would have.
ASRS:1788747.s: The pilot encountered a 50-knot tailwind and windshear during an ILS approach to Runway 06Z at ILM due to a frontal passage and lack of real-time ground wind data. The aircraft struck a treetop during recovery but landed safely with minor damage, prompting a recommendation for improved wind reporting.

ASRS:1788772.n: Climbing to FL390, at FL385 the Master Warning light flickered. It finally showed 'LOW OIL PRESSURE #2'. Engine was shutdown in accordance with the checklist. We notified ZZZ Center and we were cleared direct ZZZ1. Having departed ZZZ1 20 minutes earlier and with the Midwest in the midst of a snow storm we chose to return to ZZZ1 because we were familiar with the airport and it's current weather and surface conditions. After a slow descent and completion of all checklists we were a mere 60 from ZZZ1. An uneventful landing was accomplished.
ASRS:1788772.s: During climb to FL390, a flickering Master Warning indicated low oil pressure on engine #2, prompting an engine shutdown. The crew returned to ZZZ1 due to a snowstorm and landed uneventfully after a slow descent.

ASRS:1788776.n: I received the second dose of my Pfizer vaccine for COVID-19 yesterday at XA:00 AM. I was not feeling any immediate effects of the dose and had a flight lesson scheduled XE:00 AM and felt fine. It wasn't until this morning I was chatting with a mentor of mine and they had mentioned there being a 48 hour period of restriction for any flying for those that did receive the vaccine. I did some research of my own and found that this was indeed true. I did not feel like I was putting myself or my instructor in any immediate danger and could still perform my duties as a student pilot. Upon discovering the restriction, I scheduled my other lesson for after the 48 hours have passed.
ASRS:1788776.s: A student pilot received a second Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine and initially scheduled a flight lesson unaware of the 48-hour flying restriction. Upon learning of the rule from a mentor, the pilot rescheduled the lesson to occur after the restriction period ended.

ASRS:1788803.n: I believe this aircraft had been parked due to COVID. Apparently, when pulled out of parking, the FMS database was not updated. During pre-flight we noticed that revision 'W' and 'X' were available, but revision 'Y' was now current. I don't know how long this plane has flown without 'Y' database, but it is deferred now.
ASRS:1788803.s: The pilot reported that an aircraft parked during COVID was operated with an outdated FMS database, missing current revision 'Y' while revisions 'W' and 'X' were available. The issue was identified during pre-flight and is now deferred.

ASRS:1788804.n: We were in clear air above our altitude of FL410. we encountered unexpected continuous moderate turbulence and were unable to maintain altitude. We rapidly lost 1,000 feet of altitude.
ASRS:1788804.s: The crew encountered unexpected continuous moderate turbulence in clear air above FL410. This caused an inability to maintain altitude, resulting in a rapid loss of 1,000 feet.

ASRS:1788808.n: On approach to ZZZ gear was selected down but normal gear indications did not appear and there were no associated noises such as gear extending into slipstream, etc. PF (Pilot Flying) executed a missed approach and while being vectored we tried to lower the gear normally with the same indications and we got the L/G Gear Not Down locked ECAM. Accomplishing ECAM led us to the L/G Gravity Extension QRH and after accomplishing checklist the gear safely extended. We (advised ATC) and coordinated with Flight Attendants and Dispatch and ZZZ for subsequent runway closure and tow to the gate.
ASRS:1788808.s: During approach to ZZZ, the crew encountered a landing gear extension failure with no normal indications or extension noises. After executing a missed approach and performing the gravity extension checklist, the gear extended safely, leading to a runway closure and tow to the gate.

ASRS:1788859.n: Upon arrival at ZZZ Maintenance notified us that there were multiple damaged fan blades in the number 1 engine. While we do not know when or how this occurred, we can only guess that it was due to snow/ice ingestion on takeoff roll, improper de-icing and inspection of engine inlets prior to engine start, or de-icing prior to takeoff. While there was no active precipitation, upon arrival at the aircraft, the crew noted snow and ice on the aircraft to include in the engine inlets. Per [company] procedures, after the doors were closed, before blockout, the crew call Ramp to have engines cleared. The clearing crew showed up. The Tug Driver noted them moving around the aircraft and appeared to be clearing engines. They left shortly thereafter, and we confirmed with Ramp Tower that the clearing and inspection had been logged complete. After push back onto taxi, we noted that the taxi lane had not been completely plowed. There was a large snow berm, approximately 2 ft. high about 10 ft. left of centerline, which converged toward centerline all the way until Taxiway XX. After some discussion with Tower and the Pushback Crew, we opted to have plows come and clear an area in front of us, that they could pull us to clear of the berm before engine start to avoid ingestion. Engine start was slow, even for Pratt & Whitney, but no starter or engine limitations were exceeded. N1 started around 20-25%, well below the 40% limit. After engine start anti-ice was turned on due to temp/dew point spread. We taxied on cleared pavement to the de-ice area. The taxi took less than 15 minutes so no engine clearing was used. During de-ice we noticed B777 push back out of a gate on [taxiway XX]. It was pushed back through a berm of snow and ice. After de-ice we taxied and took off after this B777. It is possible that the B777 had some snow/ice on its trucks that was deposited on the runway on takeoff. From de-ice, we taxied to Runway XX.
