The turn from Taxiway XY onto Taxiway XZ could have been cleared of snow better, but the turn was made using minimal thrust. It is possible that some compact snow or ice was ingested here, however, once cleared for takeoff, we did a 30 second engine clearing procedure and all engine instruments appeared normal. After takeoff, the Captain mentioned a rumble, which sounded like it was coming from a pack. It was faint enough, that we didn't feel it was an issue, as all packs checked out normal. Later on climb out the number 3 engine EVM fluctuated up to 5.0, then back down to normal ranges only slightly above the other two engines. The captain sent a message to [Operations} asking about engine telemetry, and we were advised it was good, so we decided to press on.
ASRS:1788859.s: The crew reported multiple damaged fan blades in engine 1, likely caused by snow or ice ingestion during taxi or takeoff despite pre-flight clearing and engine checks. Although an EVM fluctuation occurred on engine 3 during climb, operations continued after confirming telemetry was normal.

ASRS:1788897.n: On approach, hitting sterile cockpit an unusual odor described by many crew members of dirty socks, feet, filled the cabin for the remainder of our flight as we landed. As I was sitting in my flight attendant jump seat a rancid like smell filled the forward galley, I then spoke to the Lead Flight Attendant who noticed it as well. After the detection I called the back to ask if the odor was in the back as well. The entire cabin smelt of dirty socks. As for the cause we are not sure. After informing the Captain during approach, I was then informed on why it smelt after all passengers were in the process of deplaning. He informed me it was due to the ozone layer. After the detection of the smell, I informed the lead as well as contacting 4 doors confirm if they are smelling it as well. The Lead then informed the pilots about the smell. The aroma of dirty socks, may typically be the notice of engine oil vapors seeping in. Which is usually known as 'bleed air'. If at high enough concentration flight crew as well as passengers can grow ill.
ASRS:1788897.s: A flight attendant reported a "dirty socks" odor filling the cabin during approach and landing, which the Captain attributed to the ozone layer after deplaning. The reporter noted this smell often indicates engine oil vapors from bleed air, which can cause illness at high concentrations.

ASRS:1788900.n: I take what happened seriously and will see that it does not occur ever again in the future, but please bear with me as I explain what led up to the event with a backstory. I have recently started letting my hair grow out and - up until recently - had not needed the use of hair spray. On the flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 I stepped into the forward lavatory and saw that it needed grooming. For the first time ever, after never having to use hairspray while on the airplane in my 32-plus years of flying, I retrieved my hairspray and returned to the lavatory. As I began grooming my hair with the hair spray I do not know if I had failed to recall or was simply unaware that there was the potential for that type of product to set off a lavatory smoke detector. Within a couple of seconds the alarm activated and it was then that I immediately recognized my mistake. I stepped out of the lavatory and quickly called the Captain who was also calling me. He told me the smoke alarm indicator lit up and I explained the situation to his satisfaction. I then pressed the reset button and the alarm ceased. Again, this was a first and one time incident and I will be more attentive and aware of my actions and conduct in the future so as to avoid repeating this mistake. I will review the section on hazardous materials in my Inflight Manual and, if necessary, add this event to my briefings to illustrate what can happen when one is not continuously vigilant of proper conduct on the aircraft.
ASRS:1788900.s: A flight attendant on a ZZZ to ZZZ1 flight triggered the forward lavatory smoke detector by using hairspray. The attendant immediately informed the Captain, reset the alarm, and acknowledged the error caused by unawareness of the product's potential to activate the sensor.

ASRS:1788914.n: It happened when we were doing 45 degree maneuver to enter the left downwind at OBE. We did radio call twice when we were maneuvering. While we were almost at downwind, there was another aircraft using his high speed to bypass my left side. I had to do the 360 degree to avoid it.
ASRS:1788914.s: The pilot reported that while executing a 45-degree maneuver to enter the left downwind at OBE, another aircraft bypassed their left side at high speed. The pilot performed a 360-degree turn to avoid the conflict after making two radio calls during the maneuver.

ASRS:1788927.n: We were transitioning in VFR conditions on the ZZZZZ3 arrival to the GPS approach to XXR. We loaded the approach into the FMS and set bottom attitude for the approach. I was in right seat flying and CA was in the left who is a CE510s rated pilot also. I was off auto pilot and hand flying with a different flight director display than normally used. The issue was when engaged the appr mode on flight director while still in Vnav instead of waiting until the GPS switched to LPV mode just outside of the final approach fix. The controller advised us that we had descended below the minimum vectoring altitude for that segment of the approach. The clear message here was that better crew coordination was needed.
ASRS:1788927.s: The pilot flying engaged the flight director approach mode while in VNAV before the GPS switched to LPV, causing the aircraft to descend below minimum vectoring altitude during the ZZZZZ3 arrival. The controller advised of the deviation, and the crew attributed the incident to a lack of coordination.

ASRS:1788934.n: The aircraft was on a normal approach to land at ZZZ RWY XX. During the final approach, the aircraft was within standards: the airspeed and glide path were stable, and the aircraft was aligned with the runway's extended centerline. Idle power was set about 20ft AGL causing the plane to touch down firmly on the main landing gears. This was followed by a slight bounce which caused the aircraft to lift approx 3ft off the ground. Following the bounce, I maintained aft elevator/yoke pressure to prevent the nose gear from impacting the ground first. The main landing gears then contacted the ground smoothly after this correction. As the airspeed decreased and the nose contacted the runway, I immediately felt a strong vibration from the nose followed by the nose continuing to fall to an abnormally nose-low attitude where I could see the runway directly. Seeing this happen, I immediately shut down the engine. Once the aircraft came to rest, I secured the rest of the cockpit. After exiting the plane, I was informed by the airport operations staff that they had retrieved the nose gear from somewhere on the runway (they did not specify where they found it). ZZZ Tower then closed the runway and airport for operations until both the runway and aircraft were secured. I do not believe any human performance considerations negatively affected this incident. As the events unfolded, I performed to the best of my ability to ensure that I was safe while also ensuring that the aircraft was not damaged further. while this incident ended safely, it has definitely inspired me to further my proficiency. I will focus on modules that will improve my knowledge on maintaining stabilized approaches, ADM, and preventing and recovering from bounced landings. As a flight instructor, I hope to use this experience as a lesson to any future students.
ASRS:1788934.s: The pilot executed a firm landing with a subsequent bounce on final approach to ZZZ RWY XX, resulting in the nose gear collapsing upon touchdown. The aircraft came to rest with the nose gear detached on the runway, prompting an immediate airport closure for recovery operations.

ASRS:1788937.n: During a training flight in the local traffic pattern the student pilot reported that he was unable to retard the throttle. I took control of the aircraft and too found that the throttle would not retard lower than approximately 2300 RPM. I contacted ATC, [received priority], and was able to slow the plane by leaning the mixture. Landing was uneventful but the engine stopped prior to being able to clear the active runway and required tow.
ASRS:1788937.s: During a training flight in the traffic pattern, the student pilot and instructor found the throttle stuck above 2300 RPM. After receiving priority from ATC and slowing the aircraft by leaning the mixture, they landed safely, but the engine stopped before clearing the runway, requiring a tow.

ASRS:1788939.n: After takeoff at ZZZ RW XXL, and at approximately 500 feet AGL, a slight haze was noticed in the cockpit by the flight crew. A few seconds later, the passengers also noticed this in cabin area of airplane. It was then we observed a slight pungent order typical of smoke. At this time we observed a 'baggage fire' alert on the crew alert system. Operating as a crew, we [advised ATC] at this time and made a downwind turn in the airport pattern for runway XXL. With the appropriate checklist for the indicated condition complete, we were cleared to land on runway XXL. The smoke that was observed previously had now dissipated we and turned base to final and made normal landing on runway XXL. After exiting runway XXL at intersection X, we shutdown the aircraft and executed an emergency evacuation using the appropriate checklist. Upon observation after landing no condition of heat, smoke or fire were observed. Internal engine component suspected problem. ASRS:1788939.s: The flight crew reported a haze, smoke odor, and baggage fire alert at 500 feet AGL after takeoff from ZZZ RW XXL. They returned for a normal landing, evacuated the aircraft, and suspected an internal engine component problem, though no fire or heat was found post-landing.

ASRS:1788941.n: We were flying from ZZZ to ZZZ1.We were at FL410 and given a descent to FL350. I was the PF and after the PM acknowledged the altitude and set it in the ALT selector I initiated a 1000fpm descent in vertical speed mode. At approximately 40,500 feet the aircraft pitch over 60-70 degrees and accelerated from Mach .80 to Mach .90+ in a matter of a few seconds. I turned off the auto throttles and pulled the throttles to idle while simultaneously canceling the auto pilot then extended the speed brakes. We were descending at such a high rate I had difficulty pulling back on the yoke, but was able to pull it back stopping out descent around 36,000 feet and after pulling back the aircraft climbed to almost 43,000 feet before I able to arrest the ascent and bleed our airspeed off. This entire event took place in the space of about 10-15 seconds. After bleeding the speed off and regain control of the aircraft I started our decent once again by hand and flew it down to a lower requested altitude. We were sure that our flight guidance computer was to blame and had it replaced. We were flying from ZZZ to ZZZ1.We were at FL410 and given a descent to FL350. I was the PM and after the PFrequested the altitude change and set it in the ALT selector I initiated a descent of 1000 fpm in vertical speed mode. At approximately 40,500 feet the aircraft pitch was over 55-70 degrees and accelerated from Mach .80 to Mach .90+ in few seconds. the PF turned off the auto throttles and he's pulled the throttles to idle and simultaneously canceling the autopilot then extended the speed brakes. We were descending at such a high rate the PF had difficulty pulling back on the yoke, but he was able to pull it back stopping the descent at around 36,000 feet and after pulling back the aircraft climbed to almost 43,000 feet before the PF was able to arrest the ascent and bleed our airspeed off. This entire event took place in the space. After bleeding the speed off and regain control of the aircraft the PF started the decent by hand and flew it down to a lower requested altitude. We were sure that our flight guidance computer was to blame and had it replaced.
ASRS:1788941.s: During a descent from FL410 to FL350, the aircraft pitched down 60-70 degrees and accelerated to Mach 0.90+ due to a suspected flight guidance computer failure. The pilots disengaged automation, manually arrested the dive at 36,000 feet, and replaced the faulty computer.

ASRS:1788955.n: This safety concern occurred on two flights. Same aircraft and same exact routing and runways for departure (7L) and arrival (24R). The routing was the 7L.KEENS2.MESSI ESTWD.HLYWD1.24R. The First Officer briefed all of the points, speeds, and altitudes on the SID via the FMC CDU and I confirmed them on my EFB. We completed the Before Start Origination checklist, received performance takeoff data, and completed the Before Push checklist with no issues. After pushback and engine start, we started to taxi away and when I placed the LEGS Page up on my CDU there was now a discontinuity after the first departure point, and the next point. We corrected the situation by re-selecting the SID, transition, and departure Runway 7L, which removed the discontinuity. That situation by itself would be a little unusual, but as we flew back later on and the same issue occurred yet again it appears that there is a performance software issue that needs to be looked at. The Cost Index was 15 on Flight X and 5 on Flight Y. I unfortunately did not reference the FMC software version. We had no discontinuity on our flight, so the issue could be departure related, the SID related, or performance software related. Bottom line is that there is an issue that might cause pilots to take off and soon afterward encounter a discontinuity on the route, causing a potential navigation error.Flight Ops needs to work with Dispatch and Maintenance to determine if certain weights, Cost Indexes, FMC software versions, SIDS, airports, etc, are causing a discontinuity after receiving performance takeoff data in this fleet or solely this particular aircraft.
ASRS:1788955.s: Pilots on two flights of the same aircraft encountered FMC route discontinuities after engine start while using the KEENS2 SID from Runway 7L. The reporter suspects a performance software issue linked to Cost Index or specific SIDs that could cause navigation errors if not resolved by Flight Ops, Dispatch, and Maintenance.

ASRS:1788957.n: Aircraft X was uneventful leading up to the approach at ZZZ. We had been cleared for the approach to Runway XX and were established on the localizer and glideslope. The autopilot and autothrust had been disengaged earlier in the approach and the aircraft had been configured to Flaps 3 when Gear Down was requested. When the gear lever was selected down the three indicators on the landing gear panel indicated red UNLK (UNLOCKED), no noise from the landing gear doors opening was heard. Captain [Name] and I communicated and confirmed on the Landing Gear Systems page that the landing gear had not extended. We decided to level out at 6,000 feet MSL while we confirmed the situation and attempted to cycle the gear. We communicated to the tower we would be going around for a landing gear failure approximately 3mi prior to the runway. Tower provided vectors and a climb to 9,000 feet, we initiated a go around over the threshold per ATC instructions and cleaned up the aircraft per SOP. The autoflight was re-engaged after the go around. During this time after the failure of subsequent attempts to cycle the gear and with the lever still down, we eventually got the L/G GEAR NOT DOWNLOCKED ECAM. The ECAM was run according to SOP by Captain [Name] while I flew the aircraft and handled radio calls. We [received priority], stated our intention to return to land on Runway XYR and requested CFR (Crash Fire Rescue Equipment). Gravity extension was successful and we were vectored to the approach. Approach and landing were normal with the exception of the gear doors remaining open. We landed with 8000 lbs. of fuel. We stopped on the runway and Operations was standing by to tow the aircraft back to the gate.
ASRS:1788957.s: The crew of Aircraft X experienced a landing gear failure during the approach to Runway XX, indicated by red UNLK lights and no gear extension. After a go-around and successful gravity extension, they landed safely on Runway XYR with open gear doors and were towed to the gate.

ASRS:1789040.n: We were on a Part 91 ferry flight. On climb out we noticed the ground idle annunciation light was illuminated which we concluded was not normal as the ground idle is on a squat switch and shouldn't be on in flight. We further discussed other system items which would possibly cause the issue. In addition we noticed that the takeoff V speeds were still showing on the airspeed indicator which should have been cleared out after takeoff. ATC cleared us up to FL390 and we were crossing our first fix. We tried cycling the ground idle switch during this time and were in the mid teens. The ground idle annunciation remained illuminated. Shortly after this the Captain noticed that our cabin was not pressurizing, as the cabin altitude was not increasing nor was the cabin rate increasing. He selected the cabin rate knob to high to try and get the cabin to pressurize. Shortly after, the cabin rate immediately went to approximately 6,000 fpm. He said lets get our oxygen masks on. We put them on and at this time we were at approximately FL220. Suddenly the master warning illuminated along with a cabin decompression annunciation. He disconnected the autopilot and leveled off and said lets advise ATC. I advised ATC and requested a return to our origin. ATC gave us a descent to 10,000 ft. with direct to the airport. Once we accomplished memory items for cabin decompression and emergency descent we ran the emergency checklist and returned with no further issues. I believe we handled the situation appropriately by advising ATC and going to a lower altitude and returning to our origin airport. Once we reached 10,000 ft. the cabin decompression annunciation extinguished and we landed with no further issues.
ASRS:1789040.s: During a Part 91 ferry flight climb, the crew observed a ground idle light and un-cleared V speeds before experiencing a cabin pressurization failure at FL220. The pilots donned oxygen masks, declared an emergency, and descended to 10,000 ft to return to the origin airport, landing safely after the decompression warning extinguished.

ASRS:1789048.n: After rotation PF (pilot flying) had difficulty turning left to HDG 330, I thought he was rusty. Had him hand fly to about FL180. When we put the auto pilot on we had the AP LWD Caution msg. We ran the QRH and noticed the aileron trim did not respond or move. ACARS Dispatch and they mentioned deferring the aileron trim. I then noticed the Aileron Trim circuit breaker was popped. I attempted to contact Dispatch through AIRINC prior to ZZZ. Dispatch could not hear me. We advised ATC for flight control malfunction. Test items ran no brace I briefed the passengers I did not have the go through planned diversion with passengers. I was very surprised that Dispatch had a known bad headset. She knowingly continued to act as a Dispatcher with a bad headset. I could not hear her on AIRINC and when I called on the phone I could not hear her. She said she knew it was bad and they needed a new one. If I knowingly operated an airplane with a bad headset I'd be in major trouble.
ASRS:1789048.s: The Pilot Flying experienced left turn difficulty and an AP LWD caution due to a popped aileron trim circuit breaker. The crew diverted after Dispatch failed to communicate via AIRINC because of a known defective headset, which the dispatcher admitted to using.

ASRS:1789080.n: We were given a NOTOC (NOtice TO Captain) with 2- 1.4S packages [explosives] and 1 lithium ion battery as COMAT (company materials). In order to be fully aware of what we were carrying I called Cargo OPS. The gentleman who helped me out to go over it realized that no two dangerous goods could go in one compartment and ask me to have the lithium battery removed. I requested the Crew Chief to accomplish the above request and was told that it was good and I should go. His goal was to be on time, and although I can understand his pressure, safety is our priority at all times. I asked to get it removed and was told that they have been sending airplanes like this in the previous days with no issues and I should just push. I stated that what other flights have done, is not a matter of discussion regarding this flight, and that per Cargo OPS, HAZMAT it needed to be removed otherwise I would not be pushing until it was accomplished. I was told that they were going to call the Chief Pilot on me. I'm not sure if that was a tool of intimidation or not but I told them to please have them call me. A few minutes later I received the call from Chief Pilot. I explained the situation and understood what was happening. At one point the Crew Chief wanted to place both 1.4S packages on the aft cargo which I told him not to do so. Eventually they removed the 1.4S cargo from the fwd cargo leaving the lithium ion battery on the fwd cargo and one package of the 1.4S on the aft. We departed and operated safely to ZZZ1. [Caused by] rushing to comply with departure times and not listening to what our priority is: Safety. I suggest training for our colleagues so their main focus is open communications for a safe environment so we can have a safer operation.
ASRS:1789080.s: The Captain refused to depart with improperly segregated dangerous goods after Cargo OPS advised removing a lithium battery from a compartment containing explosives. Despite pressure from the Crew Chief to prioritize on-time performance, the battery was eventually removed, allowing the flight to operate safely.

ASRS:1789104.n: We had to reopen the Main Cabin Door and the jetbridge had to be pulled back to the plane due to a change in the release requiring more fuel. I'm unsure as to how the door was missed, as I thought we had pushed on it and checked it the second time we locked it and the flight attendant even said she gave it a pull after we locked it. However, on takeoff I heard a loud bang coming from behind me and I stayed focused on my takeoff. I'm not certain at what time the captain reclosed the door, but in cruise he did mention that he had to unlock the lock in order to re latch it and lock it. My memory serves that the door was locked when we did the checklist.We had flap gap seals damaged on the aircraft on initial walk around. Maintenance came out and was irritated at the captain for writing it up. I offered a printed flap aerodynamic seal inspection task given to me from previous A&P's to help him find a quick solution as that is what previous mechanics have used for write ups for the same seals . (I typically run into these particular seals being damaged at least once per trip). He got angry at me and told me its not my place to offer help. After putting an CDL on the plane that required a lower altitude on the release due to a performance hit he sent a message saying we were released at Time. We didn't actually receive the release until around Time. The mechanic had either forgotten or based on his demeanor intentionally delayed the flight to get under our skin. After being released, we did the before start checklist again and caught that the fuel needed to be added due to the new release. We waited again for fuel and a gate agent to come. Ultimately we were delayed about 51 minutes which likely played a role.My personal adjustment to this is to make sure I push on the door every time I read the below the line before start checklist as I believe the lights on the door lock corresponded to it being locked.
ASRS:1789104.s: The pilot reported a main cabin door unlatching during takeoff and a 51-minute delay caused by a mechanic's refusal to assist with flap seal damage and delayed release. The door was later re-latched in cruise, while the delay resulted from the need to add fuel after the revised release.

ASRS:1789111.n: While on final approach the PF was having difficulty slowing the aircraft and continuing the descent. The headwind we had been fighting quickly turned to a crosswind. The PF elected to re-bug and use flaps 40 well above 1,000 feet. As the PF I selected the new flap setting in the FMC and verbally called out the Vref and target speeds. As we were slowing past our previous target speed the PF called for flaps 40. We had no amber band visible for flaps 40 placard speed, so I verified the placard, 162 knots, and selected the flaps seeing 158 knots and slowing on my tape. As I verified the speed brake was armed he again called for 40. The flaps were still at 30. At this point we were now below 1,000 feet but above 500 feet. We discussed the non-movement and load alleviation. As the PM, I suggested, pitch up and slow, the flaps moved to 40 as we suspected they would. The checklist was completed and we were able to be stable by 500 feet AGL, so we continued the landing. We did not observe any limitations being exceeded on the flaps or in procedure as the PM was able to manage the approach prior to the 500 foot gate.In discussing this event during our debrief we believe that we did meet our approach gate criteria. We were in our first 'heavy' approach in many months as the flight was full. The weight may have contributed. The wind was also a contributing factor as it shifted down the final enough that by the time we departed the traffic flow had reversed.Neither of us were averse to going around but it did not seem necessary in the moment as it seemed we met our criteria to continue. Having said that I'm certain eyes further from the instrument panel may have captured data we missed but I believe we trapped and corrected the situation. While on final approach I, PF, called for final landing flap (flaps 40) and flaps did not move to commanded position (they were at 30), despite being slower than max speed for flaps 40. Since we were within a few knots of max flaps 40 speed, I slowed further and flaps extended to commanded position. I believe the flap extension occurred right around 500 feet. The final approach speed was within stabilized approach criteria and the outcome of the approach and landing were not in doubt. Landing was uneventful.We have been flying mostly empty airplanes for almost a year and this flight was almost completely full. I believe the higher landing weight coupled with a significant loss of headwind on final contributed to the airplane taking a while to slow down to an acceptable speed for final flaps. When I called for final flaps, we were 3-4 knots below the max flaps speed and I believe the aircraft's safety system was restricting flap movement until I was a little slower. As we return to Pre-COVID passenger loads, I will have to adjust lead time for decelerating the jet. Today was a good reminder.
ASRS:1789111.s: During a heavy final approach with shifting winds, the PF and PM experienced delayed flap extension to 40 due to load alleviation near the speed limit. The crew stabilized the aircraft by slowing further below 500 feet AGL, allowing a safe landing without exceeding limitations.

ASRS:1789169.s: No safety report narrative was provided to summarize. Consequently, no details regarding personnel, aircraft, flight phase, events, or causes can be reported.

ASRS:1789180.n: The Number 2 and 4 Flight Attendants (FA) called to report strong odor in aft galley. I continued boarding while the Number 1 FA went in to speak with the Captain. She returned and said we were to continue boarding. I could hear the aft FAs calling Captain while we stood in entry area. The Number 1 would go in to cockpit to get updates from the calls. A deadheading pilot then came from the back of plane and went to the cockpit to speak with the Captain. There was some question about it being a urine smell and perhaps the cleaning of the lavs. We had neared the end and I walked through closing bins, etc. As I got to row 25 I smelled a very strong and pungent dirty sock smell. I went to aft galley and told them it was a dirty sock smell and where I began smelling it. I asked them to relay that info up front. The Number 2 and 4 wanted the Captain to come and smell because they disagreed with that assertion. I had returned to the front of aircraft and the Number 1 and Captain went to the back. When he returned he seemed perturbed that the Number 1 was not immediately behind him and wanted to close up. I said I would close the remaining overhead bins. The Number 1 returned and we departed. First, I believe we should have stopped boarding and deplaned the passengers and crew until the cause/type/potency of odor could be established. Following the operating procedures for deplaning at the gate would have allowed a quicker review of the situation and the concerns for safety until a definitive answer could be established while removing passengers and crew from a potentially harmful exposure. We commenced the boarding and Flight Attendant #2 and I walked to aft galley and both smelled a noxious odor. I called the Flight Attendant 1, three times and she in turn told the Captain. He said 'it is probably a leaky trash bag or rotten food.' Flight Attendant 2 called the Captain directly and he again blew us off. We had a deadheading pilot also go to cockpit to relay information and when he got back, he said the 'theory is that it is a leaky trash bag'. We had been on the aircraft for 4 hours prior to this event as we brought the aircraft in from ZZZ. The fumes were coming out of air vents in galley and aft lavs and was going into c zone. 33 minutes after we first notified Captain, at the end of boarding, he came to the back and said 'I don't smell anything, we are going to ZZZ1'. With that, he turned and walked back to the front. Yes, the fumes had just dissipated by that point, 33 minutes later. There was no interaction, NONE. He obviously did not care about the noxious fumes in the aft section of aircraft. For 33 minutes, he continued to disregard every attempt to tell him what was happening in the back. He's a Check Airman, really? He's supposed to be the best of the best. I felt like my safety was jeopardized and I would never feel safe flying with him again. What if I reported smoke, would he say it is stale cigarette smell on someone's shirt? The one important bit of information he might need might come from the most junior Flight Attendant or even a new hire. In this case he had 4 very senior Flight Attendants and disregarded all of us when we made 5 attempts to get his help in telling him about the noxious odors. Captain obviously needs some intense CRM training. Maybe giving a check ride to another pilot and trying to manage fume events are just too much for him. It obviously was.
ASRS:1789180.s: During boarding, flight attendants reported a strong noxious odor from galley vents to the Captain, who dismissed their concerns as trash or food and refused to deplane passengers. The Captain ignored five attempts to address the fumes, which dissipated after 33 minutes, leading the reporter to conclude the Captain's poor CRM jeopardized safety.

ASRS:1789199.n: Aircraft X was an air return back into ZZZ, for the standby display cool fan malfunction causing the display screens to overheat. This aircraft was ferrying to ZZZ1 for a repair. During troubleshooting it was decided that the problem could be relays K7HK and K11HK in JB2. The relays were replaced per the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) CH24/ESPM (Electrical Standard Practices Manual) and did not fix the problem. The next likely part was the avionics cooling control panel, it was replaced per AMM CH21 and did fix the problem. Because I had removed JB2, a retest had to be performed per the AMM CH24. The first half of this complex task was done in the hangar. The second half requires the engines to be ran. Everything was checking out good per the AMM, until the final engine start. During the start sequence on the LH (Left Hand) engine everything seemed to be normal, then I received an APU Overtemp red warning message which distracted me from watching the LH engine parameters. After the APU Overtemp message cleared I noticed the LH engine ITT (Interstage Turbine Temperature) at 998 degrees. I immediately put the LH thrust lever to fuel cutoff and motored the engine until the ITT was below 120 degrees. The MDC (Maintenance Diagnostic Computer) engine exceedance history showed the LH engine to be at 1110 degrees for 10.6 seconds. This is the first time I have ever encountered 2 overtemp events or 2 red warning indications at the same time while working one of our aircraft. I was working hard to get this task done so the crew could move the aircraft yet that day, as they were standing by in the hangar to depart after repairs were completed. I must admit I did feel pressured and hurried, however I did complete the retest task per the AMM, with everything checking satisfactory. As for the engine hot start event, I really regret it happening. It seems like it was one of those situations that does not occur together all that often. I felt I was distracted and was task overloaded for maybe a second or two which played a factor in this unfortunate event.
ASRS:1789199.s: A mechanic performing an avionics cooling retest on Aircraft X experienced a left engine hot start reaching 1110°C. The event occurred when an APU overtemp warning distracted the mechanic from monitoring engine parameters, causing a delayed fuel cutoff due to task overload.

ASRS:1789215.n: On initial approach to TRM I was announcing the arrival quite often and very diligently, in a descent of approximately 1,600 feet per minute another plane was observed on the ADS-B and was in sight. I continued the descent to fly well under the plane which was obviously VFR and as I approached the plane it turned into me with a sharp turn. The TCAS had a TA but not an RA as I had descended well below the other plane. The other plane must not have been monitoring the UNICOM or monitoring their traffic ADS-B.I realize now that I should have changed course at an earlier time, to give a much wider birth to the crossing plane. Also, I can not take into account other pilots listening to the CTAF or UNICOM frequency for area traffic. In addition, as I approached the airport to fly over and enter a left downwind, another plane was spotted that had just flown over the field with no announcements. VFR traffic in this area are not listening or announcing their intentions in the airport environment.
ASRS:1789215.s: A pilot on initial approach to TRM descended at 1,600 feet per minute and received a TCAS TA when a VFR aircraft turned sharply toward them. The reporter attributed the near-miss to the other pilot failing to monitor UNICOM or announce intentions, noting a second unannounced aircraft was also observed near the airport.

ASRS:1789247.n: We were practicing touch and go's and at the last landing we tried to brake the aircraft and I felt that the left brake was not working. I communicated to the Tower that I could not turn to the left so they cleared me to turn to the right. I cleared the runway on taxiway Alpha and I tried to stop the aircraft but we couldn't and we did the full stop at the grass. We didn't hit any light or nothing to be considered damaged. Airport operations went to the place and they saw that everything was good.
ASRS:1789247.s: During touch-and-go practice, the pilot reported a left brake failure and was cleared by Tower to turn right onto Taxiway Alpha. The aircraft could not stop on the taxiway and came to a full stop on the grass, but no damage occurred and airport operations confirmed the aircraft was intact.

ASRS:1789251.n: We departed ZZZ on DATE at approximately Time LCL with two charter pax. All preflight checks were normal. We were fully topped off with fuel. As we were climbing through 26,000 ft I noticed that the number 2 oil temperature gauge was rising. I alerted the first officer (NAME) to consult the checklist and prepare for a possible engine fire or failure. There is no guidance in the checklist so we were left to use other resources such as each other, prior experience and MX techs in ZZZ1 through conversation via flight phone. We brought the number 2 engine back to idle power and noticed a brief reduction in oil temp. Within a minute or two the oil temperature gauge was at red line where it remained for the rest of the flight. We leveled off early at 33,000 ft. and made contact with Maintenance in ZZZ2. With the number 2 engine at idle we were able to maintain altitude at a speed of .68 Mach which was sufficient to troubleshoot the issue. I transferred control of the aircraft to the first officer and spoke with NAME1 (Maintenance tech). During the phone call we tried to find other indications that would lead us to confirm that the indication is accurate or erroneous. We did notice that the oil pressure did start to rise into the yellow arc when we advanced the power lever. However this could have been normal or unrelated. We took an SPR (snapshot) of the engine settings. We also reset the Oil 2 circuit breaker which isolates the oil 2 gauge for temp and pressure. The indication was as before... a red line temperature situation. We decided the best course of action was to shutdown the engine and divert to ZZZ3 as a landing could be made safely. Our Maintenance tech agreed. Given that a more serious condition could occur, such as an engine fire, failure or an engine damage/separation event we the crew elected to shutdown the number two engine and divert to ZZZ3. We performed the engine shutdown procedure then, due to the fact we were over Max landing gross weight and would require priority handling and would be landing at a high elevation airport without one of our three engines... I elected to declare an emergency. I declared with ZZZ center at 33,000 ft. and they gave us direct ZZZ3 and began our descent. We advised approach that we would require extended vectors to run through the applicable checklists and burn fuel for a safe approach climb in the event of a two engine go around. And to land below Max landing weight. The appropriate checklists were performed as a crew and the a visual approach and landing was executed uneventfully.We taxied to flight support where we shut down and began our company reporting process.
ASRS:1789251.s: The flight crew diverted to ZZZ3 after the number 2 engine oil temperature reached red line during climb, despite troubleshooting attempts. They declared an emergency to manage high landing weight and safely landed with the engine shut down.

ASRS:1789259.n: After startup sequence exhibiting, as has been the case since last annual inspection, moderate engine skips at low RPM between 1000 and 1200 RPM, performed uneventful VFR flight from ZZZZ to ZZZZ1 and parked.Approximately 30 minutes later, taxied for Runway XX and run-up was similarly nominal. After being cleared for takeoff, initial climb exhibited a few engine misses and while continuing to gain altitude, called ATC with a request to land due to engine issue, possibly related to spark plug fouling.Received clearance to land on any runway, and chose to perform a 80/260 reversal of course right-hand (due to terrain) and established on final 06. With reduced power, engine was shaking as if a cylinder was not operating, a FADEC caution illuminated, and landing was calm and uneventful.Requested to perform a run-up, on the western taxiway, which was unsuccessful, then requested taxi back to apron and the assistance of a mechanic.
ASRS:1789259.s: The pilot experienced moderate engine skips and a FADEC caution during climb after takeoff, likely due to spark plug fouling. After landing safely on Runway 06, a subsequent run-up failed, requiring mechanic assistance.

ASRS:1789276.n: My student and I were conducting a dual pattern flight at ZZZ. We were cleared for the option number 2 for Runway XX. Number 1 was on final and number 3 was student pilot solo who was behind us in the downwind after going around after his first landing attempt. We turned based and then to final being number 1. On about a 3/4-mile final from the runway, the student pilot solo turned base and then proceeded to turn final right in front of us, and slightly below us. My best guess is that he thought he was following number 1 and that he was number 2. At best glance, they were probably 400 feet in front of us, and 200 feet below us on final. I took flight controls, queried Tower and initiated a go around left side. The student landed and was given a phone number to copy down. After we completed our lesson a few laps around the pattern later and taxied off the runway, Tower asked if we were okay with the go around. It was certainly a little close for comfort, but we had enough space to recognize the threat and execute a go around. Was the 2nd solo flight in my pilot career. I had arrived back into ZZZ traffic pattern into Runway XX. While on downwind, I was cleared by Tower as number 3 and cleared to land on Runway XX. I had identified the traffic in front of me as number 2 without any doubt. I followed that traffic and landed safely. Once I called up ground, I was notified that I had cut off the actual number 2 traffic and that traffic was forced to go around. In reality, I had incorrectly identified the number 1 traffic as number 2 and failed to see any other traffic making me believe I had the correct number 2 in sight.When I am in a congested pattern like ZZZ, I will use my multi function flight display map page and make sure there are no planes I have failed to identify. I will also start counting out traffic to make sure I have accounted for all of them.
ASRS:1789276.s: A student pilot solo misidentified traffic in the ZZZ pattern, turning final 400 feet ahead and 200 feet below the dual-instruction aircraft, forcing the latter to execute a go-around. The student attributed the near-miss to incorrectly identifying the lead aircraft as number two instead of number one.

ASRS:1789278.n: Training flight for a student who needed a 90 day solo endorsement. After doing maneuvers, I gave him a partial power loss and he decided to divert to ZZZ about 10 NM from our position. I had already checked NOTAMs and we got AWOS information twice on the way. Student announced every couple miles where we were and that we were inbound with a simulated loss of power for a straight in on Runway XX. I saw when we were about 2 NM away that the runway looked good but some of the taxiways were snowy and told my student we were not doing a full stop so we planned for a touch and go with a go-around possibility. About 1 NM away I saw a snowplow working on the taxiways. As we were in the flare, I saw the snowplow turning towards the runway. I put the flaps up and my student added power and as we climbed over the runway the snowplow turned onto the approach end of Runway XY and in our direction, we flew over the plow about 100-200 feet overhead.I believe the weather may have contributed as it was hazy on the ground, we could clearly see things on the ground but the haze may have affected the ability of the plow to see us.I think we could have made a safer decision to only do a low approach.I mostly think the situation would have not been an issue if there was any communication from the airport. There was no mention of work being done or the runway being closed in either NOTAMs or the AWOS, nor did the plow ever say anything on CTAF about their intentions. We were broadcasting our location and intentions regularly but heard no one else. We did a double check and volume was good, frequency was correct.
ASRS:1789278.s: During a student training flight with a simulated power loss, the crew executed a go-around after a snowplow entered the runway approach end. The reporter attributed the near-miss to hazy conditions and a lack of communication regarding the plow's presence on NOTAMs, AWOS, or CTAF.

ASRS:1789312.n: During flight testing of an experimental, retractable gear aircraft, the landing gear failed to extend. The failure was first noted at 2,500 feet AGL while configuring for landing stalls. The left main gear failed to lock down, as noted by the left main gear indicator light remaining red. The gear would retract normally. Several attempts at extension were made, including during pitch and yaw, to no avail. Manual extension of the gear was attempted following POH (Pilots Operating Handbook) checklist procedures, but the manual pump handle would not move. The decision was made, as recommended by the POH emergency procedure, to land with all gear retracted. The aircraft returned to the airport of origin, which also had a grass runway. Landing was made with full flaps at stall speed, and slid about 250 feet in the grass before stopping. There were no injuries to the single occupant of the aircraft.
ASRS:1789312.s: During flight testing of an experimental retractable gear aircraft, the left main gear failed to lock down at 2,500 feet AGL, and manual extension attempts were unsuccessful. The pilot executed a belly landing on a grass runway as recommended by the POH, resulting in no injuries to the single occupant.

ASRS:1789315.n: After departure from ZZZ on a southern heading, climbed to 8,500 feet with flight following to ZZZ1. After transitioning to cruise at 8,500 feet I realized my manifold pressure readings were significantly below expected (mid-20 in while expecting 30+). I informed Approach about turning back to ZZZ. The landing was uneventful. After rolling off the runway I was able to reproduce the lack of full power when opening the full throttle.
ASRS:1789315.s: The pilot reported low manifold pressure readings during cruise at 8,500 feet after departing ZZZ. The aircraft returned to ZZZ for an uneventful landing, where the pilot confirmed the inability to achieve full power with full throttle.

ASRS:1789323.n: ATC had assigned us an earlier timed descent to FL290 requiring a 2,000 FPM descent. Pilot Flying selected Vertical Speed mode to meet the descent. Prior to leveling, ATC revised the clearance to descent via the RNAV Arrival and delete the speeds. Both pilots confirmed the bottom altitude of the arrival at 13,000 feet, but failed to confirm the descent mode was in VNAV. Pilot Flying became distracted with updating the speeds on the arrival and did not see the aircraft was still descending in Vertical Speed mode. Upon passing 14,000 feet, the Pilot Flying realized the aircraft was below the arrival descent profile and began reversing the descent. About the same time ATC called to query our altitude as we had descended below their Minimum Vectoring Altitude. We were issued a climb back to 14,000 feet which we complied with and then a vector off the arrival to final and further descent. The rest of the arrival was without incident.
ASRS:1789323.s: The flight crew descended below the RNAV arrival profile and Minimum Vectoring Altitude because the Pilot Flying remained in Vertical Speed mode instead of VNAV while updating speeds. ATC queried the low altitude, and the crew climbed back to 14,000 feet before being vectored to final.

ASRS:1789361.n: On the morning of an international departure that was scheduled to depart later that evening, the Captain emailed and informed both FOs of how the flight would be conducted in regard to face masks. During the pre-flight phase, the #2 FO challenged the decision and said he was walking off the trip unless the Captain agreed to wear a mask whenever he was on the Flight Deck. In an effort to maximize safety and also to address the #2 FO's concerns, the Captain offered the solution that he would wear a mask during cruise, whenever the #2 was performing his relief duties, but, with safety concerns about glasses fogging and hindered communications during critical phases of flight, said that #2 could sit in the cabin rest seat during those phases if it would make him more comfortable (since masks would not be worn). The Captain believed this was 'legal;' since an #2 actually wasn't required by the FARs on the planned 6 hour and XX minutes flight and was also the safest option since, if the #2 dropped the trip, the flight would likely be sent un-augmented with zero inflight rest periods then available to the 'flying' pilots. The #2 agreed with this solution and the flight departed.Prior to the later descent, the #2 stated that he believed that an FAR's had been violated by him not being in the cockpit for takeoff. He said that he would be in the cockpit for descent and Captain said he was welcome to be there but reiterated that masks would not be worn during critical phases of flight. The #2 did then come up for the descent and landing.After the aircraft was parked and debrief conducted, #2 said he would be submitting a report over his belief that an FAR was violated by him not being in the cockpit for takeoff and departure.The Captain and #1 FO are not aware of any 'violations' of FAR's in this instance but decided to report the incident in case there's something they are not aware of. During takeoff, the #2 FO stayed in overhead flight crew rest area instead of on the Flight Deck. Erroneously thinking his presence was not required on Flight Deck on takeoff. Captain and #2 chose that course of action, as #2 wasn't comfortable with staying on Flight Deck with the Captain who had a cough. Captain was unable to wear a mask due to fogging of glasses.
ASRS:1789361.s: During an international departure, the #2 FO remained in the flight crew rest area for takeoff instead of the flight deck due to a dispute over the Captain's refusal to wear a mask. The #2 FO later reported a potential FAR violation regarding his absence, while the Captain and #1 FO believed no regulations were breached.

ASRS:1789362.n: Dispatch notified us that the release was not signed at cruise. I immediately realized he was correct. I added 2000 pounds operational fuel on the way to the airport and discussed this with the crew. I planned on signing the release and talking with the Dispatch in Operations (Ops), because this is one of the last places internationally that we still go to Ops. The van takes us through security then to Ops then to the bottom of the jetbridge. All 3 of us had done this recently and knew of no change and in fact the 10-7 page states that we are not allowed to go through the terminal. However, upon reaching the airport the driver brings us to the terminal, stating that this is the new procedure. We verified on our iPads and even called Ops to verify this change. Indeed, due to COVID, we go through the terminal. The security was extensive, overly extensive and time consuming. The walk to the gate is long and although we hustled, we still arrived at the jet later than desired. I called Dispatch for the brief once arriving to the cockpit and received a standard brief which included a new release, release 2 due to ZFW increase. I agree that was okay, but after the call, we realized the 2000 pounds I had added via app was not added, so I called the Dispatch back. The Fueler arrived during this call and he agreed to add the extra 2000 pounds for us and I told Dispatch it was done so no new paperwork was needed. I wondered why the Dispatcher had not included the 2000 pounds. In retrospect I should have realized something was amiss, for example, the release not being signed. We then had discussions with Ops regarding the extra 2000 pounds, but it was all resolved. During this time, the FO saw the dispatch release, stated it was #2, but neither of us noticed it said 'not signed' at the top, only noted that it was release 2 and that we were all fit for duty. We had the Oceanic checklist out and looked through it, but missed the dispatch release on it. I have been signing the release lately enroute from the hotel to the airport since we never go to Ops anymore due to COVID, except today, since this is one of the few places that we do go to Ops. However, apparently, we don't. A note in the 10-7, an Ops alert, or something stating this would have been helpful.
ASRS:1789362.s: The flight crew discovered an unsigned dispatch release at cruise and added 2,000 pounds of fuel en route. Confusion over new terminal procedures caused delays, and the crew failed to notice the unsigned release or the missing fuel entry on the second release until after the fueler added the fuel.

ASRS:1789369.n: Aircraft X departing from ZZZ bound for ZZZ1 scheduled to depart at XA:45. My FO (First Officer) and I both discussed the hydraulic maintenance write ups from the previous day and saw no obvious irregularities. All ground activities were normal, I.e. engine start and taxi. FO was the pilot flying, I was the pilot monitoring. Climb to our cruise altitude of FL380 was uneventful. Approximately 40 minutes into flight we got the B system engine low pressure light, we used the QRH procedures for this malfunction which resulted in the switch being turned off. We checked the system page and saw that our fluid quantity was rising and stabilized at 106% and pressure was at approximately 2700 psi. The #2 oil filter bypass light came on, we again used the QRH which had us reduce thrust on the #2 engine to see if the light would extinguish. After moving the throttle to idle the light was still illuminated which, as per the checklist, required us to shut down the engine. Immediately prior to shutting down the engine I contacted Purser with our plan to secure the engine, our ETA to ZZZ1, and state that no cabin prep would be necessary. He told us that a deadheading pilot was onboard so we asked that he send him forward to the cockpit. Upon completion of the Engine Failure or Shutdown Checklist we advised ATC, got a more direct turn to ZZZ1, and descended to FL240. Once established at FL240 we saw that our closest divert airport was ZZZ2, we requested and received ATC clearance direct to the field. Our decision to proceed to ZZZ2 vs. ZZZ1 was passed on to Purser. We tried initially to contact Dispatch by sending a 'Call me' message from the ACARS. It took quite a while to get a response containing a frequency and I think the actual first response we got from Dispatch was that they had noticed that we had descended and wondered if we were having an issue. We did confirm that we had shut down an engine and once a decision had been made to go to ZZZ2 we confirmed that with Dispatch through ACARS messaging. We had good communication with Center but were never able to speak to Dispatch, though as we got close to ZZZ2 we did hear ZZZ3 ARINC, though they could never hear us. At about the same time Center notified us that our company was trying to contact us on the frequency that we had previously been given, we told them that they could not hear us so they relayed our final intentions to the company. I can only assume that our altitude might have played a role in this poor communication with Dispatch, though we had no issues with ATC. In the approximately 45 minutes of cruise prior to descent into ZZZ2, we discussed steps taken, checklist to be completed (One Engine Inoperative Landing Checklist) and other considerations. As a result, I switched pilot flying and pilot monitoring duties. At approximately 60 miles from ZZZ2 we commenced our descent. With all checklists complete and planning for a flaps 15 approach to the ILS at ZZZ2, we were given an intercept heading and selected flaps 15 for landing. The flaps did not move, so we requested vectors across final while we troubleshot the flaps. At this time I assumed the duties of flying the aircraft and talking to ATC. [The other two pilots] took on the task of determining why the flaps did not extend. Shortly after, we checked our system page and discovered that we had zero B System hydraulic quantity, I do not recall the B system pressure. We decided to run the Loss of System B checklist which led us to electrically extend the flaps. After one more series of turns to intercept final, we fully configured and executed an uneventful approach and landing at ZZZ2. After being inspected by Fire and Rescue Crews we taxied to our gate.
ASRS:1789369.s: The flight crew of Aircraft X diverted to ZZZ2 after a #2 engine shutdown caused by a hydraulic B system leak and subsequent flap failure. They successfully landed using electrically extended flaps after troubleshooting the zero hydraulic quantity issue.

ASRS:1789372.n: Normal takeoff and climb out. We went to FL400 for cruise altitude. We got to cruise, made our PA turned off the seatbelt sign. I was Pilot Monitoring. FO (First Officer) said;'uh oh we have a light on the HYD overhead.' I looked up and ENG2 engine driven pump said low pressure. I canceled the master caution and got out the QRH. Simple checklist, select the HYD pump switch to off. End of checklist. We pulled up the hydraulic display on the center screen. B system 106%, normal pressure. We started a what if dialogue. We agreed it was OK to continue with present condition. We looked up Loss of System B in QRH, and discussed it. We looked at flight plan divert circles and discussed scenarios. After 5-10 min the system B quantity started to decrease, slowly at first. I asked ATC for a descent to FL 320. Now the System B started to decrease rapidly. We knew we were about to loose Hyd Sys B. We selected Autopilot A to fly the aircraft, still descending, we were now over Location X but before ZZZZZ fix. We texted Dispatch we were going to lose System B and wanted to confer if we should divert or continue, Note-Loss of SYS B checklist did not say land at nearest suitable airport. We were almost to FL 320 and the ELEC 1 low pressure light illuminated, as the system quantity reached 0 and system pressure was 0;pump switch off per checklist. We got a few more lights and confirmed we had a complete loss of system B. Unbelievably we now got an ENG 1 hyd low pressure light illuminate, pump switch off per checklist. ELEC 2 HYD pump only hydraulic pump now functioning. It held autopilot A. We looked at each other and said lets head to ZZZ1, we had previously talked about divert points and where to go if the situation had gotten worse which it did. During this time we noticed A HYD quantity decreasing from 90+% to low 80's(we thought we might loose A too)I requested a descent and a turn direct to ZZZ1 from Center for a hydraulic loss. He gave us a different heading and said to expect to hold for sequence. We were now clearer to the controller and requested priority handling. The lead FA dinged us and asked if everything was OK, I told her no, type of situation, and to prepare the cabin for a divert to ZZZ1, I asked her to have the cabin ready in 10 minutes, no evac prep necessary. We got direct from ZZZZ Center, reprogramed the FMC and let dispatch know we were diverting. We started in on the loss of System B checklist as we were making a dive for ZZZ1. We ended up taking a vector to lose altitude. We completed the loss of system B to the ALT Flap extension. I then called back to the FA confirmed TEST, no evac, trucks would be standing by, we might seem like we were landing faster. I made a PA to the passengers. The FO did an excellent job of flying the airplane first, great CRM working with me on the checklists, with ATC , keeping me in the loop where we were when we were being pulled from so many directions (We were getting pulled from ATC, Dispatch, FA, PAX, checklists...). We completed the ALT Flap extension and then landing checklist. The landing was normal for a flaps 15 landing.After the parking checklist, we debriefed. ZZZ1 station manager entered the aircraft and said they might have an aircraft swap if we could fly to ZZZ2. Sent Maintenance report. I talked to the FO and cabin crew and they all wanted to continue and fly to ZZZ2. We called dispatch and he elaborated on the possibility of us flying to ZZZ2. All the crew members wanted to finish the flight to ZZZ2, so we started in on this plan. I spoke with the Operations Manager and the ZZZ2 Chief Pilot for clearance for all of us to continue to ZZZ2. We did have to also fill out a simple report and give copies of our licensed to the [local] authorities. We informed the passengers. The plan did come together and we did an aircraft swap and an uneventful continuation to ZZZ2. In cruise, the System B Engine Pump 'Low Pressure' light illuminated. The Captain (non-flying pilot) accomplished the QRH checklist and the pump switch was deselected. Hydraulic quantity in the 'B' system was over 100%. Approximately 5 minutes later the 'B' system quantity starts to rapidly drop to zero. After reaching zero, the 'B' system Electric Hydraulic Pump unexpectedly illuminates 'Low Pressure.' We also receive the associated caution light for the flight control system. While the Captain was completing 'Loss of System B' checklist and we were discussing our options (ZZZ1 vs ZZZ2), we received another caution light for System 'A' Engine Pump 'Low Pressure.'We immediately decide to divert to ZZZ1. The Captain advised ATC, and notified the Dispatcher over ACARS. We completed the checklists, notified the Flight Attendants, and informed the passengers. There was a very clear division in the flight deck workload. The Captain worked the problems, communications with the company, and in cabin communications. I flew the aircraft and communicated with ATC. This workload division not only works well in the simulator but also in real life.We completed the 'Loss of System B' deferred items and Alternate Flap Extension procedure. We shot the ILS in ZZZ1 and landed without incident. Clearing the runway we taxied to the gate. The System 'A' Electric Pump continued to function and we fortunately had no other problems.This whole situation was extremely similar a recurrent training scenario that we had not that long ago. Having 'seen it before' was strangely reassuring.
ASRS:1789372.s: During cruise, the crew experienced a rapid loss of Hydraulic System B followed by System A engine pump failure, prompting a diversion to ZZZ1. The pilots managed the emergency using QRH checklists and alternate flap extension, landing safely with only the System A electric pump remaining functional.

ASRS:1789387.n: During descent on the arrival while speed brakes were deployed, the speed trim amber light illuminated. The master caution light also illuminated and a flight control light on the system annunciation panel also illuminated. Accomplished the QRH non-normal and proceeded to ZZZ with no further issues. Remained on auto pilot remainder of flight and successfully performed a CAT 2 auto land approach onto [Runway] 4L due to low visibility.
ASRS:1789387.s: During descent with speed brakes deployed, the pilot experienced speed trim, master caution, and flight control light illuminations. After completing the QRH non-normal checklist, the crew remained on autopilot and successfully executed a CAT 2 auto land on Runway 4L due to low visibility.

ASRS:1789388.n: TCAS RA on flight route from ZZZZ AFB to ZZZ. We were on Y52. We noticed two aircraft on TCAS and with audio in contact with Fukuoka ATC Control radio in front of us heading directly in front, 12 o'clock towards us head on. Altitude of two aircraft varied from below 1000 and to our altitude of 26000 ft. TCAS alerts were activated. One of the involved aircraft's call sign was Aircraft Y. Opposing aircraft now at our same altitude, 26000 ft., closing fast.TCAS warning, 'Traffic-Traffic;' aural followed by TCAS RA and, 'Descend;' aural warning followed. Initiated evasive maneuver. I, the Captain, with minimum map scale on display could see opposing aircraft also now descending into our flight path. Initiated flight control input with verbal command that co-pilot continue to fly while I also inputted left lateral evasive maneuver to avoid collision. I noted our separation on TCAS was less than 100 ft. in red color. Increased separation was noted and aircraft flight was stabilized back to 26000 ft. No visual contact. Possible loss of 300 to 1000 ft. of altitude of our aircraft due to evasive maneuver. Cabin crew felt evasive maneuver with no injuries reported of passengers or crew.
ASRS:1789388.s: The Captain and crew of an aircraft on Y52 at 26,000 ft received a TCAS RA while approaching two head-on aircraft, including Aircraft Y. They executed a descent and left turn, achieving less than 100 ft separation, resulting in a 300–1,000 ft altitude loss with no injuries.

ASRS:1789391.n: At cruise altitude FL380 approximately 40 minutes into the flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 the Engine 2 HYDRAULIC PUMP LOW PRESSURE light illuminated. The Captain (Pilot Monitoring) performed QRH Non-Normal procedure and selected the associated HYD PUMP switch OFF. No further action was required at that time. I don not remember exactly what Hydraulic Qty and Pressure values were at this time but I recall that they were relatively normal as the Electric Hydraulic Pump remained functional.Approximately 15-20 minutes later, the Engine 2 OIL FILTER BYPASS indication illuminated on the Upper Display Unit Primary Engine Indications page. The Captain performed the ENGINE OIL FILTER BYPASS QRH procedures. The OIL FILTER BYPASS light remained illuminated after closing the Engine 2 thrust lever which directed us to the ENGINE FAILURE OR SHUTDOWN QRH checklist and the required shutdown of Engine 2. We elected not to attempt a restart of the engine. As PF (Pilot Flying), I continued to fly the airplane. I disconnected the autopilot and auto throttles and hand flew the airplane, adjusting rudder trim to approximately 13 units of left trim in order to maintain wings level, yoke level.We advised ATC and requested a descent to FL240 due to Engine Out Altitude indication of FL245, and slowed to 233 kts. per the Engine Out speed indication. Center cleared us to descend, as requested. I descended in LVL CHG to FL240. Shortly thereafter were handed off to [adjacent] Center. Initially we elected to continue toward ZZZ1 and were cleared direct to ZZZ1 by enter. After approximately 10-15 minutes of hand flying and after reaching FL240 I engaged Autopilot A (Autopilot B was unavailable due to the non-normal events).The Captain communicated with the flight attendants, made a PA to the passengers, and coordinated with flight attendants to have a deadheading Captain join us on the flight deck as an additional resource/additional crew member (ACM). This was the Captain I had flown with from ZZZ4-ZZZ the previous day and we therefore had the added familiarity and comfort of having just flown together. The Captain attempted to contact Dispatch via both ACARS and on Comm 2 via a frequency that was received in an ACARS message. We could hear Dispatch calling us but they could not hear us talking to them (possibly due to our low altitude?). ACARS availability was intermittent in our location. At some point later on, Center informed us of the frequency that Dispatch was trying to communicate on. We told Center that we had been trying to contact Dispatch on that frequency to no avail, and asked them to relay to Dispatch that we probably had little additional information to share with them beyond what had already been successfully exchanged when ACARS was available and beyond what Center already knew about our situation. During this period of time, the Captain and I periodically exchanged communication roles as necessitated by the multiple overlapping tasks required to be completed, while the deadheading Captain also assisted with some communications to passengers, to Dispatch, and reviewed and confirmed the QRH procedures we had followed, as delegated by the Captain (PM).Approximately 10-15 minutes after shutting down Engine 2, performing associated QRH procedures, and dealing with intermittent communication issues with Dispatch, we discussed and confirmed the fact that ZZZ3 was actually the closest suitable airport and asked Center for direct to ZZZ3. Prior to that decision, given our location over the Gulf, our direct route to ZZZ1 had been taking us relatively close to what would have also been a direct route to ZZZ3. Therefore, there had been no significant delay in getting us on a course to our nearest suitable airport ZZZ3. Weather at ZZZ3 was procured, Dispatch was successfully notified of and supported the decision to divert to ZZZ3, Flight Attendants and passengers were notified, and ACARS divert communications were completed. Initially we had elected not to balance fuel but after the center fuel tanks were empty, we elected to balance fuel, opening the crossfeed valve and turning off Engine number 1 fuel pumps.The Captain discussed with me and the ACM Captain whether or not we would elect to exchange controls at some point and it was agreed upon that the Captain would fly the approach and landing. I recall that transfer of controls occurred while at FL240, approximately 10 minutes prior to descent to lower altitude. Non-Normal landing distance was calculated by me (and backed up by the ACM) and other One Engine Inoperative Landing checklists were reviewed. I made a PA to the passengers explaining that they could expect a relatively normal landing at ZZZ3 with the exception of possibly seeing fire trucks there as a precaution. Below 10;000ft. I completed the portion of the One Engine Inoperative Landing Checklist for configuring for a Bleeds Off landing. Despite having calculated non-normal landing distance, normal landing data was also procured (as suggested by the ACM Captain) in order to determine whether or not any special engine out missed approach procedures existed, which did reveal a missed approach procedure of flying runway heading to ZZZ VOR.While on a final base leg vector to final approach for the ZZZ3 ILS at 2,000 ft., the Captain called for Flaps 1. However, the flaps did not extend when selected. We discussed why that might be occurring, trying to determine whether or not it might be associated with our original HYD LOW PRESSURE situation which had initially been resolved by turning of the engine drive pump and utilizing the remaining electric pump. We informed Approach that we had a flap issue and requested vectors away from the approach. I selected the SYS page on the Upper Display Unit to observe Hydraulic indications and saw that System B Hydraulic Qty was 0 or close to 0 and Pressure was low, if not also 0 (I do not recall the exact value). In post flight discussion with the Captain we discussed that there may have been a time (when flaps 1 was selected?) that a Master Caution light illuminated, we both looked up at the overhead but did not notice any new lights illuminated that were not already part of our previous non-normals. The Captain also recalled that when I had performed the Master Caution Recall as part of the After Start Checklist, the annunciator panel lights had not necessarily all illuminated without one or both of us having to push on the panel, as is often the case, and therefore it is possible that when/if the Master Caution light illuminated during the high workload single engine approach phase of flight, we may have failed to see a HYD indication on the annunciator panel or if it did illuminate, we might have considered it to be associated with the original HYD LOW PRESS non normal. Postflight, we discussed the possibility that it was the demand placed on the hydraulic system by the selection of flaps in conjunction with some other cause of a leak that caused the hydraulic quantity and pressure to go to zero at that time. In any case, given confirmation of 0 HYD QTY on the SYS page, we now performed the LOSS OF SYSTEM B QRH checklist and procedures which eventually directed us to the Alternate Flap Extension procedure.Once we had completed and reviewed the LOSS OF SYSTEM B QRH checklist and procedures, and the Captain discussed his plan for configuring flaps (taking into account the additional time required for alternate flap extension), I asked the ACM to reference the deferred items (e.g. landing checklist) for ONE ENGINE INOPERATIVE APPROACH AND LANDING while I referenced the deferred items (e.g. landing checklist) for LOSS OF SYSTEM B, to make sure they were the same or comparable and that we did not miss anything, given that I could only run one landing checklist and we simultaneously had two separate non-normals with deferred items. When ready, we were cleared for the approach. We successfully extended the flaps to 15 usingthe alternate flap extension procedure. Upon contact with ZZZ3 Tower I informed them of our special request in the event of a single engine missed approach per the landing data information.The approach and landing by the Captain were excellent. He stopped the aircraft on the runway with manual brakes per the QRH procedure. ARFF equipment came to the runway and personnel examined the aircraft prior to our taxiing to the gate. We left the flaps extended in case Maintenance wanted them in that position and informed ops and station maintenance of their position. We discussed with a mechanic some of the details of the non-normal events. We had to wait for customs to get ready for us, which caused a delay in deplaning. I took advantage of that time to go to the cabin to talk to the flight attendants and First Class passengers to see how they were doing and talk a little about our situation and answer questions while the Captain continued discussion with mechanics and Chief Pilot, etc.One final note I would like to add is that we received outstanding, professional support from all ATC facilities during the flight and from Flight Operations (Chief Pilots, Safety Committee, etc.) postflight, and our flight attendants were totally professional and did an outstanding job. Utilization of the deadheading Captain's input and support was extremely helpful, too. Thanks to everyone who supported us.
ASRS:1789391.s: During cruise at FL380, the crew shut down Engine 2 following an oil filter bypass indication and diverted to ZZZ3. On approach, System B hydraulic pressure dropped to zero, preventing normal flap extension, but the crew successfully used alternate extension procedures to land safely with manual braking.

ASRS:1789423.n: I was deadheading in the cabin when I was asked by the Captain to come to the flight deck due to an [urgent situation]. By time I reached the flight deck the number two engine was already shut down. I assisted the primary crew anyway possible to lessen the workload and stress. I assisted with cabin and airport operations communication, checklist completion, and any other tasks the crew needed help with. The primary crew did a fantastic job and needed very little assistance.
ASRS:1789423.s: A deadheading cabin crew member assisted the flight deck crew after the number two engine was shut down during an urgent situation. The crew member helped with communications and checklists, though the primary crew required minimal assistance.

ASRS:1789468.n: During our approach briefing we planned to exit the runway at Taxiway V near the far end of the runway to facilitate our taxi to parking. After landing on Runway 31R I followed the green leadoff lights to exit the runway at what I thought was Taxiway V and was already committed to continue onto the taxiway when Tower told us to exit at Taxiway V join [Taxiways] B and S to the ramp. The First Officer noticed that we had exited at Taxiway WW and asked the Tower if okay to exit there. The Tower then advised us that [Taxiway] WW was closed but no problem. We noticed that a couple of low and narrow snow berms across the taxiway that were left over from snowplows and we continued forward without any problem. I also noticed at the time that there were other aircraft tire tracks through the snow and did not appear to affect our progress. The taxi to parking was uneventful. During the landing rollout I tried to locate our position on the moving map airport diagram which I pre-positioned as much as possible at Taxiway V area, but could not ascertain exactly our current position. I saw the green leadoff lights, and thinking that we were at [Taxiway] V continued to follow them onto the taxiway. There was also another aircraft on short final behind us and it was my intention to exit the runway expeditiously so as not to complicate its arrival. I did not see a taxiway sign prior to the taxiway and determined that we must be exiting at [Taxiway] V. The Tower Controller did not seem to be phased by our encroachment onto a closed taxiway. We were already committed to Taxiway WW and there was no way to stop the aircraft and safely make a 180-degree turn to get back on the runway to exit at Taxiway V. There were not any cones or barricades with caution lights across Taxiway WW, and as it was not a construction area I felt that we could safely exit on [Taxiway] WW. To complicate matters, taxiway signage in that area is not sufficient as I did not see a WW sign prior to the taxiway - only the sign on the right side of the taxiway after entering [Taxiway] WW. Also of concern is that the green leadoff lights were illuminated allowing aircraft to taxi off the runway onto a closed taxiway. The lights should have been extinguished. I did not see any green leadoff lights at Taxiway V.
ASRS:1789468.s: The pilot exited Runway 31R onto closed Taxiway WW instead of planned Taxiway V, misled by illuminated green leadoff lights and insufficient signage. The aircraft safely crossed snow berms to the ramp after Tower approval, though the reporter noted the lights should have been extinguished for the closed taxiway.

ASRS:1789471.n: We were flying, from ZZZ to QRO (Queretaro, MX). During preflight inspection, the FMC database was current as well as both pilots' Electronic Flight Kits. While in-flight, the weather was reporting clouds at 1,200 feet 5 mile visibility and light winds. The runway in use was [Runway] 09. While in cruise flight, Mexico Center informed us to expect VOR DME 2 for RWY (Runway) 09 approach in QRO. The aircraft was set up, and the Pilot Flying (Captain) completed all briefings. While in cruise flight, Mexico Center gave us a late descent clearance which is very common on this flight that required LVL/CHG mode and speedbrakes to get back on path. While we were descending to our first cleared altitude (around 14,000 feet MSL), Mexico switched us to QRO Approach. Upon contact with QRO Approach about 15-20 miles out, they advised of a traffic on a ten mile final, and informed us to now expect the VOR DME 1 RWY 09 Approach. We were recleared direct to QRO VOR, provided another descent, and then shortly thereafter, Approach cleared us for the approach. The First Officer went into the FMC and configured it to fly direct to QRO VOR. After the aircraft was established on course to the VOR, the First Officer selected the QRO VOR fix in the FMC and inserted the VOR DME 1 RWY 09 approach after verification with the Captain. Because of the angle the aircraft was approaching the VOR (straight in Runway 09), and relative to the approach procedure (an outbound heading 292 followed by a left procedure turn inbound), an additional procedure turn was required just to begin the approach. The procedure turn would normally be done at the VOR. Due to the FMC not having a procedure turn at the VOR to begin the approach for arrivals from the west, it immediately started auto-sequencing fixes to fly the aircraft directly to the outbound procedure turn DME 10 from the QRO VOR. The First Officer had to re-enter the VOR into Direct To and build a holding pattern into the FMC.
