There was a missed approach holding pattern depicted on the approach chart, therefore, the First Officer built a hold based on the holding pattern published. The First Officer informed ATC that a procedure turn was required at the VOR and also notified approach that the aircraft would enter holding as published to begin the approach. ATC advised us to descend to 11,000 feet and cleared for the approach. ATC seemed confused as to what we were doing. It appears that they were expecting the aircraft to make a hard left after crossing the VOR (almost a 180 degree turn) into unprotected airspace that contained mountainous terrain. The minimum safe altitude for that sector is 12,800 feet and if the aircraft would have flown that, there could have been a CFIT event. Once the aircraft entered the holding pattern, making a procedure turn to enter the crew selected IMM EXIT and the aircraft completed the current holding pattern, just a procedure turn, and exited the hold to fly the entire approach as planned and expected. There seems to be an issue regarding the Jeppesen Charts, and FMC database for this specific approach. The FMC did not contain any proper procedure to join the approach legally. Also the FMC sequencing the approach could have presented multiple issues including CFIT, TCAS, or lost of Situational Awareness. We were heading to MMQT to shoot the VOR 1 approach from the west. We were headed direct to the VOR with the approach loaded after that. Approximately 9 miles prior to the VOR the airplane started a left turn to join the outbound portion of the approach. This was not appropriate or legal. We turned the airplane back towards the VOR and realized there was nothing loaded to turn the airplane around to join the approach legally. There is also no procedure turn depicted on the chart. There was a holding pattern at the VOR and a missed approach procedure associated with the approach. We decided to enter the holding pattern at the proper altitude and told the controller we were doing that. That allowed the airplane to turn around and we were able to join and commence the approach that way. The rest of the approach was uneventful
ASRS:1789471.s: During a cruise descent to QRO, the crew encountered an FMC database error that auto-sequenced the aircraft into an illegal turn toward mountainous terrain. The pilots manually entered a holding pattern to legally execute the required procedure turn, avoiding a potential CFIT event caused by the mismatch between the FMC and Jeppesen charts.

ASRS:1789477.n: This is a report to bring to light a potential issue with a NOTAM, no pilot deviation from ATC instructions or company procedures is believed to have occurred. References you will want: Approach Chart 11-3 ILS or LOC [Runway] 24 BHM, possibly the low IFR chart for that area, and NOTAM BHM A0233/21. This NOTAM has you take a turn to [heading] 219 to intercept the VUZ radial 067. This heading does not intercept that radial, I do not know how to fly this MAP (Missed Approach Procedure) legally. We caught this and requested amended MAP from ATC before commencing the LOC [Runway] 24.This is either due to me not understanding the NOTAM or it being written poorly.
ASRS:1789477.s: The pilot reported a potential error in NOTAM BHM A0233/21 for the LOC Runway 24 approach at BHM, where the published missed approach heading of 219 does not intercept the required VUZ radial 067. The crew requested and received an amended missed approach procedure from ATC before commencing the approach.

ASRS:1789483.n: We were left base descending at 1,800 feet turning final for a visual landing 15 into MOB. As it all happens so fast there was no time to react in the moment, but as we turned to what looked like a single lone bird turned out to be a drone quadcopter zipped by me on my left at eye level and went directly over our left wing within 15 feet. I immediately reported this to MOB Tower described it as quadcopter at our altitude and within 15 feet of the aircraft and that If it had been any closer it would've struck us or potentially went into our left engine possibly causing failure. This drone was in the critical approach corridor in our path on final to land. Luckily after we landed we did a thorough pre-flight and there was no damage nor evidence of a collision. I saw the drone as we quickly passed it in a split second.Cause - Careless drone operator operating a drone illegally in vicinity of airport.Always be vigilant of the airspace and treat them as if they were birds even if not always avoidable. Report any such activity to hopefully avoid an emergency in the future. While being vector for final approach to runway 15 in MOB we experienced a near miss was a drone at approximately 1,800 feet. It was spotted at the last second because of the few clouds in the vicinity of aircraft at the time of the incident. The drone was within 15 feet of the left side of the aircraft moving in the opposite direction. ATC was immediately notified of the location and description. The aircraft was inspected for a possible strike only in parking, but nothing was detected during the post inspection.Cause - Someone was operation a drone in close proximity of MOB airport at a unsafe altitude.We did not have time to react to the drone because of the location. [We should] be cognizant of the possibility of drones operating illegally in airspace in and around airports. Report the incidents to ATC.
ASRS:1789483.s: A pilot reported a near-miss with a drone quadcopter at 1,800 feet while on final approach to runway 15 at MOB. The drone passed within 15 feet of the left wing, but post-landing inspection revealed no damage, attributed to an illegal drone operation in the airport vicinity.

ASRS:1789495.n: After an uneventful approach and touchdown with Captain as Pilot Flying, the aircraft was decelerating normally with speed brakes and reversers deployed. The crew accomplished a normal exit of the runway when smoke could be seen in the flight deck and sirens sounded in the cabin. Purser was immediately contacted and told flight crew that there was smoke in the cabin and detectors going off. The Purser was asked to assess the situation in the cabin as simultaneous contact was made with the Tower. Cabin was asked for any signs of a fire or source of smoke and none were present. The Tower advised crew that a runway treatment had been used two days prior and that upon crew request no signs of smoke or fire were visible coming from aircraft. Crew determined it was safe to exit the runway taxiway due to smoke being from possible ingestion into the packs or reversers from chemicals in the runway area and proceed to the ramp with constant contact with the cabin to ensure no escalation or fire warnings.A short time later an evacuation message and siren was triggered in the flight deck. Once again we verified with cabin crew that no fire or source of smoke could be assessed. We requested that the emergency equipment be available and accompany the aircraft to the gate out of an abundance of caution and increasing warnings in the flight deck. A normal shut down was accomplished and the flight mechanic entered the flight deck and informed crew that he had inadvertently set off the evacuate warning while trying to cancel the smoke detectors in the cabin.Crew was met by local airport authorities and emergency personnel. During the interaction with crew we were informed that two compounds 'Sodium Formate' a liquid treatment and 'Potassium Acetate' mixed in with 'aviation grade sand' had been used two days prior and could possibly have been ingested by reverser system and packs leading to smoke. A giant smoke cloud could also be seen at the midpoint of the runway at least 200 feet tall but centered in one location, the possible site where chemicals interacted with the aircraft. Crew taking over the flight was briefed on the situation and Maintenance was in the process of examining the aircraft. By all logic with no indications of a fire and smoke being generated inside the aircraft an external source was deemed the most likely cause. The pebble sized compound that may have been present along runway edge and some portions of runway, even though runway appeared perfectly clean and clear were brought by airports OPS Crew after an inspection of touchdown and mid runway areas.With the compounds mentioned not being familiar to crews not much comment can be given, I would suggest familiarizing crews with this event to help discern an actual fire with a foreign contaminant causing indications of smoke and fire. I would also point out that procedures need to be followed in regards to on board mechanics response to dealing with abnormalities, rather than helping in trying to cancel an alarm after it was deemed non-threatening the issue was compounded which could have forced an evacuation had flight deck and cabin crew had poorer communication.
ASRS:1789495.s: The crew experienced smoke and false evacuation alarms after landing on a runway treated with Sodium Formate and Potassium Acetate, likely ingested by the reversers and packs. A flight mechanic inadvertently triggered the evacuation warning while attempting to reset detectors, though no fire was found and the aircraft was safely towed to the ramp.

ASRS:1789573.n: Climbing through 10,000 feet the L Bleed Air Fail light illuminated. I called the light illumination, Pilot Flying confirmed the light. We ran the emergency checklist and returned to ZZZ. We did not declare an emergency and did not require any additional services. The flight landed without incident.
ASRS:1789573.s: During climb through 10,000 feet, the L Bleed Air Fail light illuminated on the aircraft. The crew executed the emergency checklist, returned to ZZZ, and landed without incident or declared emergency.

ASRS:1789632.n: On IFR flight plan I was cleared for an RNAV Approach. I was monitoring the CTAF while still with ATC. There was someone ahead of me on the RNAV Approach, so I was second to land. With the airport in sight, I canceled IFR and changed frequency, kept transponder number. Another plane announced it would enter downwind and land after me. Another plane announced in area and would be number four. With each new plane arriving to the area, the Fixed Base Operator announced winds and preferred runway. The plane ahead of me cleared the runway. On short final, I saw a headlight at the far end of runway rapidly approaching. I announced that I was going around for plane on opposite side of runway. I climbed and turned slightly right. The plane from the other direction was rolling on the ground and about midfield took off and turned slightly right. I then announced that I would be staying in the pattern. I then landed uneventfully. He came and found me to apologize. He said that he had keyed in the wrong frequency and had been announcing his intentions to land on the opposite direction runway.
ASRS:1789632.s: The pilot, on short final for an RNAV approach after canceling IFR, executed a go-around due to an aircraft rapidly approaching on the opposite runway. The other pilot later apologized, explaining he had keyed the wrong frequency and mistakenly announced intentions to land on the opposite direction.

ASRS:1789642.n: Upon receiving taxi instructions to return to the ramp for parking, Student Pilot under my supervision did the taxi. At taxiway Charlie, by the wash racks we turned to left. Student got off the center line and I advise him to keep centerline and prepare to turn left again by reducing airspeed. At same time I finished giving student pilot those instructions, he added full power instead of reducing it. That action was faster than my reaction time to counteract. Immediately and simultaneously, I hit the brakes steering away from the hangar on the right that we were pointed at and pulled the throttle out. The right wingtip light hit the corner of hangar door. Wingtip lights were completely broken and there was a hole the size of a lime in the wingtip. The hangar door had a scratch on the corner where the wingtip hit. No other damages were found. Airplane was placed into maintenance. Student Pilot was instructed during the post flight on actions to avoid this situation of ever happening again. Chief pilot instructed CFI to enhance attention at all times, even when student is doing well.
ASRS:1789642.s: A student pilot under a CFI's supervision applied full power instead of reducing speed while taxiing, causing the right wingtip to strike a hangar door. The impact broke the wingtip lights and damaged the door, resulting in the aircraft being placed into maintenance.

ASRS:1789694.n: We landed in BTR. We were instructed to roll out to the end of the runway and exit left onto Taxiway Foxtrot. I remember seeing a NOTAM that B between Alpha and 4R was closed. Foxtrot was on the opposite side so we confirmed that Tower wanted us to exit left onto Foxtrot. They said affirmative left on Foxtrot and we complied. The CA (Captain) slowly steered us off Runway 13 and onto Taxiway Foxtrot. He was on centerline the entire time. At this point, I was getting the flaps up, clock started, APU started, and the rest of the after landing flow. Immediately after this, I called up ground for further taxi instructions. I felt a slight dip in the left side and we were unsure of the cause. The Captain said he added some power and the airplane continued to roll forward taxiing. I was focused on getting some complex taxi instructions from ground that were abnormal and a bit confusing. It took several calls for me to clarify the taxi instructions. When we parked at the gate, I went out to do my post flight walk around. The ground crew was already taking pictures and I could see dirt on the left side wheels. That's when it clicked that the left wheel had gone into the grass. I informed the Captain of the left wheel, and he called maintenance as well as informed Dispatch.Tower advised us to 'exit left at the end on taxiway Foxtrot' and to contact ground when off. We complied with their instructions. There is no mention of wingspan restrictions or weight limits for Taxiway Foxtrot. The company documentation does not make mention of any restrictions to Taxiway Foxtrot either. While the CA was on centerline, oversteering is needed for this taxiway - there is no mention of this on the 10-09.A note should be added prohibiting air carriers on Taxiway Foxtrot. At the very least, there should be wingspan restriction or weight restrictions. Additionally, tower should have instructed us to back taxi on the runway rather than tell us to exit on Taxiway Foxtrot.A note should be added prohibiting air carriers on Taxiway Foxtrot. At the very least, there should be wingspan restriction or weight restrictions. Additionally, tower should have instructed us to back taxi on the runway rather than tell us to exit on Taxiway Foxtrot. Landed on Runway 13, rolled to the end, Tower gave instructions to turn left onto Taxiway F, I stopped the aircraft before turning asked the FO (First Officer) to query Tower if that was correct because I originally briefed that we would exit right and taxi towards the terminal located on the West side of the airport, the Tower Controller replied, yes, turn left and contact Ground Control for further taxi instructions. With my nose wheel on the centerline, I slowly and cautiously rounded the bend on Taxiway F, felt the left side of the airplane sink a little, maybe 3-4 inches, and added a little more thrust, 3/4 to a full knob of the left engine to keep rolling, after a few feet we were back on the asphalt. Once at the gate, I inspected the left gear and found dirt on the wheels, I then called Maintenance Control, filled out the LOG and contacted Dispatch.BTR ATC gave us the taxi instructions that caused this.Should have been allowed to exit right, then taxi via B, turn right on either Taxiway E or Runway 4R and then left on Runway 13/31, then left on Taxiway A into the terminal ramp.
ASRS:1789694.s: The flight crew exited Runway 13 onto Taxiway Foxtrot at BTR per Tower instructions, causing the left main gear to sink into grass due to the taxiway's unsuitability for the aircraft. The crew recovered by adding power, but the incident highlighted a lack of wingspan restrictions and improper ATC routing.

ASRS:1789699.n: While receiving an application of Type 1 De-Ice fluid to Aircraft X, EMB-145 aircraft prior to a scheduled revenue departure in ZZZ airport, FO (First Officer) was indirectly sprayed in the right eye with the Type 1 De-Ice fluid by the ground crew due to a concentrated high pressure stream of De-Ice fluid being applied directly to the seal of the Right side DV window of the aircraft for ~2 seconds. Since the aircraft was not pressurized at the time due to Standard aircraft De-Icing configuration, the seals of the cockpit windows were not air-tight, allowing for fluid passage into the cockpit. The FO was not just sprayed in the eye, Type 1 fluid also covered his forehead, right cheek, right jawline, headset, shoulder, pants, iPad resting on the window, and shelf. Type 1 fluid was seen to enter the front left and top DV window seals. CA (Captain) and FO made a crew decision to return to the gate to seek medical attention for FO for verification of the potential harm Type 1 Fluid could cause. FO got the Safety Data Sheet from a ramp manager on the fluid being applied to the aircraft. The fluid was Clariant Safewing MP 1 LFD 88 Type 1 De-Ice fluid, Substance Key 000000702835. Per instructions on the Safety Data Sheet, FO and the Emergency Response Paramedics flushed FO's right eye with Honeywell eyesaline sterile isotonic eyewash until burning sensation in FO's right eye went away. After application of the eyewash, paramedics recommended to FO to seek a follow up medical exam with an optometrist to determine if there was any further damage to the right eye or not before returning to work.[Suggest] Re-training of basic de-icing procedures required on behalf of the ZZZ de-ice crew. Due to the snow and rain showers in ZZZ the aircraft had to be de-iced/anti-iced with type I and IV fluid. While in spot XX in hold bay XX in ZZZ, towards the beginning of the type I application, the de-ice crew sprayed high-pressure type I fluid directly on and around the FO's (First Officer) DV window. The high pressure fluid entered through the seal of the DV window spraying fluid around a section of the DV window on the inside of the flight deck. The FO was also sprayed on his headset, shirt, pants, his right arm, and small amount of fluid entered his right eye. I then informed the de-ice crew that they sprayed in the inside of the flight deck via the DV window. Dispatch, the Flight Attendant, and the passengers were informed we would be returning to the gate. Once back at the gate the FO's eye was assessed and treated by EMS in accordance with the safety data sheet on the type I fluid that was provided by station personnel. It was also recommended by EMS that the FO follow up with an optometrist for further evaluation. The FO was removed from flying status. I then contacted Maintenance Control and entered a discrepancy in the aircraft's maintenance log book in regards to the DV window. De-ice fluid was observed spraying into the flight deck through the First Officer's DV window during the de-ice application. AOM Volume I section 3.2.2 defines 'sensitive areas' as 'Areas where direct high pressure fluid application should be avoided during the deice/anti-ice process'. 'Windshields' is listed as one of these sensitive areas. During the deice process, the individual applying the type I high pressure fluid directly sprayed the FO DV window causing fluid to enter the flight deck around the seal at a high rate of speed.We returned to gate, the FO received medical attention for his eye, and a discrepancy was entered into the aircraft's maintenance log book for fluid entering the flight deck via the FO DV window. I suggest that the individuals applying de-ice fluids to the aircraft are properly trained on the 'sensitive areas' of the E145 and that direct high pressure fluid application is avoided in these areas.
ASRS:1789699.s: During pre-departure de-icing of an EMB-145 at ZZZ, ground crew sprayed high-pressure Type 1 fluid directly on the First Officer's DV window, causing fluid to enter the unpressurized cockpit and spray the FO's eye. The crew returned to the gate for medical treatment, logged a maintenance discrepancy, and the FO was removed from flying status.

ASRS:1789728.n: Flight was all normal until we were cleared for a visual approach. Approach vectored us about 2 miles outside of the Final Approach Fix. When cleared for the a visual approach the First Officer turned inside of the Final Approach Fix. We had briefed the towers and their height and had them visually. The First Officer turned off the flight directors and turned directly towards the runway, about 20 degrees angle. At 1,000 feet Tower called and asked if we had the towers in sight and said he had gotten an altitude alert. At that point we were still visual with the towers and a half dot low on the glide slope. I directed the First Officer to come left and get on final. We continued the approach and landed. Found out afterwards this was the First Officer's first time to this airport and that he really didn't have a good visual on the runway. I felt his turning off the flight directors added to his lack of situational awareness. We discussed this approach afterwards and he felt I should have directed a go around. I believe he was waiting for me but I was in the green. I didn't know he was lost. I explained to the First Officer that there is a reason we brief instrument approaches at night, to use them. I shouldn't have allowed him to make the turn directly towards the runway but told him to intercept closer to the Final Approach Fix. The First Officer needed to communicate he wasn't in the green and execute a go around if he felt it was needed. Cleared visual approach after I stated to the Captain that I had the beacon in sight. I turned toward the airfield and began my descent referencing the glideslope. I only saw the beacon, not the runway. Tower issued a low altitude alert as I flew too close to the towers west of the field. I had the towers in sight and the Captain gave me verbal commands to help me orient the runway. The landing and rollout were uneventful. I accepted a visual approach based on the beacon alone. I was also distracted by the airspeed going below the hook for reasons I didn't understand. After landing, the Captain and I thoroughly debriefed the approach and landing.
ASRS:1789728.s: The First Officer accepted a visual approach based only on the beacon, turned off flight directors, and flew too close to towers, triggering a low altitude alert. The Captain corrected the course, and the aircraft landed safely, though the crew later debated whether a go-around was necessary due to the First Officer's lack of runway visual contact.

ASRS:1789744.n: During cruise descent, HYD 3 ELEV OFF level 1 illuminated. HYD 3 had 4.5. We referenced the QRH LEVEL 1 section. While still referencing the level 1 checklist, the HYD 3 QTY decreased to 4.2. Because we knew a HYD 3 FAIL was coming, we referenced the QRH HYD 3 FAIL checklist. I [advised ATC] and because we were so close to ZZZ, we continued on to ZZZ. As I was the pilot monitoring, First Officer and I traded duties making me pilot flying. We asked for and we're given direct to ZZZZZ For a visual to Runway XX. We slowed to 230 kts. around 20 miles from ZZZ and extended the gear before a failure occurred. QTY was 3.0. The gear extended fully and a HYD 3 FAIL level 2 alert followed. QTY 3 was now 0.4. Because we had already reviewed the QRH, we knew what we would have and not have for configuration. First Officer ran the HYD 3 FAIL checklist. Slats and flaps extended fully and we made a 35/extend landing with manual brakes. We notified ZZZ approach that we would shut down on Runway XX. We also confirmed this with ZZZ tower. We stopped and shutdown. ZZZ fire trucks circled the jet and said all looked OK. Maintenance came and towed us to Gate.
ASRS:1789744.s: During cruise descent, the crew managed a HYD 3 quantity loss and subsequent failure by executing QRH checklists and landing with manual brakes at ZZZ. The aircraft stopped safely on Runway XX with fire services monitoring, after which maintenance towed it to the gate.

ASRS:1789763.n: After a 2 hour delay for other related maintenance issue we took off from ZZZ on our way to ZZZ1. Right after take off as we were climbing an AMBER CAS message showed indicating IRS 1-2 COOL FAIL we were climbing to 2,000 ft. then we were cleared to 10,000 ft. we kept on climbing with CAS message still showing AMBER at around 8,000 ft. I instructed SIC to get the QRH as we were still climbing, we reached 10,000 ft. then we were cleared to FL230 as we passed 10,000 ft. we started working on the problem QRH indicated to SHUT DOWN IRSs as we kept on climbing to FL230 I was hoping perhaps the cool air would cool IRS and I wouldn't have to shut them off because if I did I will lose automatization and navegation as we were going thru the QRH the IRS 1 and 2 shut themselves OFF at that point I lost all automatization, AP AT, Yaw Damper, Navigation and DUs 1 and 6 showed a RED ATT (no attitude indicators). At that point We manually shut off the IRS and I went to the display controller and selected IRS3 the RED ATT indicator went away I had my attitude indicator back but not any automatization still no AP AT Yaw damper and Navigation then we were cleared to climb to FL320 at that point I made my mind of not more climbing did not want to get to RVSM space without automatization and I instructed my SIC to call ATC and request return ASAP and PRIORITY, ZZZ2 ATC was very busy it took some time for my SIC to get the request in so I stayed at FL230. After communicating with ATC they asked for our intentions I instructed my SIC return to airport but DIVERT to ZZZ4 (ZZZ4 has a longer runway than ZZZ they are closed to one each other and the winds when we took off were very strong) ATC acknowledged the request and were giving some turns and step descents I don't really remember what headings or what altitudes however I was trying no hand fly the airplane and land safely. It was very bumpy we had severe to moderate turbulence I instructed the Captain to go the cabin and tell passengers we are returning to airport fasten their seat belts she went back there and instructed passengers to do that then she came up front and asked if bracing position was necessary I said no but I want you seat in the back with them and make them feel comfortable she said two little girls were crying but they were OK we also had 2 Dogs on board. We started our descent and turns as per ATC instructions preparing for the visual approach latest winds were 08018G23 during the descent at some level off altitudes it was hard to keep the airplane stable or on assign altitude as it was very bumpy it fell like like the trim was working at half rate and without yaw damper I had to use rudder input also. During all the flight from the take off on I couldn't hear my SIC when she was transmitting to ATC when pushing the push to talk button on the yoke, I could hear ATC but not my SIC... I also instructed Captain to call Operations on SAT PHONE but was not working either. I hand flew that airplane for about 40 minutes almost from takeoff to landing we landed safely and exited the runway on our own, Fire trucks were waiting and asked if we needed assistance we said no, then on the ground ATC gave my SIC a phone number for me to call. I also spoke to NAME County fire and rescue they wanted a statement from me as well as my name, I called ZZZ3 ATC on NUMBER they also wanted a statement of the failure and I said we had the NAV computers overheat and the shut off we lost all automatization but I was able to control the airplane however it was very bumpy at some times....they asked for my name, my pilot certificate number, address phone number and said they will write an incident report and I should do the same. After landing I spoke to passengers I explained to them in a way that they could understand why we came back and why we choose ZZZ4 they were fine with it and just wanted a recovery flight. Captain fed them on the plane while I went to FBO I talked to chief pilot I spoke to Operations and Maintenance and I called Center as requested. I came back to plane and right at that time a recovery GV landed we helped the passengers to transfer to other plane and transfer their luggage. After they left SIC and I did a radio check on the ground checked all the buttons in the right position and they were still could not hear her were she pushed the push to talk button not in VHF1 or VHF2. We secured the airplane added some oil helped the Captain with the cleaning and got to our hotel almost 3 hours after we landed.
ASRS:1789763.s: The pilot and SIC experienced an IRS 1-2 cool failure shortly after takeoff, causing automatic shutdown of all automation and attitude indicators. The crew hand-flew the aircraft through severe turbulence to divert to ZZZ4, landing safely despite losing autopilot, yaw damper, and navigation systems.

ASRS:1789831.n: I was holding short of Runway 29R on Taxiway B2 at Stockton (SCK) in preparation for a VFR departure en route to ZZZ, waiting for a [Company] heavy aircraft to land and clear the runway. The prevailing conditions were night VFR, with unlimited visibility, clear skies, and minimal wind. Stockton Tower was closed, and traffic was coordinating via CTAF. After the heavy aircraft landed and cleared, I made my CTAF call indicating that I was taking Runway 29R for departure. The heavy aircraft crew acknowledged my transmission and noted that they were clear of all runways. While beginning my takeoff roll, a ground vehicle, self-identified as a tug, made a radio call on CTAF that they were crossing Runways 29L/29R en route to the cargo ramp. This was the first call the tug made on CTAF. I made another radio call noting that I was in my takeoff roll, and began visually searching for the tug. I reduced engine power to idle, and applied heavy braking. At that time I saw the tug's anti-collision lights cross in front of my aircraft. I stopped on the runway and made an additional radio call noting that I was aborting takeoff and returning to RWY (Runway) 29R. At no point did the tug acknowledge any of these radio calls or change behavior. I returned to RWY 29R and made an otherwise uneventful departure.Primary cause of the problem: runway incursion by airport tug vehicle that was broadcasting on, but possibly not monitoring, the CTAF frequency.Proximate causes of the problem: airport ops vehicles likely unused to operating on CTAF after-hours at normally tower-controlled airport. Night conditions may have made it difficult for the ops vehicle to see my aircraft on the runway, and made it more difficult for me to see the ops vehicle. Complacency: SCK is a cargo airport, and extremely quiet at night. It's possible that the ops vehicle crew was accustomed to only seeing large cargo aircraft operating at SCK at night, and so my comparatively smaller (and unscheduled) aircraft may have not been noticed/ignored. Finally, the airport operations staff may not have been aware that entering a runway - even several thousand feet down the runway from a takeoff aircraft - is still prohibited.Preventative measures: training for airport ops crews on proper radio use, importance of clearing runways prior to crossing, and runway incursion avoidance best-practices.
ASRS:1789831.s: A pilot aborted takeoff from Runway 29R at Stockton after a tug crossed the runway without acknowledging CTAF calls. The incident was caused by the tug's failure to monitor the frequency and night conditions, resulting in a runway incursion.

ASRS:1789839.n: Arriving at the aircraft and checking the logbook, I noticed that the last crew had written that the Takeoff Configuration light and horn activated on takeoff (speed of activation was not noted). I surmised that the crew rejected the takeoff and subsequently swapped out of the aircraft after returning to the gate and the aircraft was not flown afterwards. The corrective action was a check of the Takeoff Configuration Warning System with no faults noted. Since nothing was actually corrected, the Captain and I discussed the possibility of it activating again on our takeoff. We pushed late due to an unrelated finding of damage in the floor of the Forward Cargo Bin C. The bin was deferred and bags transferred to the aft bin. We were relatively full on this flight and our V1/VR speeds for Flaps 1 on Runway XXR were 125/135. The engine start and taxi out were uneventful with the throttle burst yielding no takeoff warning. On the takeoff roll at approximately 130 knot (5 knot after V1) the takeoff warning horn and light activated. We elected to continue the takeoff. The initial climb was normal and we discussed that we would be writing this up in ZZZ1. The Captain called for 'flaps up' at the appropriate speed and I moved the flap lever to UP. We had a few distractions from ATC due to hold-down altitude that was cancelled. Before I moved the landing gear handle to OFF, I checked the flap indicator and noticed that the flaps were still at 1 with the LE FLAP EXT green light illuminated. After confirming that the flap handle was up, I told the Captain the issue and that we need to keep our airspeed below 250 kts. and level off to handle the problem.After notifying ATC that we would need to level off, they gave us vectors for terrain while we ran the QRH for Trailing Edge Flap Disagree. Since the QRH doesn't really address the disagreement when attempting to RETRACT the flaps and only deals with setting the flaps for landing, we turned our attention to coordinating the air return. Dispatch was advised of the return as well as Station Ops in ZZZ. Our current gross weight was a little over 130,000 pounds so we extended the gear to add drag and burn off excess fuel for landing. The F/As (Flight Attendants) and passengers were notified of the return. Since this was a flight control issue, we [received priority handling] and notified ATC that we were requesting [Runway] XYL but would need time to reduce our landing weight to 128,000 pounds. We felt this was the safe option as time was not an issue. We then ran the QRH, ran the performance calculation for the Trailing Edge Flap Disagree QRH, and then the brake cooling module. The flaps extended normally with the Alternate Flap system to 15 degrees. The only slight issue was although I read the section directing the flap lever to be moved to the final flap position (15), we were sidetracked by discussing slowing during the extension and this was not done until after the QRH was completed. This allowed us to see our Flaps 15 maneuvering speed. After the delay vectors were complete and we were below the maximum landing weight, we made an uneventful landing on [Runway] XYL. Brake cooling allowed us to take right to the gate and the ARFF (Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting) trucks followed. No other issues occurred. We swapped into another aircraft and continued the pairing. The aircraft was an originator. The previous day a takeoff had been rejected because of a spurious Takeoff Config Warning and the maintenance resolution was no faults noted. The F/O (First Officer) and I discussed possible reasons for a false warning lasting a few seconds, which refreshed our memories of the warning system and thankfully prepared us for a repeat occurrence. We pushed late due to an unrelated finding of damage in the floor of the forward cargo bin. The bin was deferred and bags transferred to the aft bin. On takeoff, approximately two seconds after the F/O's V1 call, the configuration light illuminated and the warning horn sounded. The F/O called VR, and we lifted off. The light went out and the horn stopped about the time the wheels left the ground. The F/O's performance and adhering to procedure during this event was flawless, which combined with our earlier discussion allowed the situation to be handled easily. We briefly mentioned writing the issue up again in ZZZ1. I called for Flaps Up, from their takeoff '1' setting. F/O moved the flap lever to Up, and then moments later told me the flaps didn't go up, and instructed me not to go over 250 [kts.]. We were still at about 200 knots, so no airspeed issues. I told F/O to tell ATC we needed to level off and maintain low airspeed. Initially we told ATC we would follow the SID and get back to them. ATC gave us a terrain clearance altitude. We confirmed the flaps were not up. I called for the QRH and we agreed that 'Flap Disagree' was the appropriate checklist. The checklist starts off by saying 'to prepare for landing' so we paused the checklist, agreed we were not going to ZZZ1 with flaps out, and I messaged Dispatch we were returning to ZZZ, told ATC, and received clearance to return to ZZZ. I notified the F/A (Flight Attendants) and told the passengers we were returning to ZZZ. We ran the QRH for Flaps Disagree, the procedure went mostly uneventfully. We were at 130,000 pounds, so we took delaying vectors to burn fuel to 128,000 [lbs.]. We checked the brake cooling for Autobrake 3, no issues. We did [receive priority handling]. We landed Flaps 15 and taxied to the gate. Positive takeaways. The CQT training from (year)?, (year)? that emphasized flap malfunctions prepared us well to handle the stuck flaps. Negative takeaways. The QRH for Flap Disagree was obviously written with a failure occurring during approach in mind. For our situation of failure on takeoff, the procedure kept us with the flap handle up until we had returned to ZZZ and were preparing to land, which meant we had flaps out, but no maneuvering speed. We know that Flaps 1 speed is 180 knots approximately, but it would have been one more item in our favor if we had moved the flap handle to match the flaps to give us the normal sight picture on the displays. While we were extending the flaps with the alternate switch, between watching the flap gauge and calls from ATC, we momentarily missed the instruction in the QRH to move the flap handle with the flap movement. We followed proper flap speeds as flaps were extending, but that that was because of our experience, not the display. The QRH should have the instruction to move flap handle with flaps before the actual instruction to move the flaps so that crews can discuss the handle in advance. We ran the brake cooling for Autobrake 3, and then tried to run again for Autobrake 2. The brake cooling module did not work the second time. We recalled a recent (Company communication piece) about Dispatch doing something to mess up performance calculation results, which could be rectified by requesting landing data again, but that did not work. Something in the performance calculations needs to be corrected so that brake cooling can be run more than once. Brake cooling was not an issue, even with Autobrake 3, so this was a small nuisance. Based on passenger comments, F/As did a great job. F/O's performance was excellent, our teamwork together allowed the situation to be handled easily.
ASRS:1789839.s: The flight crew experienced a spurious takeoff configuration warning followed by a trailing edge flap disagreement on departure, prompting a return to the origin airport. They successfully landed with flaps extended to 15 degrees using the alternate system after burning fuel to reduce landing weight.

ASRS:1789863.n: Shipment labeled for cargo only aircraft was intercepted prior to acceptance by dock agent. Shipper was under the impression that because this was a cargo flight product was able to fly on aircraft.
ASRS:1789863.s: A dock agent intercepted a shipment labeled for cargo-only aircraft before acceptance. The shipper incorrectly assumed the product could fly because the flight was a cargo operation.

ASRS:1789890.n: At or near ZZZ VOR, I noticed the aircraft started to turn when on a direct clearance to fix ZZZ1. Followed quickly by an Unable RNP. I quickly went to heading mode and requested and was given a heading from ATC. Aircraft was about a mile left of course. Trouble shooting looked to be a GPS issue. Turned off GPS navigation and used IRS function and aircraft tracked courses normally. We changed flight plan with ATC to no GPS and continued on with a normal flight and approach and landing.
ASRS:1789890.s: The pilot experienced an unintended turn and Unable RNP alert near ZZZ VOR while on a direct clearance to ZZZ1, likely due to a GPS issue. After switching to IRS navigation and coordinating a heading with ATC, the crew continued the flight and landed normally.

ASRS:1789892.n: Climbing out of ZZZ on the ZZZZZ TWO on our flight plan. After a short delay ATC cleared us direct to the ZZZZZ1 Intersection followed by the ZZZZZ2 and ZZZZZ3 intersections which are on the ZZZZZ2 THREE departure.During the departure briefing both the FO identified our lack of recency experience as a threat. When the clearance was sent to the FMC with the new routing the FO was not aware of the LOAD FMC prompt so the new routing was never loaded. When I reviewed the print out of the PDC clearance I remember being confused by the clearance.I should of voiced my concern to the FO when I did not understand the clearance. Unfortunately, I got distracted and never resolved the discrepancy. There's no substitute for diligence when it comes to the route check.
ASRS:1789892.s: The Captain and First Officer departed ZZZ on the ZZZZZ TWO flight plan but failed to load a direct routing clearance into the FMC due to the First Officer missing the LOAD prompt. The Captain admitted distraction prevented resolving the discrepancy despite initial confusion, highlighting a lapse in route check diligence.

ASRS:1789902.n: While taxing to the gate and on the terminal ramp the 4th Flight Attendant called up and stated there was smoke in the cabin. She stated 'could be electrical'. I stopped the aircraft, I got a minor whiff of something but it dissipated immediately. FO (First Officer) smelled nothing. We reported smoke in the cabin to ground and requested Airport rescue and Fire Fighting. We considered running the Smoke/AVIONICS SMOKE/Fumes but needed more information, (global assessment). I called up the 1st and she stated she was unaware of what was going on. I called back to the rear of the aircraft and 2nd stated it had begun to dissipate. After a brief discussion with FO, I elected to taxi to the gate and have Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting follow us and access the situation. Aircraft deplaned normally. 1st was unaware there was an issue 4th thought it was an electrical odor 2nd stated there was an odor but not a burning odor. He noticed a lite haze in the reading lights. [The possible cause] was primarily due to the dark cabin, communications among cabin crew. In a perfect world, there would have been better communication between all of the flight attendants, prior to calling up the flight deck. A more concrete assessment could have made with all eyes on the situation. Then the degree of urgency, and solid information can be transmitted more efficiently to the Captain. Taxiing to the gate on the terminal ramp we received a cabin call from the #4 FA (Flight Attendant) reporting smoke in the cabin. CA stopped the aircraft to assess the situation and asked if I smelled smoke or odor. I did not see or smell smoke or odor in the cockpit. CA said he sensed a brief odor but not burning. We called ground to request Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting due to the cabin smoke report. We discussed completing the Smoke/AVIONICS SMOKE/ Fumes checklist but after a follow up call to the FAs about the cabin environment the #1 said she didn't see or smell smoke or odor and #2 and #4 said the smoke/odor had dissipated. Due to close proximity to the gate CA decided to continue to the gate for further evaluation by the Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting personnel. The smoke report was entered in the AML and the fumes report [was] completed.
ASRS:1789902.s: During taxi to the gate, the 4th Flight Attendant reported cabin smoke, prompting the Captain to stop and request fire services. The odor dissipated quickly, and the crew continued to the gate for evaluation, attributing the incident to poor cabin crew communication and low lighting.

ASRS:1789904.n: Upon arriving at aircraft, noticed the crew O2 supply read zero. I reviewed the AML (Aircraft Maintenance Logbook) and found the aircraft had been on the ground for approximately 5 days. I also noticed the last MX (Maintenance) action taken was to change the crew bottle due to low crew O2. That got my attention. The bottle had been changed 5 days ago and the bottle had emptied while the aircraft sat on the ramp. So, I went further back into the AML pages and found the crew O2 bottle required changing 4 other times in 30 days (meaning this was the 5th time it required changing in a month). This led me to believe there was a deeper problem with the crew O2 system. Therefore, I refused the aircraft. Lack of meaningful automated historical oversight of AML discrepancy/corrective actionAs AMLs are being moved to more remote electronic system with less transparency to the flight crews, a system that compares discrepancy code numbers so that when one is able to detect a system failure that is repeated often. As this aircraft has been imported to the new AML storage system (which is MUCH less accessible to flight crews than the old [software] system), the only reason I was able to see the problem was because the old AML discrepancy book hadn't been removed from the book yet.
ASRS:1789904.s: A flight crew member refused an aircraft after discovering the crew oxygen bottle had emptied within five days of replacement, marking the fifth such failure in a month. The reporter attributed this to a lack of automated historical oversight in the new electronic maintenance log system, which obscured the recurring discrepancy.

ASRS:1789909.n: While cruising at 0.82 Mach at FL350 with an FMC calculated optimum altitude of FL370, aircraft experienced unforecasted severe turbulence with the autothrottles immediately becoming disconnected and the airspeed immediately accelerated to approximately 320 kts. 0.85 Mach (5 kts. over VMO Max speed). As Pilot Flying, I manually managed the throttles to avoid any further overspeeds and requested that Pilot Monitoring coordinate for a descent to FL330. This request was made and we received a 'Standby' message. [Two minutes later], the airspeed fluctuations became more severe and the autopilot had trouble maintaining altitude. I then advised the Pilot Monitoring that I was initiating a descent to FL330 and to advise Gander that were doing so prior to receiving ATC clearance. The PM sent this message to Gander that were descending due to severe turbulence and as we were descending through FL33.5, Gander approved our previous request for descent to FL330. The plane was in cruise at FL350, the aircraft entered abruptly into severe turbulence without warning. The auto-throttles disconnected and the airspeed accelerated into the barber pole (approximately 3-5 kts. overspeed) for approximately 2-3 seconds. Followed by an abrupt deceleration and continuous vibrations of the aircraft. Previous cruising airspeed was .82M. The PF (Pilot Flying) was manually controlling the throttles to the best of his abilities. We then asked for FL330 via CPDLC. The aircraft was becoming extremely hard to control at an appropriate airspeed and altitude. We received a Standby message. [Two minutes later], the aircraft began to enter constant severe turbulence and the decision was made to descend immediately to FL330 for the safety of flight. I advised Gander Radio that the decent to FL330 had been initiated due to the severe turbulence. We received an approval to descend to FL300 at approximately FL350. No other deviations were noted. We called Gander Radio to issue a Pirep and contacted the Dispatcher or subsequent Pireps and reports.
ASRS:1789909.s: The flight crew encountered unforecasted severe turbulence at FL350, causing autothrottle disconnection and a brief overspeed. They initiated an immediate descent to FL330 for safety, notifying Gander ATC before receiving clearance.

ASRS:1789931.n: We were at FL320 on the HLYWD arrival into LAX, and we had been given a vector off course for spacing. Upon rejoining the arrival we were given slower speeds until we actually saw an aircraft 5 nm in front of us. We were then assigned a speed of 250 kts indicated, then descend to FL240, followed by a clearance to descend via the arrival. I was concerned as we started our descent as we were clearly descending at a higher rate than the aircraft ahead of us and would be flying through their flight path at a close proximity plus winds at altitude were approximately 110kts. Suddenly our airplane began a roll to the right, I would estimate 20-25 degrees of bank, then it began rolling to the left at least 30 degrees of bank if not more and the autopilot disconnected itself. We were having an upset due to wake from the aircraft ahead of us so the Captain quickly recovered and I advised ATC what was happening and that we needed something different. They approved an offset to our course, and then advised the aircraft ahead was a B777. 5nm is inadequate spacing between a heavy aircraft and others. Fortunately we recovered well and landed safely. 99 percent of the time our folks in ATC do an absolutely outstanding job, and we couldn't do this without them! This event is unusual, but highlights an opportunity we can improve.I would also like to see better communication from ATC and a better understanding of the safety ramifications of wake turbulence - I frequently get the impression that they don't understand this risk adequately. I want to know if I'm in trail of a heavy aircraft! Sooner than later! It matters, it changes my expectations and I'm not consistently getting this information. I recommend more spacing, more and consistent communication about heavy aircraft ahead, and if I need to be vectored for spacing then let's address speed at the same time so I'm not constantly changing my configuration when I need to focus on flying.
ASRS:1789931.s: Pilots on a flight descending from FL320 to FL240 on the HLYWD arrival into LAX experienced an upset with autopilot disconnect due to wake turbulence from a B777 ahead. The crew recovered after ATC approved a course offset, prompting a recommendation for increased spacing and better communication regarding heavy aircraft.

ASRS:1789972.n: I was conducting a stage check for my student and we were practicing engine out approaches. On the first attempt a slip was attempted but the nose was too high and the airspeed dropped dangerously low. I took over and attempted to initiate a go around but the aircraft landed on all 3 gear to bounce sharply. I proceeded back to our base and the student and I attempted to get his power off approaches cleaned up and we did multiple touch and goes. After several landings we decided to end the lesson but I noticed that the left brake lost all authority when trying to stop. I took over and prevented a [runway] excursion and tried to slow down in a controlled manner. When I tried to exit [the] taxiway the wind pushed my tail around faster than expected and the plane skidded to a stop just before the hold short line with the nose gear and left main in the grass and snow. No damage to the plane or taxiway lights occurred. No injuries occurred.
ASRS:1789972.s: During a stage check practicing engine-out approaches, the instructor prevented a runway excursion after the student's left brake failed. While exiting the taxiway, strong wind caused the aircraft to skid into the grass and snow, resulting in no damage or injuries.

ASRS:1789976.n: During flight unexpected moderate rime ice was encountered. Upon encountering the ice I requested a higher altitude of 13,000 [feet] to attempt to escape the conditions which ATC approved. However, at that point, buildup had accrued and the aircraft was struggling to maintain 12,000 [feet]. I then requested 11,000 [feet]which Center also approved. The aircraft continued to have difficulty maintaining altitude and fell below the minimum IFR altitude for the area several times resulting in a terrain alert and several terrain vectors from ATC. An aircraft coming from the other direction advised that the area a couple miles ahead from the aircraft's current position was clear, so I elected to get to that area and the rest of the flight was completed normally. Lack of positive icing PIREPs in the vicinity of the route of flight informed that encountering icing would be unlikely. In the area where the icing occurred it seemed that the combination of location and temperature were contributing factors.
ASRS:1789976.s: The pilot encountered unexpected moderate rime ice, causing altitude loss below minimum IFR levels and triggering terrain alerts despite ATC-approved altitude changes. The incident was attributed to a lack of positive icing PIREPs and specific local temperature and location conditions.

ASRS:1789991.n: During initial climb (FL280) TR [Thrust Reverser] #1 unlock light illuminated and horn sounded. We ran the unlock light in flight checklist with no effect on the TR light and horn. In the interest of safety we performed a Precautionary Shut Down Checklist to avoid possible TR deployment in flight. We [advised ATC] and diverted to [a suitable alternate airport]. During initial climb - TR [Thrust Reverser] #1 unlock light illuminated and horn sounded. We ran the 'unlock light in flight' checklist with no effect on the TR light and horn. In the interest of safety we performed a 'precautionary shut down' checklist to avoid possible TR deployment in flight. We [advised ATC] and diverted.
ASRS:1789991.s: During initial climb at FL280, Thrust Reverser #1 unlock light and horn activated. The crew performed a precautionary engine shutdown to prevent in-flight deployment and diverted to an alternate airport after advising ATC.

ASRS:1789999.n: I departed from an airport which lies in a cutout from the adjacent airport Class C airspace. My desired on-course heading was 021. I knew that the adjacent airport Tower handled the nearby airspace, and I was comfortable contacting them and requesting clearance through Class C toward my destination.Immediately after lifting I established contact with Tower. Tower responded, and I requested clearance through Class C climbing to 3,500 feet. The Tower controller responded with the phraseology 'Cleared to operate in Class Charlie;' approved my course heading and told me that he only controlled to 2,500 feet. I took that as an altitude limitation, and continued north north eastward. About the time I was getting ready to level off at 2,500 feet, the Tower Controller cleared me to 3,500 feet, and handed me off to Approach.Upon establishing contact with Approach, that controller asked me if I was familiar with Class Charlie airspace and scolded me, telling me words to the effect of 'You can't just fly around here not talking to anyone.' I informed her that I had been in contact with Tower and he had handed me off to her however, I sensed that explanation didn't satisfy her. She then gave me a phone number that I could call later if I needed to talk with someone about it.At my next fuel stop, I contacted TRACON at the phone number that was given to me, and I was told that I had violated Class Charlie airspace. I explained to the gentleman on the phone that Tower had cleared me using the proper phraseology, 'Cleared to operate in Class Charlie.' The gentleman from TRACON went on to say that the Tower Controller shouldn't have done that. At this point, I didn't know what to do, and I certainly couldn't undo what I had done, so I thanked him for his time and told him I'd be filing a Report when I reached my destination.This airspace is remarkably busy with training aircraft. That is why I contacted Tower immediately with my request. If the Tower Controller didn't have the authority to grant me clearance then it's my opinion that he should have told me to remain clear of Class Charlie airspace, but he didn't do that. Instead, he specifically used the clearance phraseology that is taught in flight school and my company's recurrent training. Given those circumstances I proceeded in good faith with the clearance given to me by the tower controller. I believe that air traffic controller communications are recorded and stored. If so, I believe someone with the proper authority can verify this narrative and correct whatever caused this potentially dangerous situation.
ASRS:1789999.s: A pilot departed from an airport near Class C airspace and received a "Cleared to operate in Class Charlie" clearance from Tower, which included an initial 2,500-foot limit later raised to 3,500 feet. Despite this, Approach and TRACON later informed the pilot of a Class C violation, attributing the error to the Tower controller's improper use of clearance phraseology.

ASRS:1790003.n: We were flying to ASE and I was the Pilot Monitoring. As we approached Aspen, we were given vectors to intercept LOC E into ASE. We accepted clearance to maintain 13,000 ft until established and clearance to execute LOC E approach. As we were intercepting LOC we picked up visual with the airport and commenced descent towards it while having visual reference with the airport and all the terrain around. In the midst of all things happening quickly and the excitement of having visual with the airport, I failed to communicate to ATC my intention of executing visual approach. At some point we lost the visual with the airport due to a cloud layer just ahead of us, but not the terrain. At the same time ATC issued an altitude alert to us due to us being lower than what LOC approach altitudes called for. I advised that we had terrain in sight but lost the visual with the airport and said that we would be going missed and starting a climb. We got another altitude alert from ATC. We advised we are in a climb and asked vectors, until we decide what to do. We proceeded to ZZZ airport afterwards. At no time we were in IMC conditions and maintained visual clearance from all the terrain. My mistake in this case was deviating from ATC clearance and going visual without communicating that to ATC. And also, not staying on a LOC due to a cloud layer over the airport. At no time was the aircraft in IMC conditions and we were maintaining clearance with terrain at all times. By all means the aircraft was never put in any unsafe condition. I did learn from this experience to clearly and concisely communicate any and all of my intentions with ATC, so there is no misunderstanding at any point of the flight.
ASRS:1790003.s: The Pilot Monitoring deviated from an LOC E approach clearance to Aspen by descending visually without notifying ATC, triggering altitude alerts when the airport was obscured by clouds. The crew executed a missed approach, climbed, and diverted to ZZZ, attributing the incident to poor communication and unauthorized deviation.

ASRS:1790004.n: I was doing my first solo for my CFI training so I was alone in the aircraft in the right seat. I was performing engine start up procedures and had to lean over to the complete left side of the flight deck to crank the ignition switch. As I was leaned over the engine started and my feet slipped off the brake pedals. The plane moved forward and as soon as I could react I moved the throttle to idle and my feet back to the brakes. I then taxied back into the parking spot, shut down the aircraft, and canceled the flight.
ASRS:1790004.s: A CFI trainee alone in the right seat of a training aircraft experienced an unintended forward movement during engine start after slipping off the brake pedals while leaning to crank the ignition. The pilot immediately returned the throttle to idle, re-applied brakes, taxied back to the parking spot, and canceled the flight.

ASRS:1790012.n: Runway was extremely slick. There was nothing on the METAR or the NOTAMs that indicated the braking action. The 210 overran the runway end by 8 feet. Local Airport Manager and his handyman helped push it aircraft onto the pavement. The maintenance personnel after looking at the airplane deemed nothing was wrong so [I] departed for destination airport. No anomalies or problems found with gear, no prop strike occurred.
ASRS:1790012.s: The pilot reported that a Cessna 210 overran the runway end by 8 feet due to extremely slick conditions not indicated in METARs or NOTAMs. After airport staff pushed the aircraft back, maintenance found no gear anomalies or prop strikes, allowing the flight to depart.

ASRS:1790013.n: Precautionary right engine shutdown because of fuel contamination.
ASRS:1790013.s: The pilot performed a precautionary right engine shutdown due to fuel contamination.

ASRS:1790021.n: Position was CORKR intersection to directly over SFO [VOR] at approximately 8,000 MSL. Had navigation flag on GNSS from GPS jamming Was tracking fine up to SFO, Over SFO GNSS made a turn directly to ZZZ or so was thought, however, it was off course, Controller asked what our previous clearance that had been given, which was HOLLR, GRIJO, CORKR, SFO, ZZZ. Original clearance was GPI DIRECT to ZZZ. On the NW side of Nevada, there was GPS jamming was in progress. We reported it, and checked with controllers to see if our course was accurate. They informed us it was, and that if necessary they would give us a heading. Upon changeover to Oakland Center, we advised the Controller that GPS jamming had been in progress, and that we still had a navigation flag. He then issued a clearance to follow the fixes listed above, and we then asked how much longer the GPS jamming would continue. He said a few more miles. we advised him we still had a navigation flag on our GNSS, but apparently he was distracted, and told us to continue without issuing a heading. We were then turned over to another controller who apparently had not been informed of the ongoing issue. Hence once over SFO VOR, was when the issue listed above was encountered. We were not told if there was a near miss, he just gave us a heading to 180 and vectored us to the airport after that. Once on the ground, we were advised to call approach control for a possible deviation. We attempted to call but could not get through to anyone. We advised the Tower we were not able to reach anyone, so he tried to call and failed, but then he got through with another number. They said to disregard, and we then proceeded to ZZZ1 where the flight terminated.
ASRS:1790021.s: Pilots reported GPS jamming and a GNSS navigation flag while flying from CORKR to SFO at 8,000 feet, causing an unintended turn off course. Controllers eventually vectored the aircraft to the airport, and post-landing inquiries regarding a potential deviation were dismissed by approach control.

ASRS:1790109.n: Was cleared visual approach [Runway] 23 / asked to turn short final inside of GS Intercept Altitude for traffic. Changed Alt Select from 2,300 feet to 1,500 feet and selected VS (Vertical Speed) descent of 700 rpm to get below GS. Descending below 1,800 feet or so, received Low Altitude Alert from ATC / Tower. Deactivated AutoPilot, added power and initiated climb to intercept GS.ATC Low Altitude Alert followed later (approximately 5-10 sec of 'Glideslope' call-out from GPWS.Two causal items: short turn to final / cleared for visual approach at altitude that would put us above glide slope, so selected lower altitude and initiated descent. Second causal item was over aggressive selection of Altitude Select to 1,500 feet . . . In retrospect should have selected something like 1,900-2,000 MSL given field elevation of 700 feet.De-selected AP and climbed to 2,000-2,100 feetWe actually discussed not accepting a short turn to final as part of approach briefing . . . When cleared for the visual, initially turned right to extend final leg, but then was asked by ATC to turn to a left heading given other arriving traffic behind us. In retrospect, could have indicate unable, but that seemed unnecessary given overall regime, weather, etc. Second suggestion would be to double-think / exercise caution in selecting an altitude above the DH but below the FAF / GS Intercept Altitude.
ASRS:1790109.s: The pilot, on a visual approach to Runway 23, received a Low Altitude Alert after aggressively descending below the glideslope intercept altitude to accommodate a short turn. The pilot attributed the event to the clearance geometry and an overly aggressive altitude selection, subsequently climbing to intercept the glideslope.

ASRS:1790145.n: Prior to departure Maintenance was called due to FOs (First Officer's) MAP failure on navigation display. Maintenance did a reset and signed off logbook as reset ok for service. FOs MAP was restored. Approximately 2 hours into flight and approximately 30 mins from ZZZZ1 enroute to ZZZZ, FOs MAP failed, followed by Captain's CWS (control wheel steering) fail, autothrottle failure, and SINGLE FMC operation message. Very shortly later, approximately 10 seconds, LNAV/ VNAV failed, both FMCs failed. Opposite autopilot selected, autopilot B. Captain's CWS was restored and one FMC was restored allowing for the engagement of LNAV/VNAV, and autothrottle was restored. FOs MAP still indicated a failure. Within approximately 60 seconds we had another dual FMC failure, followed by another LNAV/ VNAV failure, autothrottle failure, Captain's CWS failure. At this time with over two hours left to ZZZZ and navigating by raw data we decided it was the best course of action to divert to ZZZZ1 where the weather was favorable for landing with these navigational failures. We notified ZZZZ1 Center of our issues and intent to land in ZZZZ1. Around this time the Captain's FMC was restored automatically and we were once again able to navigate with LNAV/VNAV and the autothrottle and Captain's CWS was restored and autopilot was operational. As we neared ZZZZ1 we informed ATC of the need to hold to burn off fuel due to being overweight for landing which took approximately 10 minutes. The remainder of the flight was uneventful, we landed on Runway X and commenced the ILS approach in VFR conditions. The FOs MAP warning flag remained in view for the rest of the flight. My FO, Fas (Flight Attendants) did outstanding jobs. Great communication. ZZZZ1 ATC also very professional and helpful. In the 21 years I've been on the 737 both as an CA (Captain) and FO I've never experienced a dual FMC failure. I've experienced several single FMC failures, but not dual failures leading to several other navigation failures.
ASRS:1790145.s: The crew experienced recurrent dual FMC, LNAV/VNAV, and autothrottle failures en route to ZZZZ after a pre-flight MAP reset. They diverted to ZZZZ1, held to burn fuel, and landed safely while the First Officer's MAP failure persisted.

ASRS:1790157.n: The aircraft had several maintenance scheduled items that needed to be addressed before we could fly the aircraft. It was supposed to be the first revenue flight after long term storage. There was one maintenance schedule item X which needed to be accomplished before the aircraft can be used for revenue flight with passengers. The item was signed off on the completed items sheet and the aircraft was released for flight. When we were taxing, Dispatch notified us to hold. We called them and they said there was a maintenance schedule write off not signed off properly. So, we returned to the gate to have to addressed. The reason for this report is that you cannot leave the gate with passengers unless maintenance schedule item X had been signed off. Our paperwork showed it was signed of yet the electronic AML [Aircraft Maintenance Logbook] said it was not. We returned to gate. We found out later that it was a clerical data entry error made by someone in maintenance and the maintenance schedule item sign off was entered incorrectly.The cause is easy to figure out. The only way to fix it is to have a computerized completed items sheet that only shows items cleared and then the computer copy and paper completed items sheet would always match!After items are cleared in computer, print out new completed items sheet for AML so paper and computer always match.
ASRS:1790157.s: The crew of a revenue flight departing long-term storage returned to the gate after Dispatch halted taxi due to an unsigned maintenance item X. A clerical data entry error caused a discrepancy between the paper and electronic maintenance logs, requiring the aircraft to be held until the sign-off was corrected.

ASRS:1790174.n: Upon arrival the inbound crew advised us that the nose strut might possibly be low. I advised them that we would look at it on the walk around and that we would write it up if necessary after doing the walk around. Prior to boarding with the only occupants on board being the two flight attendants and myself, my FO (First Officer) went out and did the walk around, he motioned for me to come down and look at the strut which was nearly fully collapsed and not showing any chrome. Not having a ruler or protractor available we took an informal measurement. The distance between the top and bottom was two fingers or less, which was certainly less than two inches. At this point, I contacted Dispatch and Maintenance Control to advised them of the situation, at which point Contract Maintenance was dispatched. I made an entry into the logbook stating that the nose strut was nearly compressed and needed to be serviced. Once Contract Maintenance arrived, he originally rolled out the tanks, as if he were going to inflate the cylinders, he attempted to open a valve in the nose wheel strut area and then after some difficulty stopped. He then made a phone call to Maintenance Control. After this phone call, he said that per the AMM (aircraft maintenance manual) the measurements that he took indicated that the strut was showing 2 inches and was legal for dispatch as outlined in the AMM as is and that he was to sign it off as instructed by Maintenance Control. At this point we boarded, and just prior to closing the door, under all prudence and caution, I decided to do another inspection of the nose wheel strut to find it fully collapsed and actively leaking foamy fluid. I contacted Maintenance Control and advised them that the strut was compressed and leaking foamy fluid, which I then entered into the logbook. We deplaned and Contract Maintenance then added nitrogen to the strut and signed it off again. At this point, the on duty pilot, Name 1 called me to gather more information on the situation. I informed him of all the events that had occurred up to this point. He then asked me why I would do a preflight walk around with passengers onboard and he stated because we aren't really sure of what the strut compression should look like after passengers had boarded and additionally why would I need to do that after I had a legal sign off. I informed him that in the interest of safety that I felt it was OK to do a walk around after a maintenance procedure and, as well as to comply with the CFM (company flight manual) guidance for exterior inspection, which is to ensure that gear struts aren't fully compressed and that there are no fluid leaks. I also added that we should still be able to see some chrome on the strut and that there shouldn't be any leaking fluid. After the Contract Maintenance inflated the strut we then began to board again as we waited for the book to be signed off. As the FO and I were briefing, the Contract Maintenance asked me to step outside. After stepping outside, the Contract Maintenance guy pointed out the strut which may have been inflated to the legally required two inches and but was leaking a solid stream of foamy liquid and not just a couple bubbles as Maintenance Control contends. I then contacted my Dispatcher Name 2 and Maintenance Control. They then advised me that they would remove the aircraft from service and schedule us to take the RON aircraft that was coming around XA:15pm. I also sent pictures of the compressed strut and leak to Maintenance Control. I attempted to send the video too but was unable to do so because of the file size. The following morning, I was contacted by Chief Pilot Name 3, who asked if I was OK with how everything turned out and to get my side of the issue. He also said that I was scheduled to fly the airplane several more times the following day and would I be OK with taking the aircraft. I told Name 3, that I'm perfectly fine flying the aircraft as long as it's legal and safe, which in this case would mean the strut would be showing a normal amount of chrome and not streaming foamy liquid from the cylinder. He also shared an email outlining the events from Name 2 which directly contradict several key facts from the evening. 1. The inbound crew didn't write up the aircraft. I wrote up the aircraft three times. 2. When Maintenance came back there was foaming bubbling liquid coming from the strut which can be be seen in the pictures and videos that I took or are visible on the ground which appears wet from the leaking fluid. Name 2's email incorrectly characterized this leak as a couple small bubbles. The cause narrative for this series of events is pretty straight forward. I feel like my Dispatcher was very accommodating and I feel that the real issue here lays with how Contract Maintenance, Maintenance Control, On Duty Pilot and indirectly Name 2, Maintenance Control, Maintenance Director interact with the pilots after the fact. Contract Maintenance from the very beginning expressed his hesitation with the situation once he saw the foamy liquid coming from the cylinder. Finally, his insistence that I look at the leaking cylinder after we boarded and he once again expressed his hesitation and ultimate concern about the issue thus giving me a moment of pause. I had the opportunity to speak to Maintenance Control several times and they didn't really seem to understand why we wouldn't go because in their opinion, because they signed off on it that it was good to go, even though it was leaking. The On Duty Pilot questioned why I would do a walk around after Maintenance was performed, expressing that we didn't know what the nose strut would look like after boarding and why would I do that even though I had a legal sign off, as if I was supposed to accept the sign-off carte blanche. I expressed to him that I needed to be not only legal but safe and that I could do a walk around whenever I felt it was needed on confirm to expectations set forth in the manuals. I didn't see that email from Name 1, until Chief Pilot contacted me to inquire if I was OK with flying the aircraft on my next trip. I told him that I was was fine with flying the aircraft in the future, as long as it was in serviceable condition, which would mean showing a normal amount of chrome on the strut and not leaking fluid. The concerning part of Name 2's email is where he ends with 'This is bad when Maintenance is using appropriate AMM references for the checking of proper servicing being refused with a legal sign off, but we are taking the delays for no reason at this point.' This sentence is challenging because it assumes that I'm making a refusal for no good reason and that the sign off were legal to begin with. If it had only a couple bubbles as his email suggests then I would have certainly taken the sign off but upon receiving the sign off and seeing the stream of foamy fluid still coming from the cylinder, along with input from the Contract Maintenance and my First Officer we needed to again assert our concern with the aircraft. Fortunately Name 2 wasn't there, he doesn't know the extent of the issue and his comments are a direct challenge to the safety reporting culture that the Company has developed.
ASRS:1790174.s: The captain and First Officer found the nose strut fully collapsed and leaking foamy fluid despite a maintenance sign-off, leading to a second inspection that confirmed a solid stream of fluid. Consequently, the aircraft was removed from service due to the unsafe condition, contradicting Maintenance Control's claim that the leak was minor.

ASRS:1790183.n: Captain (CA)=Pilot Monitoring (PM), First Officer (FO)=Pilot Flying (PF). Discovered pressurization outflow valve in the full open position during the after takeoff checklist (no Auto Fail lights, both Packs, ISO valve and bleeds all in proper position). Discussed with the FO and advised ATC we needed to level off at 10,000 ft to investigate an issue and asked for straight ahead to avoid terrain (initially assigned 15,000 ft on the SID). FO was PF and had them take the radio. Pulled the QRH and referenced AUTO Fail or Unscheduled Pressurization Change 2.2. At this point we discussed and surmised we did NOT have an AUTO Fail issue nor and unscheduled pressurization change as the Cabin appeared to be modestly, although suspiciously pressurizing, as we were building some differential and the cabin altitude was relatively low. Troubleshooting forbids switch manipulation unless inclusive of a QRH or other written procedure hence we chose not to manipulate cabin pressurization controller from AUTO to ATLN. Additionally, we recalled a bulletin from Standards Department dated 7/xx/2020 titled 'Cabin Pressure Controller Blinking/Blanking issue'. This bulletin states that on our 900ER fleet from (tails)(we were in tail) the digital controller can blank and or blink or become so dim its unreadable. Additionally, the bulletin states the controller should right itself shortly...We did not have any blinking/blanking or dimness. Our outflow indicator was bright and solid indicating full open and remained so for the duration of our flight. In an attempt to determine if the cabin would hold we elected to continue our climb to 12,000 ft at which point we got a significant bump felt by the entire crew.... At this point I attempted to contact Dispatch via ACARS to establish two way radio communications. We had plodded along south at a low altitude for a good duration in an attempt to solve the issue. I became concerned with our flight plan fuel. We were dispatched with no reserve for ZZZ1 (weather severe clear at arrival time). Was there enough to complete the mission or might we find ourselves having to divert for fuel 'if' we felt the cabin psi was solid enabling us to continue? We we're now down near (mountain) at 12,000 ft IMC picking up a fair amount of ice as weather was now an issue. After multiple attempts to get a hold of Dispatch to no avail, Flight Attendants complaining about ears, a QRH procedure that didn't quite fit, no ability to troubleshoot, a bulletin that didn't match enough to convince me and a possible fuel stop with an open maintenance issue stranding passengers....in consultation w/ my FO I made the command decision to return to ZZZ. In my mind, this was the safest option and provided our passengers an opportunity to reset. Additionally, it brought the aircraft back to a maintenance base for investigation and repair. We informed Dispatch via ACARS and setup to return and received an amended release via ACARS. We did not declare an emergency as it did not appear warranted/necessary. We ran performance including our LTP (landing threshold point), discussed our TPC and landed significantly under max landing weight as we had a light load.
