During block in as L1 was opened we felt another pressure bump despite the outflow valve remaining in the full open position. I greeted all deplaning passengers and answered questions, debriefed full crew and discussed scenario and concerns. Flight Attendants met with supervisor and were replaced. No crew members/ nor passengers asked for medical attention. Swapped aircraft, checked duty time and pressed on.Lesson learned:I should have used SATCOM to raise Dispatch in lieu of ACARS. We traveled a fair ways south and company frequency became weak. We switched to XXX.X and sent a message but never could get radio contact. We became distracted by the accumulation of ice buildup at that point in the journey. Bulletin concern: If it is related to the digital controller bulletin why would the company continue to allow problematic controllers be installed? NOTE: The original design Pressurization Control Panel may be installed in any 9ER aircraft from (tail) and subsequent as a repair for a Pressurization Control Panel issue. Therefore, even though (tail) and subs were delivered with the upgraded panel, this issue may occur on these aircraft if the upgraded panel has been replaced with an original panel.
ASRS:1790183.s: The crew of a 900ER discovered the pressurization outflow valve stuck full open during climb, causing cabin pressure bumps and ice accumulation. Unable to resolve the issue or contact Dispatch via ACARS, they returned to the departure airport for maintenance, landing safely with no injuries.

ASRS:1790208.n: During the approach we were cleared direct down to 8000 feet from 12000 feet. During the descent Autopilot was engaged and following LNAV and VS we were encountering continuous light to moderate turbulence throughout the descent. As we passed through approximately 12000 feet and beginning to slow, we experienced severe turbulence mixed with continuous moderate [turbulence]. When we initially encountered the severe turbulence, the Autopilot disengaged, the aircraft was changing altitude and air speeds abruptly with several hundred feet of altitude change and at least plus or minus 20 to 30 knots airspeed changes. The Captain was thrown hard enough to hit the overhead panel with his head and we received a report one of our Flight Attendants had been hurt and several passengers had hit their heads. I as the Pilot Flying took manual control of the aircraft and flew the remainder of the descent and approach. The aircraft was extremely hard to control throughout most of the descent and approach as we continued to encounter continuous turbulence, strong crosswinds and wind shear. During the ensuing descent and approach the aircraft was extremely hard to control as we continued to experience moderate to severe turbulence, strong crosswind and wind shear throughout the approach. Once established inbound and cleared for the approach we were pushed several degrees off course and had some airspeed fluctuations of plus or minus 20 knots. We quickly discussed missed approach but prior to reaching 1000 feet we had regained the course, were on glide path and stabilized (properly configured) to continue the approach. We continued the approach while receiving some lower wind shear of plus or minus 10 knots down to approximately the 500 foot call. At 500 feet we were still stabilized and continued the approach to landing without further issue. Throughout the approach and landing, we had airspeed, altitude variations and heading deviations that were extremely hard to control due to the turbulence and wind shear events we were experiencing. I do not believe at any point we had any exceedances or violations, however, it was a very task saturated environment. There were no reports of the severity of the turbulence ahead of us and it was a very unexpected event.This was an example of good Crew Resource Management as the Captain and I maintained good communication throughout the event and helped to cross monitor the aircraft systems and instruments. As the pilot flying, I was entirely focused with aircraft control and the Captain doing the pilot monitoring was ensuring all the descent and approach tasks were completed. We kept good crew communication with what was happening with aircraft control and situational awareness. A recommendation is for pilots to ensure they continue to practice hand flying skills for situations like this. The autopilot was unusable, and I was thankful I constantly practice hand flying the airplane. It helped me with confidence to control the airplane to the best of my ability in a situation where the aircraft is being tossed around by turbulence.
ASRS:1790208.s: During approach, the crew encountered unexpected severe turbulence and wind shear that disengaged the autopilot and caused injuries to the Captain, a flight attendant, and passengers. The Pilot Flying manually controlled the aircraft through difficult handling conditions to complete a stabilized landing without exceedances.

ASRS:1790218.n: As [aircraft] was being loaded, a cart was brought to my airplane that contained a bunch of dry ice boxes. 16 boxes in total, each containing a reported 18kg of dry ice. I multiplied 18 by 16 and got 288kg. I remembered that there had been an alert bulletin released recently that limited the Aircraft X to what I thought I remembered was 320kg of dry ice, and I confirmed this number with a pilot standing near me. However I didn't recall that the limit was in pounds, not kilograms. So I completed the PNF, submitted it to Dispatch via email and completed the flight as scheduled. I then received an email several days later from the director of safety asking to confirm the weight of the dry ice, we spoke on the phone and he informed me that the limit was in fact 320lbs and not 320kg. We discussed the issue and I now have this number etched in my brain.[Weight limit issue clarified] when the director of safety spoke with me on the phone about the discrepancy.[Captain further stated the following statements]. Instead of breaking out my GOM or confirming in the hazmat binder, I verbally discussed the weight with another pilot and thought that 320kg was the correct limit for the Aircraft X. This was compounded by the fact that the jet was several hours late and thus everyone was in an enormous rush to get the cargo loaded and sent on its way.I felt rather crestfallen, as I pride myself on doing everything in exactly the same way and by the regs/procedures to the letter. When in doubt I will always refer to documentation in the future instead of verbally discussing it with someone or relying solely on my memory.Confirming with actual paperwork instead of verbally with another pilot. As I am the PIC the responsibility falls directly on my shoulders to ensure each flight is flown in compliance with company policy/procedure and the FARs and I shouldn't rely on my own memory and word of mouth information when I have questions with regard to important matters such as this.
ASRS:1790218.s: The Captain loaded 288kg of dry ice on Aircraft X during pre-flight, mistakenly believing the limit was 320kg instead of 320lbs due to relying on verbal confirmation rather than official documentation. The flight departed as scheduled, but the error was later identified by the Director of Safety, prompting the Captain to commit to verifying weight limits against paperwork in the future.

ASRS:1790221.n: During our initial climb-out we noticed the rate of climb on the pressurization gauge was acting erratic with various climb and descent rates. As ATC continued to assign higher altitudes we both noticed that the cabin altitude was climbing but the differential rate needle was not increasing like normal. As we climbed through 10,000 feet the cabin altitude needle started to decrease and the differential rate needle started to increase. After leveling off at 23,000 feet everything appeared to be stable. The cabin altitude was decreasing below 9,000 feet after nearly getting up to 10,000 feet and the differential rate needle started to increase between 5 and 6 psi showing that cabin was pressuring like normal. After ATC clear us to 25,000 feet I then requested climb to 27,000 feet because of the moderate chop/turbulence at 25,000 feet. Once we reached 27,000 feet we proceeded with running the cruise checklist. Moments after completing the checklist our pressurization rate of needle showed a descent of 6,000 feet depressurizing the cabin, triggering the cabin high altitude annunciater and the master warning lights. At that time we both donned our oxygen mask, performed abnormal checklist and asked ATC for a lower altitude because of our depressurization issue. Once we reached a safe altitude we removed our oxygen masks and decided to return back to our departure airport.Although I believed this incident was handled safely, declaring an emergency would have been the right thing to do. Anytime an emergency checklist is used or a return to field situation arise should trigger one to declare an emergency regardless of the severity. By doing so helps the pilot in handling the emergency more effectively. Upon initial climb out we felt our ears straining and popping so I as Pilot Monitoring looked at the pressurization gauge, and it was fluctuating between climbs and descents. We continued to monitor it and it stabilized acted as normal as we climbed through about 10,000 to 11,000 feet. The cabin needle stabilized just below 10,000 (cabin altitude) feet and started a slow descent down to 9,000 (cabin altitude) feet. As we climbed into the Flight levels up to our cleared altitude of 23,000 feet, it appeared stable at 9,000 feet, and the differential needle pushed to a higher differential as its design to do.ATC then cleared us to our filed altitude of 29,000 feet. As we continued the climb, the pressurization continued to operate normally, with the differential increasing and the cabin altitude slowly descending just below 9,000 feet. The Pilot in Command asked me to asked ATC for 25,000 feet as a level off altitude. We leveled there and were getting continuous moderate turbulence at 25,000 feet so we requested 27,000 feet as our final. We climbed up to 27,000 feet. We leveled off, and shortly after running the cruise checklist, we both felt high pressure in our ears, and I instantly saw the cabin needle jump up too a 6,000 foot a minute climb and then the Red Cabin above 10,000 foot annunciator illuminated and as well the master warning. We then both put on our mask and made sure oxygen was 100% and notified ATC that we were having an issue and needed to descend. The decision was made to return to our point of departure. ATC cleared us direct to the field and we descended down to 6,000 feet. We ran through the abnormal checklist for the cabin above 10,000 foot annunciator. Once were low enough to safely remove the oxygen masks we did. We did not declare an emergency. We continued without any further incident and landed safely.
ASRS:1790221.s: During climb to 27,000 feet, the crew experienced erratic pressurization followed by rapid cabin altitude increase, triggering master warnings and requiring oxygen masks. They descended to 6,000 feet and returned to the departure airport without declaring an emergency, landing safely.

ASRS:1790248.n: In flying return flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 at 3,000 feet, we were anticipating B clearance into the ZZZ 1,500 feet shelf northeast of ZZZ VOR. This expectation was due to the fact that clearance was received shortly before going the same route but opposite direction, and that ZZZ was landing Runway XX, so arrivals would not be a factor in receiving clearance. We were receiving VFR flight following from ZZZ1 followed by ZZZ1 [TRACON]. Upon hand off to ZZZ Approach frequency from ZZZ1 [TRACON], the frequency was extremely congested. We established two-way communication and made initial Bravo request with ZZZ around ZZZ [VOR], but only received 'radar contact' in return with no further clearance. I queried the Controller at least two more times for clarification, but communication was blocked and the frequency was extremely congested. We initiated descent near ZZZZZ [Intersection] to avoid the 1,500 feet class B shelf, but may have penetrated the B airspace in the descent down to 1,400 feet MSL. We remained below the floor of the Bravo and received no further communication from ZZZ until handoff to ZZZ2 Approach near ZZZZZ1 [Intersection].Contributing factors leading to this possible deviation are that the PF was the senior pilot on the flight and is very experienced in the area but may have been somewhat out of practice as COVID has significantly decreased flying. Also, the Controller seemed to be slightly overwhelmed, possibly working multiple frequencies, we weren't anticipating the business of the frequency although we should have known better. Additionally, the strong tailwind increased ground speed, although the descent was rapid, the ground covered during descent was greater than normal. Finally, as we just flew the same route the opposite direction, we were (falsely) anticipating the B clearance.While these factors are no excuse for possibly entering the airspace without clearance, the notion that business is picking up again means we all need to be more diligent in our planning and flight execution. As Captain, I should have anticipated not receiving the B clearance, and planned descent accordingly.
ASRS:1790248.s: The Captain and crew of a return flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 possibly penetrated Class B airspace while descending to 1,400 feet MSL due to frequency congestion preventing clearance receipt. Contributing factors included false anticipation of clearance, high ground speed from tailwinds, and the pilot's reduced recent experience.

ASRS:1790276.n: In the course of a [mission type X] using a DJI magic Zoom, I got confused with the workflow of Kittyhawk and believed it created a LAANC authorization as part of the mission set up. This was an incorrect assumption and I realized after the flight that the program did not automatically create the LAANC authorization as I expected. In the future, I will always verify and have a valid LAANC authorization code for the location of my flight prior to beginning operation of my drone.
ASRS:1790276.s: A drone pilot operating a DJI Mavic Zoom during a mission assumed the Kittyhawk app automatically generated a LAANC authorization. The pilot realized post-flight that no authorization was created due to this incorrect assumption and plans to verify codes before future operations.

ASRS:1790287.n: Entering the traffic pattern for the airport I turned to enter final which positioned my aircraft directly into an extremely bright setting sun. The sun then blinded me at that point and I lost visual contact with the airport and runway and altitude information. After regaining sight from the sun and while establishing my position along with altitude in relation to the airport and runway I observed another aircraft that appeared to be flying in the opposite direction about 200 feet away. I then took an evasive maneuver and cleared the traffic. At that point I was no longer in position to continue the landing and I executed a VFR go around and re entered the traffic pattern and landed without further incident. What caused this incident was turning on final directly into the extremely bright setting sun which blinded me. To prevent this from happening again I will use a runway if available that is not in line of sight with the sun or fly to an alternative airport without conflict with the setting sun or wait until sunset.
ASRS:1790287.s: A pilot entering the traffic pattern turned final into a setting sun, causing temporary blindness and loss of visual contact with the runway. The pilot executed an evasive maneuver to avoid another aircraft 200 feet away, performed a VFR go-around, and landed safely after re-entering the pattern.

ASRS:1790342.n: While approaching Mt Jefferson area on course direct ELKES at 14,000 aircraft encountered a mountain wave. First indications were not unusual, a loss of altitude followed by the autopilot pitch correction to maintain and resulting indicated airspeed loss. It is not uncommon for a momentary loss of a couple hundred feet and airspeed to drop to 90 KIAS, however, at the point where it would 'normal' the situation quickly escalated into an uncontrolled altitude loss as the autopilot rapidly pitched above 15* and I noted a 90+ headwind on the G600 wind vector indicator. I immediately contacted ATC that I was unable to maintain altitude, which they issued a lower clearance (13,000) and vector away from terrain. With the autopilot turned off, I maintained about 10* nose up at 75 KIAS, flaps 10, full throttle and noted a 1200FPM altitude loss. As I approached 13,000 I informed ATC I was unable and inquired about the MVA. I was fully prepared to activate emergency power, declare, and turn back, however ATC stated that the heading I was on gave me about 9000 for an MVA. I elected to ride the wave as the uncontrolled altitude loss was trending up and was able to stabilize as I approached 12,000. While altitude was stable, I remained below the MEA and published minimum off route altitude unable to climb or increase indicated airspeed above 80KIAS for several minutes. As the aircraft exited the mountain wave to the south, I was able to recover the airspeed slowly back to normal cruise as the aircraft moved over the ridge lines.This is the second time a mountain wave event has resulted in altitude loss of more than a few hundred feet. During the 'normal' events I have always notified ATC that I was encountering a wave and only one time previous did the incident result in the necessity for a lower clearance at 13,000'. However, in this event, I would characterize the resulting altitude loss as uncontrolled at minimum control airspeed and max continuous power for the altitude. I would consider this to be an escalation of what might be a normal inconvenience, and causes me to inquire about alternate routing. In all cases of my experience, these waves seem to be encountered over the Mt Jefferson area and a southerly re-routing of to the south is the normal avoidance procedure when the waves are encountered. But why wait until one is encountered? Might it be more prudent to take a different airway further south to begin with? Might be worth exploring.
ASRS:1790342.s: A pilot flying direct ELKES at 14,000 feet encountered a severe mountain wave near Mt Jefferson, causing uncontrolled altitude loss and airspeed decay to 75 KIAS. ATC issued a lower clearance to 13,000 feet and vectors away from terrain, allowing the pilot to stabilize at 12,000 feet after exiting the wave.

ASRS:1790344.n: Cruise flight at FL 390. Smooth air while overlying thunderstorms and VFR conditions. ATC authorized deviations left and right. Captain (CA) made PA call to Flight Attendants (FA) and passengers to all be seated and fasten seat belts. As the aircraft approached the far end of storm, severe turbulence rocked the plane and stick shaker and high speed warning activated twice. CA corrected and re-established control each time, but lost approximately 600 feet in so doing. Pilot Monitoring (FO) called FA's and FA1 reported FA2 was injured. They found her on the floor. FA1 asked for help from medical personnel and they responded. Destination was only 25 minutes away so we continued heading there in case medical attention was needed. Reported injury to ATC. Below 10,000 feet personnel in back advised paramedics were needed. Called for them to meet us at gate and proceeded direct to airport with ATC approval. Emergency vehicles were at the gate, but no ramp personal. FA2 was conscious but confused. She was taken to hospital. Dispatch and Maintenance contacted. I (Captain) called hospital from hotel and spoke to FA2. She was coherent but had no memory of any events previous to people talking to her from the passenger seat. Captain was Pilot Flying. Cruise at FL390 with smooth air flying over a thunderstorm. Deviations left and right approved. PA call to FA's (Flight Attendants) and passengers to all be seated and buckled. Far edge of storm was in sight. Severe turbulence, as published, was encountered. Stick shaker activated twice and Hi Speed aural warning twice. Both times, stick shaker stopped quickly before throttles were advanced to maximum thrust. Loss of altitude approximately 600 feet. Control was re-established. Called FA's and heard FA2 was injured. They found her on the floor. FA1 asked for help from medical personnel, two nurses and one flight attendant responded. Destination was only 25 minutes away so we continued heading there in case medical attention was needed. Reported injury to ATC. Below 10,000 feet, personnel in back advised paramedics were needed. Called for them to meet us at gate and proceeded direct to airport with ATC approval. Emergency vehicles were at the gate. FA2 was conscious but confused and in pain from a hip. She was taken to hospital. Dispatch and Maintenance contacted. I (Captain) called hospital from hotel and spoke to FA2. She was coherent but had no memory of any events previous to people talking to her from the passenger seat.
ASRS:1790344.s: During cruise at FL390, severe turbulence near a thunderstorm caused a 600-foot altitude loss and activated stick shaker and high-speed warnings twice. The Captain regained control, but Flight Attendant 2 was injured and required hospitalization after the flight continued to the destination.

ASRS:1790360.n: At Time ZZZ ramp loader [namd] walked on flight deck with Dangerous Goods Form showing Dry Ice was loaded in the forward compartment and stated he had loaded it himself in the rear. I asked him to correct the Dangerous Goods Form to show that it was loaded in the rear. We received an ACARS message from company at Time showing AUTODangerous Goods Form notification. The corrected Dangerous Goods Form was brought to the flight deck at approximately Time. We had a takeoff time slot of Time to ZZZ1. On taxi out we received our load close out that did not have the R/A (Restricted Article) Dry Ice on it. We contacted company via ACARS and Aircraft X replied at Time that Dry Ice of less than 5lbs will not show on close out and that our close out was good. We finished all takeoff checklists and lined up for takeoff and departed at Time. At Time some time during takeoff roll we received an ACARS message that said our load closeout had been cancelled. Then, multiple company messages that followed updating the load closeout and that it was determined to be 8 lbs of Dry Ice. The corrected load closeout was received at Time. The flight was operated to ZZZ1 uneventfully.[Situation was caused by] I believe that the casual factors are a communication disconnect between the ZZZ base and loaders to loads and planning in ZZZ2. Captain [recommends] a fix [to correct] the way we automate the communication of Hazardous Goods to Load Control & Dispatch.
ASRS:1790360.s: The Captain and a ramp loader experienced a Dangerous Goods documentation error regarding Dry Ice location and weight during taxi and takeoff roll. The incident resulted from a communication disconnect between base operations, loaders, and planning, prompting a recommendation to automate Hazardous Goods communication.

ASRS:1790417.n: When accepting the flight the Wx (Weather) report at base/sending hospital was 10 sm and clear. Wx at receiving hospital was 6 sm and clear. Although cameras showed haze down the mountain I was confident with the visibility reported and knew that the sun set made it look worse. Descending down the mountain the layer of haze did look more dense than forecasted and arrived at receiving hospital without issues. I checked all weather before return back to base and all were still reported the same. Now it was fully dark and cameras gave a clear view of the basin. I chose the return leg through ZZZ as this gives a good indication of visibility due to the lights up the mountain and all the way. Due to 0% moon there was no reference than the lights on the ground. I climbed to 8,000 ft. which provided proper clearance along that flight path. From ZZZ I could see the lights at the airport from about 10 sm. When I got to ZZZ1 valley the visibility rapidly decreased and within seconds we were IMC. I started my climb to about 9,000 ft. and because my crew did a fantastic job immediately giving me report on visibility left and right, I made a left turn which got us out of the clouds fairly quickly. My crew kept on briefing me their view/visibility on both sides which got us back on track on the north side of the lake. Here we could see the haze/fog/clouds spilling through and over the south mountain range. From that position we had a clear path to the airport and landed without further incident. Weather reporting in our area is spotty. We have wx reporting up in the mountain at the airport and down the mountain at two other locations. The weather 'out of control' factor here is the mountain ranges. There are several tools like cameras that supply information and you make your best judgment, but if the weather is very dynamic you can be caught by surprise like we did on this incident. The additional factor of 'no-moon illumination' added to the fact that we did not see the forecasted clouds rolling in. The 'in-control' weather factor here was that I could have been severely cautious and decline the flight on the haze shown on the cameras. Although I kept positive control over the aircraft when initiating IIMC [Inadvertent IMC] protocol I do want to mention that an autopilot would be a great tool in circumstances like this. When practicing the IIMC procedures in the SIM I am spoiled with the situational awareness and added 'second pilot' of the autopilot. Due to the fact that we are dealing with mountain obscuration and often weather that is not reported and can only be identified with visual cues, we should be first in line for a helicopter with these kind of capabilities.
ASRS:1790417.s: A pilot and crew encountered inadvertent IMC while returning to base in a helicopter due to unforecasted haze and lack of moonlight. They recovered by climbing to 9,000 ft and turning left based on crew visibility reports, landing safely without further incident.

ASRS:1790467.n: On Aircraft X from ZZZ to ZZZ1 we had smoke in the aft cabin and diverted to ZZZ2. We were in cruise at 13,000 ft when the CA (Captain) saw the smoke. We descended to 10,000 ft right away and turned off the bleeds. The smoke in the aft cabin cleared. We landed in ZZZ2 with no further issues.[The first detection occurred] when the CA saw the smoke in the aft cabin.[Captain suspects] something in the Bleeds and/or Packs.
ASRS:1790467.s: The Captain detected smoke in the aft cabin of Aircraft X during cruise at 13,000 ft, prompting an immediate descent to 10,000 ft and shutdown of the bleeds. The smoke cleared, allowing a safe diversion and landing at ZZZ2, with the Captain suspecting a fault in the bleeds or packs.

ASRS:1790494.n: Earlier in the day I wrote up the airplane for a pack 2 overheat. We were flying an airplane with an MEL on pack 2. We were cruising at FL250 about 90 miles north of our destination when we got a red 'bleed 1 leak' warning message on EICAS. I notified ATC that I wanted an immediate descent to 10,000 ft. for a bleed leak. The FO (First Officer) handed me the QRH and we began the descent and notified the FA (Flight Attendant) to take her seat because hot air was going somewhere it shouldn't and that we would call her back. I began to run the QRH. ATC gave us FL200 as the initial descent. He asked if I was requesting priority handling, I said YES. He asked for clarification on what a bleed leak meant for us and gave us 10,000 ft. subsequently. Our initial descent rate was about ~3500 fpm, faster than normal, to get out of the icing conditions and closer to a safer pressure altitude. I ran the QRH as written until I reached END. Once I finished running the QRH and put it back in the storage cubby, we began to breathe a sigh of relief that things are probably going to be okay. I directed the FO to slow the descent rate to ~1000 fpm. We were at about 16,000 ft. by this point. The FO then pointed out to me that cabin pressure dropping as indicated by the amber boxed Cabin Alt reading on the EICAS. Cabin altitude was at roughly 9,800 ft. and climbing. We elected to keep pace down to 10,000 ft. in order to get in front of the reducing cabin pressurization. The checklist list was not written with a pack 2 MEL in mind. I began to realize the ramifications of what I had just done by turning off Bleed 1, Pack 1, and closing the cross-bleed switch.The priority handling request with ATC and the events we had just gone through had my mind racing from adrenaline. I decided that 'worrying' about the pressurization system wasn't necessary. We were at 12,000 ft. and descending and if I recall correctly cabin pressure differential was about 2.2 psid. I decided to press dump on the cabin pressurization controller after looking over at the FO and mentioning that pressing the dump button wouldn't harm anything and that we weren't in dangerous territory as far as what happens if I press it. We felt a minor pressurization change as the airplane equalized. In hindsight, this was entirely unnecessary. I should have simply let the airplane depressurize on its own.I then began to evaluate how much fuel our descent to 10,000 ft. would burn instead of being at FL250. It took a minute for the FMS to catch up to the descent we had done. The initial fuel numbers it gave us led me to believe we would be very close to divert. I gave it some time and the numbers got more accurate for fuel calculations. I determined we had no need to divert on account of fuel. I notified dispatch, ATC, and the FA that the urgency was over and we would continue to our destination.Next, the airplane began to get hot and stuffy. One consideration was diverting to the nearest airfield. I didn't want to have a heat casualty in the back. The other was to get air into pack 1 so that it was useful in cooling the cabin. I looked at the overhead panel and discussed with my FO the notion of starting the APU to feed pack 1. This was a risky decision because if the leak was closer to pack 1 then feeding APU bleed air into the system would induce basically the same situation. I figured that I could simply turn the APU back off if that turned out to be the case. I figured the air and pressure coming from the number 2 bleed was hotter and higher pressure than the APU. The checklist had given me the steps to solve the problem perfectly if only my number 2 pack weren't MEL'd. I had a short mental struggle with my decision to do something that contradicted what the checklist had just made me do a few minutes earlier and really felt strange using Captain's authority to bypass it. I pride myself on checklist discipline and following the books as best I possibly can. In hindsight, I think alittle thermal discomfort and more rigidity with regards to the checklist would have been wise.I selected auto on the cross-bleed switch and turned on the APU and fed the number 1 pack. The airplane cooled down inside. I spoke with the flight attendant once more to ask about the faces of the passengers and if anyone knew about what just happened. She said they didn't have any idea and that we would keep it that way. We shot an ILS approach and landed normally.This situation was a learning experience of the highest caliber for me. I have since re-learned how the cross-bleed switch logic works. I have studied the layout and function of the bleed and pneumatic systems and learned much more about airplane pressurization. Pressing dump was not the right decision and I wouldn't do it that way again. Selecting the recirc fan off to bring in fresher air would have been a better choice than turning on the APU.
ASRS:1790494.s: The Captain and First Officer experienced a bleed 1 leak warning while cruising at FL250 with an MEL on pack 2, prompting an immediate descent to 10,000 ft. The crew unnecessarily dumped cabin pressure and later activated the APU to cool the cabin, resulting in a normal landing after the Captain acknowledged these deviations from the checklist were incorrect.

ASRS:1790495.n: Strong burning smell like hot wires shortly after departure. Since bleed air (heater) was on, my first step was to turn bleed air off assuming that is likely engine fumes. The switch would not turn off air, and hot air continued to enter and smell persisted. Thermostat control also would not change the air flow. Since the smell was abnormal and stronger than a common smell of TKS entering the engine (the TKS system was not used), I elected to return to ZZZ which had airport fire facilities and was only a few minutes away. In the event that were was a fire or something was about to catch fire, I elected to request priority handling and executed the in cabin fire checklist. Upon landing at ZZZ, no further indication of fire was present and I meet the airport fire on the ramp. Their investigation did not find anything that was or had been burning. Aircraft was secured on the ramp for inspection by a mechanic.
ASRS:1790495.s: The pilot reported a strong burning smell shortly after departure with inoperative bleed air and thermostat controls. The pilot returned to ZZZ for priority handling and fire inspection, but ground crews found no evidence of fire or burning.

ASRS:1790524.n: On departure from SEA, ATC warned us that a drone had been sighted at approximately 6,000 feet at the cloud tops in the vicinity of our flight path. Both my First Officer and I maintained a lookout. Climbing through 6,100 feet, I spotted the drone about 200 feet off my right side, about 100 feet below our altitude. Due to the clouds and small size of the drone, I spotted it less than one second before we crossed its position. Had there been a conflict, I would not have had enough space to execute an avoidance maneuver. The drone near miss was promptly reported to ATC with the recommendation to not send any aircraft through this airspace. There were no TCAS indications of the drone. A timely report from ATC alerted us to that hazard, but ATC did not provide any specific instructions to avoid the traffic.ATC knew a drone was operating in the vicinity of NEVJO, but continued to send aircraft on the SUMMA 2 departure. A simple vector on departure would have eliminated this potential threat to our aircraft. The drone was large enough and our rate of closure was great enough, that if could have caused significant damage to our aircraft had there been a midair collision.
ASRS:1790524.s: During departure from SEA on the SUMMA 2 route, the crew spotted a drone near 6,000 feet despite ATC warnings but received no specific avoidance vectors. The pilot reported a near miss with insufficient time to maneuver, noting that a simple vector could have prevented the potential collision hazard.

ASRS:1790538.n: I was in command of Aircraft X schedule service from ZZZ to ZZZ1. We departed normally and were climbing to our assigned altitude of 32,000 ft. when just prior to level off our Flight Attendant called us in the cockpit to report that she had a smell of smoke in the cabin. We maintained communication with her as she said it seemed to be coming from Row 4 emanating from the lighting valance on the aircraft left side. We told her to monitor the situation and let us know if there was any sparking visible. She told us that she physically checked the valance and PSU's and they were very hot to the touch and that the smoke and heat was migrating rearward now from Rows 4 thru 10. I told the FA to get the PBE [Protective Breathing Equipment] out along with the fire extinguisher and prepare to fight a fire if one erupted. I then told the FO (First Officer) to notify ATC of our situation and that we needed to return to ZZZ. We were then cleared to return and given a decent clearance to 24,000 ft. Still not sure what type of smoke we had in the cabin I asked the FA to come forward so we could have the FO check the smoke for type of odor (electrical or engine based). FO advised me that the smoke odor seemed to have been not electrical. I then had him get the QRH out and run the procedure for SMOKE IN THE CABIN procedure. We accomplished the memory items and in coordination with ATC requested priority handling and were given an unrestricted decent to 8,000 ft. and vectors to a visual approach to Runway XX at ZZZ. The ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) trucks were standing by for our arrival. The QRH procedure was completed and the smoke seemed to dissipate a little according to the FA. We landed without incident and upon initiation of communication with the ARFF commander we were told there was no smoke evidence on the exterior of the aircraft. Since it appeared the internal situation was under control we decided to taxi to the gate for normal deplaning. Fire Dept. followed us to the gate and upon arrival , they boarded the aircraft and I advised the commander of what had happened and where it had been located. The ARFF members then checked the aircraft over with their thermal heat locater and found no heat source in the Valance or PSU. They then left the aircraft. Dispatch and MX were notified of the situation. Aircraft passengers were deplaned without incident.
ASRS:1790538.s: The Captain of Aircraft X reported smoke and heat from the left lighting valance and PSUs during climb to 32,000 ft., prompting a return to ZZZ. After executing the smoke procedure and landing with ARFF standby, ground crews found no heat source, and passengers deplaned without incident.

ASRS:1790572.n: Boarding a nearly full flight began at XA:30 AM. We had power (i.e. lights) but, we did not have any airflow (air conditioning). We were beginning to sweat profusely. I (FA) contacted the terminal Supervisor who patched me through to Agent, in the tower. I told him of our plight and passenger complaints and concerns. He said he would send someone immediately to turn on the air. This was approximately 20 minutes later. About 15-20 minutes later we still had no air. Passengers were getting very upset and many took their masks off. We made announcements stating that without airflow, it was even more important to keep their mask on since they could not social distance. I contacted the Supervisor again and insisted the passengers be let off the aircraft if we were not going to get airflow and we still didn't know anything about when the pilots would arrive. Approximately 10 minutes later the pilots boarded and stated we should never have begun boarding under those conditions. They got air up and we departed 15 minutes later. 1 hour and 10 minutes after boarding. I felt very, very unsafe in those conditions as did many passengers.We should never board without air conditioning during COVID. If the pilots are running late, a mechanic should be brought down to turn on the air. A few minutes would be acceptable but when the tower is contacted, something should be done in a timely manner. Flight attendants should be allowed to let passengers deplane under such extreme conditions where everyone's safety and health are put at risk.
ASRS:1790572.s: A flight attendant reported that during boarding of a nearly full aircraft, a lack of air conditioning caused passenger distress and mask removal for over an hour. Pilots eventually arrived, restored airflow, and departed, though the crew deemed the initial boarding unsafe and recommended deplaning passengers if airflow is not promptly provided.

ASRS:1790588.n: I had just departed Manassas (HEF) Runway 34R. Tower had me maintain runway heading, then turned me on course to the west (out to the SFRA FLUKY gate), and switched me to Potomac Departure. On my ADS-B in, I noted a target 100 feet below me, and simultaneously Potomac Departure called out that traffic and asked if I had it in sight. I replied, 'No because it is directly under me.' The low-wing light sport aircraft passes the wing directly under the pilot, so nothing directly under me can be seen. I started to climb but Departure warned me there was also traffic above me. It was then that I noticed that I had climbed into the bottom of the 2,500 foot ring of the Class Bravo. Then Departure informed that traffic was no longer a factor, and I descended back below 2,500 [feet]. I believe Manassas Tower had me continue on runway heading to clear traffic that had just departed Runway 34L. Perhaps Tower was not aware of the traffic which eventually found itself under me. HEF traffic is very constrained by Class Bravo to the North, the East and directly above, and R6608 directly south, leaving only two narrow paths for arrival and departure--to the west toward the FLUKY gate, or narrowly to the SSE between the Class Bravo and FRZ to the East and R6608 to the West.
ASRS:1790588.s: A pilot departing Manassas Runway 34R reported a light sport aircraft 100 feet below and traffic above while climbing into the 2,500-foot Class Bravo ring. The pilot attributed the conflict to constrained departure paths and potential Tower unawareness of the traffic under the aircraft.

ASRS:1790605.n: We were flying from ZZZ to ASE and I was the pilot flying. As we approached Aspen, which at that time was reporting VFR, we were given vectors to intercept LOC DME E into ASE. I looked over and noticed the LOC approach was not properly set up. I warned the monitoring pilot of this but at that point we made visual contact with the airport. We accepted clearance to maintain 13,000 ft until established and clearance to execute LOC DME E approach. Having visual contact with the airport we started our descent. A layer of clouds moved in below us as we made the final turn inbound. At the entire time we had full visual contact with all the terrain around. We lost sight of the airport due to the cloud layer, at the same time ATC issued an altitude alert. I emphasize that we were in full visual contact with all the terrain and that visibility at our flight level was unrestricted. The pilot monitoring advised that we had terrain but lost a visual with the airport and said that we would be going missed and starting a climb. We got another altitude alert from ATC. We advised we are in a climb and asked for vectors to give time to decide what to do. We proceeded to ZZZ1 airport afterwards. We were NOT in IMC conditions at any phase of the flight and we maintained visual clearance from all the terrain. The mistake was communication breakdown with ATC and in part CRM in regards to the intentions to execute a visual approach. At no time aircraft was in IMC conditions and we were maintaining clearance with terrain at all times. The aircraft was never put in any unsafe condition. I learned from this how CRM and communication has to be mastered the entire time.
ASRS:1790605.s: The pilot flying and monitoring pilot on a ZZZ to ASE flight lost visual contact with the airport due to clouds while descending for a LOC DME E approach, triggering ATC altitude alerts. The crew executed a missed approach and diverted to ZZZ1, attributing the incident to communication breakdowns with ATC and CRM issues regarding the visual approach.

ASRS:1790620.n: I was PF in the left seat and we were cleared for take off on Rwy XL. As we were lining up on the runway, I heard the Tower clear a helicopter for an eastbound departure from the ramp, but I did not visually see the helicopter yet. Once we were on the takeoff roll, I saw the helicopter lifting off from the ramp (ahead and to our left), but it appeared to be turning parallel to our runway to I diverted my attention back to the runway. Right after initiating rotation, I saw the helicopter begin to cross over our runway, left to right, at approximately 200 feet AGL. Because we were past V1 and already rotating on a short runway, I quickly determined an aborted takeoff was not an option so I continued our rotation. During these few seconds, there were some communications between the Tower and the helicopter, but I did not comprehend them due to my focus on avoiding hitting the helicopter. Shortly after liftoff (~100 feet AGL), I had to make an evasive maneuver to our left and reduce our climb rate for a few seconds to avoid hitting the helicopter. Luckily, there was no terrain or obstacles to the left of our runway heading. Once the helicopter passed off our right at what I estimate was 200-300 feet, I resumed a normal climb rate and a right turn back to our departure heading. The Tower controller apologized and then handed us off to Departure. Looking back on the scenario, I believe continuing the takeoff roll as we did was the right call, as we certainly would have had a runway excursion if we had attempted an abort at that point in the roll - passed V1 and already rotating. Additionally, I am not sure how I could have anticipated the impending conflict earlier because helicopters maneuver on a dime and it was hard to tell its intending heading after liftoff. After the event, I listened to the ATC recording on a publicly available website and it seems the controller tried to tell the helicopter pilot to remain north of the runway at all times, but that transmission was not acknowledged.
ASRS:1790620.s: The pilot flying a fixed-wing aircraft on takeoff from Rwy XL encountered a helicopter crossing the runway at 200 feet AGL after the helicopter failed to acknowledge ATC instructions to remain north. The pilot executed an evasive left maneuver and reduced climb rate to avoid a collision, continuing the takeoff past V1 as an abort was not an option.

ASRS:1790626.n: While performing a charter flight under FAR part 135 departing off of runway 25 at EGE we were assigned the BEEVR2 SID. After programming the FMS I noted that the FMS did not include the initial turn to a 206 heading, I told the Captain that he would need to use heading mode on the SID and he immediately dismissed it as incorrect, even after me bringing up the chart and the active legs page for him to review. This resulted in us not making the turn at the correct time and triggering a GPWS Warning accompanied with the 'Pull Up' 'Pull Up' annunciator to go off. Eventually he did disconnect the auto-pilot but went direct to the first fix instead of the 206 heading.
ASRS:1790626.s: During a Part 135 charter departure from EGE on the BEEVR2 SID, the First Officer warned the Captain that the FMS lacked the initial 206-degree turn, but the Captain dismissed the concern. This caused a GPWS "Pull Up" warning, after which the Captain disconnected the autopilot and flew direct to the first fix instead of following the required heading.

ASRS:1790628.n: Both the preflight check and weather were confirmed to meet solo flight requirements. During takeoff, and prior to rotation, the aircraft veered left and exited the runway. The aircraft struck a construction berm which caused it to veer further left where it struck a second construction berm parallel to the runway and damaged the nose and left gear. Emergency procedures were conducted and both power and fuel were cut off. I exited the aircraft and contacted emergency services. No one was injured.
ASRS:1790628.s: A solo pilot exited the runway left during takeoff before rotation, striking two construction berms that damaged the nose and left gear. Emergency procedures were completed, and the pilot evacuated with no injuries reported.

ASRS:1790632.n: While operating on a VFR training flight out of ZZZ, I noticed the voltmeter on the aircraft was beginning to fluctuate slightly. We decided to continue flight but eventually noticed the volts were dropping significantly. At the time we had been in contact with Approach but decided to turn back to ZZZ and notified Approach we were turning back hoping to avoid any serious problems. Within minutes, we notice the volts had gone below 10 volts. At that time, we decided to head to ZZZ1 because it was closer, we were also worried about losing all electrics at night. As we started our initial approach into ZZZ1, we lost all electrical power, transponder, radios, electric instruments and lighting. We decided to continue and eventually landed at ZZZ1 without any problems. After a few minutes we located a phone number for Approach, we were able to contact them to let them know we were alright.
ASRS:1790632.s: During a VFR training flight, the pilot and student experienced fluctuating then total electrical failure, losing radios, transponder, and instruments. They diverted to ZZZ1 and landed safely without incident, later contacting Approach to report their status.

ASRS:1790636.n: When reviewing my logbook on Date 6, I discovered that what I thought was a BFR completed on Date 2, was an IPC only. I did however complete a BFR on Date 1, eight months before the IPC. I made two flights after Date 3, one on Date 4 and the other on Date 5. I believed at the time that I made these flights that my last BFR was completed on Date 2, and thus that my next BFR was not due until Date 8.However, since I only completed an IPC on Date 2 (and not a BFR), even allowing for an extension provided by the SFAR in response to the COVID-19 health emergency, it appears that I made two flights after my previous BFR (the Date 1 BFR) expired.Upon discovering this inadvertent error, I immediately contacted my flight instructor and scheduled an appointment to complete a BFR with him today, literally one day after discovering my mistake.In order to prevent this from happening again, I have calendared the due date for my next BFR on an electronic calendar, with an automatic reminder set 30 days before my current BFR expires.
ASRS:1790636.s: A pilot inadvertently conducted two flights after their Biennial Flight Review expired because they mistakenly believed an Instructor Proficiency Check on Date 2 was a valid review. Upon discovering the error, the pilot immediately scheduled a new review and implemented electronic calendar reminders to prevent recurrence.

ASRS:1790654.n: I was 10 miles north of ZZZ and flying heading 220 at 1,500 ft. MSL and 105 knots in a Mooney inbound for a VFR traffic pattern entry on a right downwind to Runway XX. Three airplanes had just landed and I was maneuvering for the 45 degree entry to Runway XX. I heard the Cessna announce it was 4 miles ahead and also maneuvering for the same entry to Runway XX. The sun was setting to the west which made it difficult to spot aircraft to the southwest and west of my flight path. I announced on CTAF that I was 10 miles north and maneuvering for the 45 degree entry right downwind Runway XX. At 5 miles northwest of ZZZ, I announced that I was 5 miles northwest maneuvering for the 45 degree entry, right downwind, for Runway XX.At that point, I heard the Cessna was on the 45 entry to right downwind Runway XX. I turned to a heading of 180 at 1,300 ft. MSL, 113 knots, and remained 5 miles west of ZZZ, while visually scanning ahead, left and right, for the Cessna. It was very difficult to see southwest and west due to the sun setting. At 5 miles west of ZZZ, I announced Mooney is 5 miles west of ZZZ maneuvering for the 45 entry, right downwind, Runway XX".Within a minute, I spotted the Cessna approximately 100 ft. below and 400 ft. to the right. The CFI onboard called on the radio, and said "did you see us?" I responded, "Yes I just did. Would you like to go ahead of me or do you want me to proceed on the 45 entry?" He responded that they would continue the entry and go ahead of me. I continued to fly a heading of 180 and then executed a turn to the west followed by a 360 degree turn to the east to enter the pattern after the Cessna. I landed and did not see the Cessna on the ramp.Afterwards, I called the CFI in the Cessna, whom I've known for years. I listened to his remarks and explained that I had no intention of overtaking him in The Cessna. This is not something I would ever attempt nor have I ever done in 18 years of flying. He mentioned they had requested my position in the air (around 5 miles out) and I said that I never heard that request nor that they were in the Cessna. I was only monitoring CTAF and visually scanning for traffic. I heard they were already on the 45 degree entry to Runway XX. I believe that 1 or 2 of their position reports or requests for my position were not transmitted or heard because we may have both pressed the mic button at the same time to give or request position reports. One of the Cessna's communications may have been incomplete which could explain why I heard that the Cessna was on the 45 degree entry to Runway XX, as I was 5 miles west northwest of ZZZ."
ASRS:1790654.s: A Mooney pilot and a Cessna flight instructor experienced a near-midair conflict while both maneuvering for a 45-degree entry to Runway XX at ZZZ. The reporter attributed the incident to sun glare and potential simultaneous radio transmissions that caused missed position reports.

ASRS:1790658.n: Landed on the runway at ZZZ. Several seconds after touchdown I felt nose shaking followed by loss control of the nose wheel. Stopped on Runway XXR had operations determine I need a tow back to the FPO. Was towed back and no other damage to the aircraft
ASRS:1790658.s: The pilot landed at ZZZ and experienced nose wheel shaking and loss of control seconds after touchdown. The aircraft was stopped on Runway XXR, towed to the FPO, and found to have no other damage.

ASRS:1790667.n: Student pilot with instructor doing pattern work at 33N in crosswind leg. During turn to downwind in left traffic pattern Aircraft Y entered the pattern in crosswind leg and was operating dangerously close to my aircraft creating a collision hazard. Aircraft Y did not enter 33N left traffic pattern correctly and executed an unsafe maneuver putting myself and other aircraft in the pattern at risk.
ASRS:1790667.s: A student pilot and instructor on a crosswind leg at 33N reported that Aircraft Y entered the left traffic pattern incorrectly and flew dangerously close during a turn to downwind. The reporter stated Aircraft Y's unsafe maneuver created a collision hazard for their aircraft and others in the pattern.

ASRS:1790676.n: I departed from Runway XX at ZZZ. At the departure end of the runway, the aircraft backfired and power fluctuated. I was able to return and land at ZZZ. Prior to flight, I had sump-checked each fuel tank and the fuel selector valve, at the low point. All fuel samples were found to be clean, with no contamination. The engine run-up was normal. I departed with 70.1 gallons of usable fuel. The engine ran smoothly while utilizing the electric auxiliary fuel pump. Subsequently, the JPI930 Engine Monitor's memory indicated a fuel delivery issue at the time of fluctuation. I checked all fuel lines and found them to be clear and free flowing. I then sent the suspected failed engine-driven fuel pump out for assessment and overhaul.
ASRS:1790676.s: The pilot reported a backfire and power fluctuation shortly after departing Runway XX at ZZZ in an aircraft with a JPI930 engine. The event was attributed to a suspected failed engine-driven fuel pump, which was sent for overhaul after the pilot returned to land safely.

ASRS:1790677.n: Landing Runway XX in ZZZ experienced a bump on the runway after landing which was coupled with a wind shear causing a directional control problem. Pilot made control inputs to correct situation. Wind speed and direction varied greatly. Pilot was unable to maintain directional control. Aircraft ground looped to the right approximately midfield. No human injuries were sustained.
ASRS:1790677.s: The pilot experienced a runway bump and severe wind shear while landing Runway XX in ZZZ, causing a loss of directional control. The aircraft ground looped to the right approximately midfield, but no injuries were sustained.

ASRS:1790681.n: Tower closed, multiple airplanes in pattern using Runway 14 for favorable winds (170 about 15 knots). I was on short final, less than 200 AGL over clearway for runway. Jet lands straight in on Runway 32. No calls were made from the jet on CTAF announcing position or intentions. Jet landed, I added power and went around, overflying the jet. All other airplanes in the pattern were using 124.125 as the CTAF as published. Brief phone conversation with Houston Approach confirmed that the jet landed straight in apparently on an RNAV 32 approach. Jet would have landed with excess of 10 knots tail wind. ASOS was broadcasting at the time.
ASRS:1790681.s: A pilot on short final for Runway 14 executed a go-around after a jet landed straight in on Runway 32 without CTAF calls. The jet likely used an RNAV 32 approach, resulting in a landing with over 10 knots of tailwind despite favorable winds for Runway 14.

ASRS:1790701.n: A flight of 2 helicopters called Ground Control on for VFR flight following. They were on a non controlled ramp. Ground Control issued departure frequency and squawk. No readback was heard. Generally, this is an issue with military helicopters, and they usually call up local shortly after, when ready to depart. I reached out several times on Ground Control, inquiring if they had the ATIS information, and if they wanted to taxi to a runway or a present position departure. They were non responsive.I passed the strip to Local Control, thinking they would call him. Moments later a Aircraft Y who had been in the pattern was departing and I saw the 2 helicopters departing the ramp, right in the path of Aircraft Y. I alerted Local Control and he had the Aircraft Y make an evasive left turn to avoid the traffic. Both Local Control and myself on Ground Control made multiple attempts on all frequencies to reach the Aircraft X flight. They both almost had a NMAC with the Aircraft Y. TRACON was calling on the shout line and I answered on Ground Control as Local Control was trying to move the Cessna to a safe position. The TRACON controller alerted me Aircraft X had called them and they mistakenly thought they were calling from a different airport so the TRACON controller gave them a departure clearance which resulted in the unauthorized departure from ZZZ and the NMAC. Once Aircraft Y was safe Local Control and Ground Control both advised TRACON to issue a brasher.Military helicopter pilots need better training on how to depart here and learn to give appropriate readbacks. TRACON should have verified where the helicopters were. Assuming they were at ZZZ1 created a dangerous situation. The VFR flight plan was in the system. TRACON Flight Data should have seen it originating from ZZZ. Aircraft Y departed climbing to remain in closed traffic for stop and goes. Aircraft X helicopters on a ramp near the departing Aircraft Y began to lift climbing in front of the Aircraft Y who did not have them in sight. Local Control issues immediate traffic for the Aircraft Y and told to turn left immediately. Local Control called out to Aircraft X on Local Control frequency several times and on guard frequency. Aircraft X did not answer and continued to fly toward Aircraft Y which was maneuvering to avoid the helicopters. Aircraft Y made an inadvertent low altitude turn to avoid colliding with the helicopters. Coming out of the turn the Aircraft Y reported them in sight.Approach Control called Local Control in a panic about Aircraft X saying she gave permission for departure to the helicopters saying she thought they were at another airport nearby. She did not know they were actually located at this airport. Aircraft X continued toward the Aircraft Y and eventually called local control once they departed the airport. Local Control told Aircraft X that they were not cleared by Local Control for departure and advised that they almost hit Aircraft Y that was climbing directly toward the helicopters.Aircraft X replied that Ground Control gave them the departure frequency. In error Aircraft X thought that they needed to contact Approach for takeoff from the airport. When Aircraft X called for VFR departure, Ground Control issued Aircraft X a squawk code and told them the departure procedure which is normal handling for VFR aircraft. The next expected sequence of events is that the VFR aircraft then contacts Local Control for takeoff clearance. Aircraft X bypassed Local Control and went directly to Departure Control thinking that is who they needed for departure.My recommendation is that there is clarity made to pilots that their receipt of the departure frequency is not a directive to contact them to depart while the Tower is actively controlled by a Local Controller who is issuing control instructions and safety alerts.
ASRS:1790701.s: Two military helicopters (Aircraft X) departed a non-controlled ramp without Local Control clearance after mistakenly contacting TRACON, nearly colliding with a Cessna (Aircraft Y) in the pattern. The near-miss resulted from the helicopters' failure to readback instructions and TRACON's incorrect assumption of their location.

ASRS:1790703.n: Aircraft X was inside of a quarter mile final on the ILS Runway 31C approach. I turned around for a second to tell the supervisor about the visibility getting better on final when the supervisor noticed an airport vehicle going onto Runway 31C. At that point I issued a go around to the aircraft and to climb and maintain 3,000 ft. MSL and turn right to a heading of 110. I also let the aircraft know the reason of the go around. They were able to respond in time and were re-sequenced for another approach and landed without incident. I understand it was snowing and airport markers are difficult to see. I suggest airport vehicles be more vigilant of their position on the airport before moving anywhere. Driver refresher course recommended.
ASRS:1790703.s: An air traffic controller issued a go-around to Aircraft X on the ILS Runway 31C approach after an airport vehicle entered the runway. The pilot complied with the climb and turn instructions, and the aircraft landed safely on a subsequent approach despite poor visibility from snow.

ASRS:1790720.n: My second report regarding aircraft from the Palm Springs area performing erratic maneuvers in the face of IFR arrivals. Aircraft Y departed Palm Springs and terminated services outside of the PSP Delta. They proceeded to fly just north of UDD and start performing aerobatic maneuvers between 050 and 060. This aircraft climbed right in front of Aircraft X, who was cleared for the RNAV visual 31L approach. Traffic alert was issued to Aircraft X and while the pilot did not say 'near midair', they did say 'he's right in front of us!' and the altitudes were the same.The pilot for Aircraft X said they had to respond to two RAs for that one aircraft.The pilot of Aircraft Y may have also been in violation of FAR Sec. 91.303 which prohibits aerobatic flight within 4 miles of a federal airway (V137) and over an area of congested population.I am requesting, again, for the PSP airspace to have a Charlie or Bravo airspace. My colleagues and I deal with dangerous situations every day that could easily be avoided by having non-voluntary protected airspace. This is the second event in one day where PSP Tower has terminated a VFR aircraft who ultimately got much too close to an IFR arrival. A Class C/B airspace and a requirement for Tower to hand off departures to approach, would allow the radar Controller to determine if a dangerous situation is imminent.As of now, the only controlled airspace in the Palm Springs valley is the Tower's Class D. Class E airspace exists around TRM, but only prohibits flight for poor weather. This airspace is a free-for-all with half of the aircraft talking to ATC and the other half are not, and just blasting through everyone else. This needs to change.Also, the local pilots should know better than to be flying in these congested areas doing aerobatics. The safety culture of these pilots is questionable and should be discussed.
ASRS:1790720.s: An air traffic controller reported that Aircraft Y performed aerobatics between 5,000 and 6,000 feet near V137, climbing directly in front of Aircraft X on an RNAV visual approach. This caused Aircraft X to receive two resolution advisories and prompted the controller to request expanded Class C or B airspace to prevent future conflicts.

ASRS:1790722.n: Training was in progress on Local control. Aircraft X was sequenced to follow Aircraft Y. Aircraft X had the wrong aircraft in sight and turned base early and at the same time as Aircraft Y. Aircraft Y had to maneuver off final to the north for spacing. Aircraft Y called the tower and spoke with me, the CIC (Controller in Charge), and said Aircraft X got as close as 50 ft. prior to him maneuvering. Aircraft X was also on his check ride. I was training on the Local Control position. There were 4 VFR aircraft in the traffic pattern for RWY XX and 1 VFR aircraft on practice approach RWY YY. Aircraft Y was VFR in left traffic for RWY XX and given a sequence to follow Aircraft X. Aircraft X was VFR in right traffic for RWY XX. Aircraft Y was given a sequence of number 4, to follow Aircraft X on right downwind. Aircraft Y was extending their downwind until they had their traffic in sight. Aircraft Y asked if their traffic was turning final RWY XX. I visually scanned the traffic pattern to verify Aircraft X position. I saw Aircraft X on final for RWY XX. Aircraft X was the 3rd aircraft on final at the time and was on an approximately 4NM final. I cleared Aircraft Y to land RWY XX after my visual scan. Aircraft Y must have had the incorrect aircraft in sight, the aircraft preceding Aircraft X was an Piper. Aircraft Y flew into the flight path of Aircraft X, cutting them off. Aircraft Y had to make a quick turn north bound to avoid Aircraft X. Aircraft X saw Aircraft Y, after Aircraft Y turned to the north, and Aircraft X made a south turn to avoid Aircraft Y. At this time Aircraft X made a call to Local Control that he was making his north turn to avoid Aircraft Y. I did not see the two aircraft turning to avoid until Aircraft X made his call for the north turn. Aircraft Y rejoined the RWY XX final, in front of Aircraft Y, and was reissued a landing clearance for RWY XX. Aircraft Y was instructed to make a 270 degree turn back to final and rejoined RWY XX final behind Aircraft X. Aircraft X was reissued a landing clearance for RWY XX. Both aircraft landed without further incident. About 10 minutes after Aircraft X landed, the pilot called the tower to let us know that Aircraft Y was within close proximity to him and he would be filing a safety report.
ASRS:1790722.s: A VFR pilot on a check ride and another VFR pilot on Local Control training experienced a loss of separation while sequencing for Runway XX. The second pilot misidentified traffic and cut off the first, forcing both to maneuver to avoid a collision before landing safely.

ASRS:1790723.n: Aircraft X was on a visual approach about 1 NM north of WIGZU. VFR Aicraft Y was 2 NM east of WIGZU tracking westbound. I issued the traffic to Aircraft X and let them know where the traffic was, where it was headed, and that the aircraft was not in communication with ATC. I issued the traffic again when Aircraft X was crossing WIGZU and the VFR aircraft was 1 NM east of WIGZU. It appeared they must have seen Aircraft X because the VFR aircraft made a sharp northbound turn. The CA alarm did sound between Aircraft X and Aircraft Y.I recommend a shelf or a key added to AFW Class Delta. There are many, many instances where VFR aircraft are transitioning at WIGZU, at the same altitude as arrivals or departures, but are not in communication with ATC.
ASRS:1790723.s: An air traffic controller issued traffic advisories to an arriving aircraft regarding a non-communicating VFR aircraft near WIGZU, resulting in a CA alarm and a sharp turn by the VFR pilot. The controller recommends adding a shelf or key to AFW Class Delta to address frequent altitude conflicts with uncommunicating VFR traffic.

ASRS:1790729.n: I was working the Springs sector and noticed a high performance aircraft depart PSP and then the tower dropped them and they went to a 1200 code. I kept my eye on them because we have had high performance aircraft interfere with arrivals/departures before. Over the next 30 minutes, the aircraft flew around the airspace, but it wasn't until around XA:45z that they started doing maneuvers around UDD. I believe it was Aircraft X that was doing aerobatic maneuvers just east of the UDD airport. The aircraft rapidly change altitude, turn very quickly, and all of this at a high rate of speed. It's next to impossible to anticipate what their intentions are and makes it very difficult to keep other aircraft out of their way. These aircraft fly through the airspace, creating havoc, and then just call the tower for pattern entry, instead of calling approach for sequencing. One of the aircraft was right next to a regional jet, but below, and keeping up with them, while they were trying to descend on a visual approach in to PSP. This aircraft called the tower, instead of approach, and was sequenced by them. I, however, was left focused on the situation, unsure what this aircraft was doing, and if they even saw [the regional jet].The lack of a mandatory controlled airspace in the PSP area makes it very difficult to make any sort of plan, since anyone who wants to can fly right down the final legally. PSP tower is also terminating these high performance aircraft, right as they leave their Delta airspace, where they go on to get in the way of arrivals coming in PSP or other nearby airports. These high performance aircraft are out every weekend, constantly getting in the way, and making the approach controllers bend to their will. The workload on the Springs sector is already very high, but add in the lack of guaranteed controlled airspace makes everything much more difficult. We are approach, departure and clearance delivery, all in one sector. It is incredibly frustrating to make sense of all the aircraft criss crossing, formulate a plan, and then have someone who deems it not important to participate in the TRSA, blow up your entire plan, making you change everything. While that did not happen exactly in this instance, it has happened many times before, and is what has brought me to file this report in hopes to prevent it from happening more.I recommend that we change the airspace around PSP to something that is mandatory controlled airspace. The voluntary participation makes sequencing and separation difficult, and in the cases of these high performance aircraft, they are creating an unsafe situation, but still 'following the rules'. Some sort of protection needs to be added to the area to help us ensure our separation and allow controllers to have a safe space to sequence.I would also request that someone look in to the legality of the aerobatic activities that these aircraft are doing in the Palm Springs valley. Are they aware what they are doing is unsafe and potentially illegal?
ASRS:1790729.s: An air traffic controller in the Springs sector observed a high-performance aircraft performing unpredictable aerobatic maneuvers near UDD and PSP, flying close to a regional jet on visual approach. The controller attributed the safety risk to voluntary TRSA participation and the lack of mandatory controlled airspace, which complicates sequencing and separation.

ASRS:1790733.n: Aircraft X checked in for Runway XXC was told descend and maintain 040 and good rate down, leveled off at 050 while being vectored to final and told to parallel final on heading 350 and expedite down to 30, shortly after looking 1,000 feet at 2.7 miles he saw the field and was cleared.There was approximately 10 read back errors during this push due to the new mask mandate, control instructions had to be repeated to this pilot 2 times. With the new mandate and tower restrictions forces us to land Runway XXC and XXR in IFR weather this operation is unsafe with the new altitude restrictions implemented by our supervisors.For the past 2 weeks management has told the arrival wall to not go below 4,000 feet until north of ZZZZZ (the dual fix) regardless of where the aircraft's flight path will be, this makes IFR operations very difficult to accomplish at ZZZ and is a very poor knee jerk reaction to a Controller making a simple mistake. These type of rule changes mean that every single transmission on that wall need to be 100% clear and any read back error will cause an aircraft incident, we cannot continue with frivolous rule changes and a mask mandate unless we would like a major incident or accident at ZZZ.Allow us to use judgment and common sense on where to turn our own airplane. These unnecessary rule changes will cause more incidents than they will prevent.
ASRS:1790733.s: A pilot flying Aircraft X reported unsafe IFR operations at ZZZ due to new altitude restrictions and mask mandates causing communication errors. The reporter attributed these risks to management's rigid rules and poor judgment, warning they could lead to a major incident.

ASRS:1790734.n: Aircraft X arrived from the south east at 110 where ZZZ has a MVA (Minimum Vectoring Altitude) at the highest point of 115. I do not know if ZZZ1 has the same or lower MVA in that area. Per the LOA with ZZZ1 any arrivals in this area 130 or lower, must be on an airway and verbally coordinated. There was no coordination from ZZZ1. OJTI was being conducted at the Approach position, I was the OS in the TRACON. Due to COVID social distancing requirements the OJTI was working from the 'B' scope, the trainee was working from the 'A' scope and I was at the OS desk. There is no radar scope or secondary monitor available at the OS desk to observe traffic, so I was unable to see the altitude of the aircraft. A regional jet that was about to be switched to the Tower told approach that an aircraft was trying to call approach and at that point I was able to observe Aircraft X at the altitude below the MVA. Aircraft X eventually was able to reach approach on radio and landed without incident.-Review ZZZ1-ZZZ LOA-Add a non-certified radar display at the ZZZ TRACON OS desk-Check the MVAs to the south east of ZZZ to see if there are any discrepancies between ZZZ1 and ZZZ MVAs. I am training the trainee on approach control. Three arrivals scheduled with close arrival times. Trainee accepted all three handoffs back to back well outside of our airspace boundary, further away than normal. He was not aware that Aircraft X was flying a wrong altitude for direction of flight as well as 500 feet below the MVA we have depicted on our maps until after accepting the handoff. Neither of these two issues were coordinated between either facility. Aircraft landed without issue.We need to have matching MVA maps with ZZZ1. This could be a real issue in the future. That aircraft was 500 feet below our MVA and could not reach us on radio due to the terrain.
ASRS:1790734.s: An OJTI trainee accepted a handoff of Aircraft X, which was 500 feet below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude and uncoordinated with ZZZ1, while the OS could not monitor altitude due to scope limitations. The aircraft eventually contacted approach and landed safely, though the incident highlighted MVA discrepancies and communication gaps.

ASRS:1790751.n: Recently we were told we had to wear masks while on sector. Following the rules I was wearing a mask, and multiple aircraft could not understand what I was saying. Multiple times I was told to 'Say again' until I pulled the mask down to give the aircraft the transmission. After I pulled the mask down they said they could understand me better. This is a safety issue. If the aircraft can't understand what we are saying and takes the wrong altitude this could be disastrous.Since Coronavirus started we were told we only had to wear masks when we couldn't be socially distanced. What has changed? Why do we have to wear masks all the time even if we are socially distanced?
ASRS:1790751.s: An air traffic controller reported that mandatory mask-wearing caused multiple aircraft to request repeated transmissions due to poor audio clarity. The controller stated this communication barrier creates a safety risk where pilots might misunderstand altitude instructions.

ASRS:1790756.n: With new guidelines for wearing mask on position. (With no one around) I am having multiple read back errors. Aircraft X miss read his restriction and frequency. The issue was corrected.When there is no one is close proximity controllers should not be made to wear mask.
ASRS:1790756.s: An air traffic controller reported multiple readback errors, including Aircraft X misreading restrictions and frequency, while wearing a mask alone on position. The controller attributed the errors to the mask and recommended that controllers not be required to wear them when no one is in close proximity.

ASRS:1790762.n: I was working Local Control and had four aircraft waiting to depart with Aircraft X on short final to an intersecting runway and Aircraft Y still about 10 mile final for the same runway on an instrument approach for a option back to radar pattern. There was also two VFR picture taking aircraft around the Tower airspace at 2700 feet. I asked Aircraft X if he could land to hold short of the intersecting runway. He said he could, though hesitantly. I cleared him for LAHSO(Land and Hold Short). I began to depart the other aircraft of the crossing runway with turns and to also have them stop at 2000 feet for the picture takers. When Aircraft Y checked on, I cleared him for the option. My biggest mistake was putting expeditiousness over safety. I overlooked Aircraft X in two important ways. I had an expectation bias that he would exit the runway before the intersection and even the I scanned the runway, I missed him sitting at the intersection. The color of the plane and the concrete made it difficult to notice him. Not until Aircraft X keyed up to talk did I remember he was there but by then Aircraft Y had touched down, saw the aircraft and was stopping to avoid.This situation very poignantly reminded me (because it was a very close call and so thankful it was not more serious) that safety is our number one priority. As a facility we need to have a clear reminder that a runway is occupied as opposed to one single light that carries multiple meanings. We should clearly define a procedure for LAHSO as well.
ASRS:1790762.s: An Air Traffic Controller cleared Aircraft X for a LAHSO landing while managing departures and an instrument approach for Aircraft Y. Due to expectation bias and visual difficulty, the controller overlooked Aircraft X holding at an intersection, causing Aircraft Y to stop short to avoid a collision.

ASRS:1790765.n: Aircraft X on an IFR flight plan was being vectored for an ILS approach. The weather was marginal but apparently had some very strong winds aloft as the aircraft kept flying off course when given any heading. The initial heading of 115 looked like a 125 heading. I gave him a 115 heading down to 1800 ft. for the ILS approach but when I saw that he was heading toward the higher MVAs, I asked him to turn 10 degrees left. The pilot asked if I was painting any weather but I didn't see anything and I told him that. I also told him to advise if he wanted to deviate for weather. It looked like the weather was clearing up and the winds were calm enough for an approach. Since he kept getting blown off course toward the shoreline and away from the water, I asked him if he'd like an instrument or visual approach instead.
